speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the most important issues to Canada's continuing prosperity is youth development.
While this government claims to care about global competitiveness, unfortunately it often takes steps to undermine Canada's competitive position.
The government talks about a learning culture while it cuts its spending on post-secondary education and imposes a 3 per cent tax on student loans. It says it wants to fight illiteracy while at the same time it imposes a tax on books.
It pretends to care about training while this department has seen drastic cuts. Between 1985 and 1990, the government cut the budget of the SEED program in half from $149.5 million to $77 million, depriving many young Canadians of job opportunities. Last year alone it cut $100 million from the Canadian Jobs Strategy.
It is time for this government to stop sending out mixed signals on the issues of education and training. It is time for this government to act in a consistent, constructive manner which will guarantee that Canada's young people get the education and training which will enable them to compete against the rest of the world.

Mr. Speaker, from today until November 8, an exhibition of life-size bronze busts of Canada's 18 Prime Ministers will be held to mark the 125th anniversary of Confederation. These busts were made by Dr. Joseph Adrien Letendre of Amos. On the base of each is a short biographical note giving the Prime Minister's main achievements.
Dr. Letendre is an orthopedic surgeon by profession. On a sabbatical year in Oxford, England, he developed a particular interest in sculpture. He spent ten years of his leisure time to complete this collection.
Mr. Speaker, I invite all my colleagues and all employees of the House of Commons to visit this exhibition, located in Room 525 of the Wellington Building in Ottawa.

Mr. Speaker, Grant Devine and the Saskatchewan Tories could not pull it off but a Pennsylvania Democrat did. Last night Harris Wofford overcame a 40 per cent deficit in the polls to beat Republican heavyweight Dick Thornburgh in the Pennsylvania senatorial race. Wofford won on a platform of advocating nationalized health care in the United States and Pennsylvania voters sent a clear message to their President. They agree with Wofford.
Americans have heard about the efficient, affordable and universal Canadian health care system and have decided that they no longer want an expensive user-pay system which leaves 37 million Americans without adequate health care.
This victory should serve as a reminder to Canadians of the value of medicare and how fortunate we are to have it. It should serve to remind the present govern-

ment that the commitment to medicare in this countiy must be preserved and the cutbacks stopped. Finally it should serve as a warning to politicians across the countiy who wish to win the next election that to back away from the principles of universal medicare and to campaign for a user fees will mean certain defeat.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all Canadians know that Canada's national financial burdens of debt and deficit are both federal and provincial partnership challenges. All know in their hearts that the goods and services tax is a necessary response to those burdens and is here to stay.
The constitutional proposals call for harmonization of federal-provincial interests in economic planning and financial budgeting. A good place to start that harmonization and that partnership is here and now with the goods and services tax in the interests of all Canadians.
Provincial initiative and leadership is required. I call on my own province of New Brunswick, which has long been a model for Canada, to lead again by the integration of the New Brunswick and federal sales tax systems as an expression of that leadership now.

Mr. Speaker, I find it difficult to believe that the NDP government of Ontario has accepted the Conservative government's federal-provincial forest agreement when the federal contribution has been drastically reduced from $15 million a year to $6 million a year.
The 1984 to 1989, $75 million agreement saw 100,000 hectares of forest regenerated, 166 million seedlings purchased and 400 kilometres of access roads constructed. The 1984 agreement was considered inadequate at the time and the future agreement should do more.
How can this government present this agreement as progress for the future of northern Ontario and its ailing forest industry? This is just another slap in the face of the working people of northern Ontario as a tonne of
newsprint sells at 1982 prices and the softwood lumber industry has lost its markets because of the 15 per cent export surtax.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada is home to many refugees from terrorism and inhumanity, some of whom owe their very existence to the heroism of individuals who stood up to tyranny and fear itself.
John Fulop of Budapest, Hungary is such a man. Between October 15,1944 and January 20,1945 he saved the lives of my constituent Dr. Thomas Szirtes and five other Jews by hiding them first in his one room apartment and later in a 12 foot by 5 foot cellar.
As Dr. Szirtes has stated: "He did it because of his supreme dedication to helping the oppressed, his calling to save the persecuted and to alleviate the suffering of the sufferers. His bravery, his skill, his tenacity to keep our moral and physical beings alive were exceptional. He never lost his cool and he always had his presence of mind which was so essential to make possible our survival against overwhelming odds."
I would call upon all members of this House to recognize John Fulop's outstanding heroism and humanity.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Canadian health care system was given a show of support by our southern neighbours. Democratic candidate Harris Wofford defeated Republican Dick Thornburgh in the United States Senate elections. Mr. Wofford's campaign focused on the need for an affordable health care system based on the system we have in Canada.
At a time when the United States is moving toward a Canadian-oriented health care system, it seems rather ironic that this government is trying to phase out ours so that by the year 2000 the Canadian health care system as we know it will cease to exist.
November 6, 1991

Perhaps our health care system was one of the tradeoffs in negotiating the U.S.-Canada free trade deal. Unfortunately I fail to see what Canada is getting in return.
In words of defeated candidate Dick Thornburgh: "The issue of health care commanded greater attention than we had anticipated. I guess we underestimated voters' concerns".
I would urge the Prime Minister and this government to stop underestimating the concerns of the Canadian voter and restore health care funding instead of making the mistake of listening to President Bush again.

Mr. Speaker, this is Canada Career Week and I would like to take this opportunity to tell you how urgent it is to do something about education and careers. When we talk about the recession, unemployment, training, research and development, and high technology, we too often forget that education is the key to our economic progress. We are in the midst of an education crisis.
In Quebec, nearly 40 per cent of young people drop out of high school before graduation. It is time for all concerned, whether in the federal or provincial governments or in the labour movement, to agree to develop a strategy to rectify the situation. A complete, stimulating, well-directed education is essential to our prosperity. Young people have lost confidence and we must do our homework again. I hope that our jurisdictional quarrels will not compromise our young people's future and that everyone will open their eyes to reality, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, all future agricultural policies are supposed to be market responsive, product neutral, sustainable and competitive.
I assume these four pillars apply to the distribution of the $700 million to non-horticultural crops announced
during the Saskatchewan election, in which case there should be no question about including cultivated forages. They are good for soil. They take pressure off grains, oilseeds and pulses.
I am talking about good farm land above class 5 that can be easily converted back to other crops. I am talking about farmers who made good market decisions to switch to forages to reduce losses and to put nutrients back into the soil.
These crops have suffered from lower prices too. Surely the proposed assistance package must include all cultivated land whether seeded to cereals, oilseeds, pulses or forages. To do otherwise ignores the four pillars and common sense.

Mr. Speaker, our government's commitment to research and development will help secure Canada's future and ensure that our nation remains one of the best countries in the world in which to live.
It gives me great pleasure to inform the House that this Conservative government has committed $7.4 million to an industrial research and development institute to be established in Midland, Ontario. The institute will assist in the advancement of the tool, die and mould industries.
Universities, community colleges, and the industrial sector will work together to make the institute a leader in its field. Research in the industrial sector is vital. It goes to the very heart of all of our economic activity. The new technology and subsequent jobs which will emerge from this centre is one step toward ensuring Canada's continued prosperity and competitiveness.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to endorse the sentiments of my hon. friend who just spoke.
If you based your understanding of the government's proposals for a renewed Canada just from what is in the media, your view sure would be distorted.
We hear lots about the distinct society clause and other things which cause controversy.
But where is the debate on the elimination of interprovincial trade barriers? Where are the arguments for and against new powers of economic union? Why are Canadians not getting the facts about harmonizing budgets and tax systems? How about the division of powers which would cut duplication and bring government closer to the people?
I would like to urge all Canadians to demand an intelligent and comprehensive debate on these important economic initiatives. We have stared at our constitutional navels for long enough.

Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada and the Government of British Columbia will spend close to $1 million to commemorate the Alexander Mackenzie Bicentennial in 1993.
Two hundred years ago Alexander Mackenzie was the first white man to cross Canada by land and the first white man to make contact with the 30,000 Indian people
who lived in the Bella Coola Indian territory. The white men who followed Alexander Mackenzie spread disease, alcohol and firearms. They stole Indian land, resources and Indian artefacts. They destroyed Indian society and Indian people.
A hundred and fifty years after Mackenzie's visit there were only 239 Bella Coola Indians left on the face of the earth. Thirty thousand people had been annihilated.
Mr. Speaker, from you and other honorary patrons of the Alexander Mackenzie Bicentennial, the people of Bella Coola today would like to know what is there to celebrate about a genocide?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. According to the CFIB, for every dollar of sales tax in Germany it costs businesses less than half a cent to collect the tax. For every dollar of sales tax in the U.K. it costs businesses less than four cents to collect the tax. But in Canada it costs businesses 40 cents for every dollar of GST collected. It costs Canadian businesses nearly $7 billion to collect the GST.
You can say "bull" et cetera all you want, but these are the facts.
If the GST is such a simple tax, why is the collection cost to business in Canada one hundred times higher than that in Germany?

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member would be honest with herself, she would realize that the statistics which she just quoted are hogwash. They are based on a survey which has no evidence, no support data, no proof of cost and is based on flawed methodology.
In fact I think that the respected columnist, Mr. Terence Corcoran in The Globe and Mail put it the best way this morning when he wrote: "Mr. Bulloch's $10 billion, essential to his sensational claims, is the product of fine but preposterous statistical manipulation". I agree with Terence Corcoran.
November 6, 1991

Mr. Speaker, my follow-up question is for the Minister of National Revenue, he who claims to be fighting cross-border shopping.
Everyone knows that the GST is largely responsible for a flood of cross-border shopping which is costing thousands of Canadian jobs.
Can the government explain why, on the one hand, it is telling Canadians that we are going to cut back on cross-border shopping and on the other hand, in the government's GST Consumer Information Office bulletin released this week, the minister's office is suggesting: "The GST reminds holiday travellers that domestic flights are taxed at 7 per cent; all flights to Mexico, the Caribbean and to overseas are GST free. Bus and train trips within Canada are taxable, but there is no GST on bus and train trips to destinations outside Canada".
Why is the minister responsible for the GST also killing us with more calls for cross-border shopping in his own document?

We appreciate that the process is critical here in terms of providing ample opportunity for all Canadians to participate if they wish to. The minister has set the deadline of February 28 as the time for the committee to report. Will the minister indicate some willingness to reconsider this deadline to provide ample time, acknowledging the fact that we are getting into a pre-Christmas period in terms of Canadians' attention being perhaps turned to other than constitutional issues? Will he consider that date being put off a few weeks to enable the committee to do its job more properly?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows as well as I do the rules of this House and its requirements. A report will be presented to this House by the special joint committee on its reporting day. There will then be a reply by the Government of Canada which will constitute the position of the Government of Canada which will be interpreted in Quebec in accordance with their Bill 150 as an offer, and which will be interpreted in other ways elsewhere in the country.
The time frames are very tight. They are not all of our making. I would not anticipate that there would be a change in the reporting date of the special joint committee that has been established by a resolution of this House.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary for the same minister.
Obviously Canadians have indicated that when they are responding to what they see as a committee on the renewal of Canada that much of the discussion has taken place beyond strict constitutional matters, that they have also included matters of fair taxation, economic development, job creation and so on.
Will the minister responsible recognize that these are in fact appropriate interventions on behalf of Canadians concerned about the renewal of Canada and will he
November 6, 1991

make some effort to communicate to the two chairs that they be more tolerant in terms of a much more widespread debate on some of the critical issues facing the country's renewal?

I would also repeat to him what I think is known to all in the House that if there is an individual, a political party or a government of a province that has a proposal to make on an issue related to, for example, a social charter, we would be very interested in seeing the detail of that proposal.

We were informed this morning about some potentially very unfortunate remarks that one of the co-chairs made regarding the premier of the province of Quebec.
My question to the minister responsible is that if these quotes that are alleged to have been uttered by one of the co-chairs are in fact true in any form whatsoever, will the minister consider replacing that particular chair of the constitutional committee?

speakerposition: Speaker pro tempore
speechtext: I do not know that the minister can replace the co-chairperson of the committee. The committee is the master of its own procedure and that would have to be a matter for the committee.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Knowing that the plans to harmonize the GST fully with the provincial
Oral Questions
sales tax clearly cannot be implemented, is the government now telling us that we will continue to be the only country with two retail sales taxes that are completely inconsistent and not harmonized?
Is the government now prepared to work with Canadians to clear up this disaster of its own making?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, discussions are in fact continuing. As the hon. member knows, Quebec saw fit to postpone the implementation of the harmonization for six months but it has certainly in no way backed away from the implementation of it.
There are other discussions going on with other provinces. I can only indicate that there is the prospect of success and achievement in these particular areas.
The hon. member says name them. My understanding is that talks are continuing with respect to the province of Newfoundland which has expressed an interest in the harmonization in order to improve efficiency and to reduce the administrative costs.
My own sense is that what is required now is the support, in fact the encouragement of all politicians and leaders and people who represent special interest groups to encourage the harmonization of the tax because in that way it can reduce the administration costs and make the whole tax system much more effective.

Mr. Speaker, I think the minister is living in a dream world if he thinks that harmonization is still going to occur.
Let me ask him this. He surely knows that one of the things that Canadians find most unfair about the GST is the fact that it taxes things that they consider to be essential in their daily lives. Yesterday, and we welcome this news, the minister announced among other things that lancets, button infusers, aerosol chambers and extremity pumps and guide dogs for the hearing impaired are going to be exempt from the GST.
Why will the minister consider exempting and zero rating other things that are essential to Canadians in daily life, things like fuel to heat their houses, children's clothing, other things that people need daily?

November 6, 1991
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is progressive enough to recognize that the old federal sales tax that was in place was not an appropriate tax for a modem economy and that there needed to be reform and a value added tax like the GST was the most appropriate.
The hon. member refers to the fact that some changes were made yesterday. This is the fourth occasion on which there have been changes implemented. I think he should also bear in mind that the object of the exercise was to reduce the over-all rate from 13.5 per cent, which was the tax under the old manufacturers' sales tax, to a lower level, but in so doing it had to cover a broader range of services and to generate essentially the same amount of tax revenue.
The hon. member knows and understands that the minute you start providing for more exemptions, you will either end up with less revenue or a higher tax rate. I guess what we are trying to do is implement the system so that it will be fair and equitable to all concerned.

My question is for the Minister of Finance. Does he think that Atlantic small business has suffered enough? Will he act today to make the major change and end this punitive tax?

November 6, 1991

figures indicated that there was an increase in housing and an increase in the merchandise trade balance.

Oral Questions TAXATION

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
The Minister of Finance stands up in this House repeatedly and makes the claim that the cancellation of the manufacturers' sales tax is a great benefit to our manufacturers. Yet 80 per cent of the job loss in the province of Ontario is related to our manufacturing.
How does he square his claim that the cancellation of the manufacturers' sales tax is benefiting our manufacturers when we have such significant job loss?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member does understand that in fact the manufacturing sector has suffered not only in Canada and the United States, but indeed throughout the world there has been a substantive decline and a substantive decline in relationship to the other sectors, i.e. the service sectors.
I think that as we go through the process of globalization and attempting to compete more effectively in the globalized economy, there are certain adjustments and economies of scale that have be created in order to be competitive.
I think the hon. member would understand-and I am sure he does-that there is that adjustment and restructuring going on and a bit of that fall-out is recorded in that decline in unemployment in the manufacturing sector.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Finance.
There are 900,000 entrepreneurs in this country who are opposed to the GST. They are our greatest hope for job creation.
The Minister of Finance and the minister of trade state repeatedly in this House that they are going to listen to Canadians and they are going to consult with Canadians. Who are his consultants that are telling him and his government that the GST is a good tax for the economy of this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, committees of this House, successive royal commissions and studies into the manufacturers' sales tax all recommended that it be

November 6, 1991
Oral Questions
scrapped and that a more modem tax such as a value added tax or a GST be implemented. It was on that basis that this was done.
The federal sales tax, the manufacturers' sales tax, was archaic. It was a silent killer of jobs. It was not the kind of a tax to have for a country in a modernized global community. Therefore it needed to be changed.
There are refinements and improvements that have to be made and we are doing that. Yesterday we announced the fourth batch of improvements and refinements. We believe it is the best tax system to preserve jobs, to create new jobs and to maintain Canada's competitiveness.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on August 17, the Montreal Gazette published an article on the Meme breast implant, alleging that it did not comply with the Medical Devices Regulations. Following that article, I asked my department to examine the issue of the Meme implant, to find out if these allegations were true. I have now received the department's report, which I am pleased to table in the House today.
First, I want to respond to the allegation that the Meme implant had not been checked before it was put on the market. I am convinced, given the information that the department has, that the Meme implant was available to Canadian surgeons before Part V of the Medical Devices Regulations took effect on October 8, 1982 and that it was not necessary then for the manufacturer to make a submission.
As for the second allegation, that the Meme implant has been modified many times since 1984, the manufacturer has given the department written assurances that only the size, shape or volume of this device has been changed. Without any scientific evidence to the contrary, we should take the manufacturer, who did not inform the department when those changes were made, at his word.
However, the report indicates a discrepancy between the strict interpretation of the regulations and the administrative practices of the department when the

November 6, 1991
Routine Proceedings
ownership of the maker of medical devices that can be implanted changes. I want to dispel any other suggestion that the department would have been at fault regarding this medical device. That is why I want another opinion on the department's findings.

I have asked my deputy minister to have an audit firm from outside the government examine the department's actions on demand and to determine whether officials follow the appropriate administrative practices. My deputy minister has consulted with the Auditor General on the terms of reference for the outside audit.
My main concern is for the women who have these prostheses. We will continue to make available to these women and their physicians any new information regarding the safety of these products.
I encourage women who want information on the Meme or other breast implants to write to my department.
[Translation\
On the basis of our present knowledge, we can say that the main risks to women are those related to the actual surgery: complications as a result of anaesthesia and post-operative shock, infection and scarring. These risks are no greater with the breast implant that with other protheses, and the type of implant does not seem to make a noticeable difference.
At the request of the department, the Canadian Medical Association assembled a group of specialists to advise physicians on the use of polyurethane-coated breast implants, including the Meme implant. The group's report is published in the 1991 November 1 issue of the Canadian Medical Association's review, which is sent to all Canadian physicians. I will send a copy of the report to my provincial counterparts, to inform them of the results of the study and the recommendations formulated by the group, and I will ask for their views on the recommendations concerning jurisdiction.

We will also conduct a survey to obtain information from Canadian women regarding their experience with
breast implants. We will request the collaboration of I Know/Je sais Network.
I encourage all women with breast implants to participate in this survey. The department will also be asking doctors to make their patients aware of this study.
The regulation of medical devices is a very serious matter. In March of this year we established the Medical Devices Review Committee under the chairmanship of Dr. Ambrose Hearn. The committee is examining the regulatory framework under which medical devices are sold on the Canadian market and will make recommendations for regulating devices over the coming years.
The committee will hear from consumer groups as well as from the medical, scientific and manufacturing sectors. It will report in the spring of 1992.
In closing, I want to assure Canadians, especially those women who have the Meme implant, that Health and Welfare Canada will continue to monitor the safety and effectiveness of these devices.

Madam Speaker, I am delighted to respond to the minister's statement on the Meme breast implant. I applaud his statement.
There are certainly two issues and they are quite clear. These are the same issues that have been before us for some time. They are the safety of the product, the health of Canadian women and the reliability of the Research Branch of the Ministry of National Health and Welfare in deeming something safe or unsafe.
The history of the Meme has been chequered, to say the least. Its manufactured name has changed several times over the years. As a result of a grandfather clause it has had open access to the Canadian market without scrutiny and has been exempt from government checks.
At least five of the minister's own scientists have said the product was unsafe and women across Canada have also said that it was unsafe and should be withdrawn from the market. Yet in those months when it was very much under discussion the ministry did not act until the U.S. Food and Drug Administration withdrew the product from the market.
I raised this issue on several occasions in this House of Commons. Due to the unsatisfactory response of the then minister and the government I introduced a private member's bill, C-279. It is an act to amend the Food and
November 6, 1991

Routine Proceedings
Drugs Act (breast prostheses). This bill has had first reading in this House and waits its turn for full debate in the House of Commons.
The purpose of Bill C-279 is to ensure that people are protected from dangerous or potentially dangerous breast prostheses, including the Meme.
I welcome the minister's decision for an independent review of his research practice within his own department. Earlier the ministry review was made by a surgeon who implanted the Meme in her patients, an obvious conflict of interest.
You do not ask a user surgeon if the product is safe. You do not ask the head of your own research branch if the department is acting properly with regard to medical devices. You do not ask the manufacturer of a product, such as the Meme, if its product is safe. You go to an outside source for an independent review. This is exactly what the minister is going to do.
We need only to go back in history to find a few examples of medical devices that can kill or maim. The one that immediately comes to mind is the IUD. Yet many stay on the Canadian market without meeting proper safety standards.
I am not scare mongering and I do not think anyone in this House has ever meant to scare monger. However we need to be concerned about safe products and good health practices, as well as about standards within a department that is responsible for the health and welfare of all Canadians.
Again I applaud the minister for this step forward and an enlightened approach. I will closely follow and monitor the minister's survey and encourage Canadians, especially women who have had implants, to participate in the process.
I thank you very much for the opportunity to respond to the minister on this very important subject.

Madam Speaker, we are cautiously optimistic about the minister's statement. It is not often that we can applaud what the other side of this House does but this is one day I think we can. Much of what we have asked for the minister has given us today.
The government has admitted that it is willing to correct a wrong. The wrong it is going to correct is a
wrong of the government's own making. We are going to see an audit which is something that our party and the women involved in I Know/Je sais have asked for for a long time.
We will see what actually transpired between the government's regulations and its dealing with the manufacturer of the Meme transplant. In looking over the minister's statement I find that he makes a kind of half-hearted admission that the government made a mistake. He seems to say: "We did not do anything quite wrong, but I am not quite sure because there seems to be something that could have been done better."
I applaud the fact that the government side is going to look into this mistake and is going to have an outside scientific audit once and for all to determine what dangers are associated with this implant. That is very important.
It seems when you look at the consumer history of implants and women and the control of their bodies, that women have been guinea pigs. Women have been testing devices on the market which have never really been fully tested before being marketed. I hope that perhaps when the government makes its audit and comes up with its conclusions that it will be very quick and forthright in giving its conclusions to the Canadian public. I believe the government can only learn from its mistakes and by being forthright, open and transparent with the people who are most affected, the people who have had these implants as well as the public in general.
Another important statement made by the minister is that there is going to be a general survey not just on the Meme implant but on breast implants generally. That is very important and it is very important that the people in the I knowlJe sais network be consulted. They have had first hand experience. They have created their own network and because of the self-help they have been responsible for I think they are the best placed people to contribute to this survey.
Only last week our party was calling for this type of action from the government. I want the government to know that the problem is not going to go away. I just learned from my colleague who has been responsible for the dossier that just last week two women were offered the Meme implant again. Now the minister probably does not believe that but I will be very happy to supply him with the information on the incident and he can look into it. The minister says it cannot happen, these implants are not available in Canada and then you come

November 6, 1991
Routine Proceedings
up and see a woman who has had these implants. I mean that is the reality that we are faced with as a political party. That is the reality that women are faced with when they come up against this government and tell it: "Look, I have one reality and you have another, I do not believe you know what is really happening on the market."
In conclusion I want the minister to know very clearly that the offer to consult and collaborate with the I Know/Je sais Network is one which is going to be taken up by the women in this network. I would like the minister to know that this group of women will not be drawn in to any co-operation without assurances from his department that all-and I mean all-will be done to correct past errors. When I say all, the minister is aware of a letter that was sent to him quite recently by my office that women who want these implants out of their bodies should have, with his provincial counterparts, all the financial support needed to get these devices out of their bodies.
I hope the minister will look at the request made from my office and at the same time start this scientific technical audit as soon as possible as well as have this survey with the Je sais I I Know Network.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald S. Merrithew (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my proud duty today as Minister of Veterans Affairs for Canada to remind this House and indeed all Canadians that Monday, November 11 is Remembrance Day. It is certainly a very special day for the free world.

Considering that the future of our country is at stake, I think it would be appropriate if we were all particularly attentive this year to the significance of Remembrance Day.

Just a couple of months ago I had the honour to lead a pilgrimage of Canadian veterans. They returned to Sicily and Italy for the first time in six years to visit the graves of some 6,000 compatriots. The Mediterranean campaign
lasted 20 months and was the longest campaign waged by the Canadian army in the Second World War, yet it was fought in relative obscurity and unwarranted anonymity.
I cannot help but wonder whether our country would have benefited had Canadians been exposed to the hour by hour television coverage of the battle for Ortona-Montecassino or the Hitler line and all the other battles of the two world wars and Korea, in much the same manner as we received almost instant news from the Persian Gulf. We would have known so much better the sacrifices made on our behalf and the horrors our veterans faced. I think Canadians would have even better appreciated our Canadian veterans.
We might also have appreciated Canada better. Viewers would have seen young men from the prairies sailing with their countrymen from the maritimes. They would have seen regiments raised in Quebec City and Winnipeg battling side by side in the futile effort to save Hong Kong. They would have seen air crews from Canadian cities thousands of miles apart flying together in the Battle of Britain. Viewers would have seen not western Canadians, not central Canadians, not Atlantic Canadians but Canadians. They would have seen Canada at its very best.

If television cameras had existed at the time, they would have shown us men and women rising above all petty concerns, involved in a tremendous joint effort, ordinary Canadians from all the provinces and territories acting as one to accomplish a task and risking their lives in the name of the traditional virtues of duty and patriotism.

It is no surprise that our veterans' organizations are once again fighting for Canada as they conduct vigorous national unity campaigns. They do not want to let down the 115,000 men and women who were killed with the Canada flash on their shoulders.
Next April we will be commemorating the 75th anniversary of Vimy Ridge, Canada's greatest victory in time of war. General Byng, Commander of the Canadian Corps recalled the victory in these magnificent terms:
There they stood on Vimy Ridge that 9th day of April, 1917. Men
from Quebec stood shoulder to shoulder with men from Ontario, men
from the maritimes with men from British Columbia and there was

forged a nation tempered by the fires of sacrifice and hammered on the
anvil of high adventure.

If we allow these words to become a mocking echo in the future, it seems to me that we will have failed those we are commemorating on Remembrance Day. That will be more than a shame for Canada, it will be disgrace.
Let this be the time for us to show courage and commitment to our country Canada. Let this be the time for new generations of nation builders. On November 11 let us all remember the sacrifices of those nation builders who died so our country and the free world could prosper.
Madam Speaker, we owe that to them.

Madam Speaker, on each November 11 we make statements to commemorate the supreme sacrifice made by many young Canadians so that we and future generations could speak freely inside and outside the Parliament of Canada in this rich and magnificent country.
We gather around more than 1,700 cenotaphs of the Royal Canadian Legion across Canada to lay wreaths and poppies in their memory.
As time goes on there is a danger that some people will consider it a common practice or just simply the "thing to do".
For all of us every day of our lives should be a Remembrance Day because many young Canadians gave up their lives so that the rest of us could continue to build Canada into a great land of opportunity for all.
If we do not continue to build Canada into a strong and united country, if we do not continue to build Canada into a great land of opportunity for years to come then we will not be remembering the serious cause for which more than 112,000 young Canadians died in World War I, World War II and the Korean conflict. Tens of thousands more brought their lifetime wounds back home with them.
Canadian historians have stated that Canadian nationhood was born on the battlefields of Europe. One has only to visit and witness the massive but beautifully maintained memorial cemeteries in Europe and Korea, where the grave markers remind us of the teenagers and
Routine Proceedings
early 20-year olds who never returned to Canada and who are resting far from home. They never had the opportunity to participate in and live out their days in their beloved Canada. At this early age they answered the call to responsible duty and left their native land, never to return. Dreams lie buried in those foreign fields, dreams of families left behind, dreams of families yet to be bom, dreams of careers, dreams of peace and dreams of home.
Those young Canadians who never returned to their homes and families never knew what they did for all of us, and what their sacrifice meant to the entire world. But we know and we must remember.
We all tiy in our own way to honour both the casualties and the survivors of those terrible wars. We have as a society tried to pay back some of the debt which we owe. We have developed veterans' benefits programs which are the envy of the world but we must do more.
Those young men and women who died in foreign fields and those who came back did not fight for benefits or pensions. They fought for ideals, they fought for freedom and they fought for justice.
They fought for what was right. They fought for Canada and the free world. In this place as we pay tribute we must, each of us, re-dedicate ourselves to seeking solutions to our problems in their and our beloved Canada.
Just as one of our respected House of Commons constables salutes and turns a page in the Book of Remembrance in the Peace Tower of this Parliament each day of the year at eleven o'clock, we as living and gifted Canadians must work toward turning a new page in Canadian history. We must set this great nation of ours and theirs on a renewed course toward a Canada that is strongly united and a Canada that is clearly a great land of opportunity.
It is within our power to guarantee that they did not die in vain. On Remembrance Day let us make their memory the inspiration which will lead us to maintain and indeed improve the country which they died to defend. They accepted the responsibility to fight for the rights and privileges of each and every one of us.
Let us remind ourselves constantly that we too have responsibilities and obligations to our country. They managed the wars for us. It is now our duty to manage

Routine Proceedings
the peace for them. In all of these ways we will be remembering them.

Madam Speaker, it is an honour and a welcome duty to be able to rise in my place on behalf of my colleagues in memory of those men and women who served our country during her armed conflicts.
I also want to urge all Canadians to remember with me those who have suffered most from the insane cruelty of modern warfare; the innocent civilians of many lands, the men, women and children who endured hardship and death during wartime.
Canada has been at war a number of times this century. On each occasion the burden of service has been borne mainly by Canadians of unspectacular origins, by the sons and daughters of farmers, foresters, fishermen, miners, nurses, doctors and factory workers.
When Canada called they rose from their native soil. They left their families, their communities and their work to face the guns of the enemy. Too many did not come home.
We can never repay those who returned. We must never forget those who did not.
I want to compliment the minister on his statement, particularly the part pertaining to keeping this country whole. Those in Canada who want to break up our country had better explain to Canada how they can callously disregard those who gave their lives for this country.
About 110,000 Canadians-French, English, aboriginal, Metis and those who immigrated from other countries-fought together not for western Canada, Atlantic Canada, Ontario or Quebec. They fought for all of Canada.
When I visited cemeteries in Europe there were many instances where I saw English names, French names and Indian names on gravestones side by side. I thought about my country. Are those who would break up our country or who do not care if it does break up telling us that those who gave their lives or suffered their wounds did it for nothing?
Since the end of the Second World War, Canada has tried to repay its veterans and generally has done well. As a nation we have keenly felt our duty and obligation to those who risked so much in our name.
However, it gives me great pain to have to remind this House and all Canadians that some of our bravest souls have received as part of their reward indifference and neglect.
The first Canadians to fight fascism in the Spanish Civil War have never received even the thanks of the government of their country, nor have they received the slightest compensation for the risks they faced for the sake of democracy.
Many members of Canada's First Nations contributed mightily to our nation's efforts in World War II and Korea. In many cases their armed service created problems they had not faced before. We as our nation's parliamentarians are only now learning of these difficulties. Aboriginal veterans are entitled to the fullest veterans' benefits and to any benefits denied them. They must be given the most sympathetic review and reconsideration retroactively.
There is one group whose members have been denied their rightful reward and may be standing on the verge of receiving the full recognition they have earned.
On October 2 the Standing Committee on National Defence and Veterans Affairs tabled its first report of this parliamentary session in the House of Commons.
I was very glad to have the privilege of working with the other committee members on that report. I am even more pleased to be able to endorse without reservation its recommendations.
The committee recommended unanimously that Canadian merchant mariners with one or more high seas ocean-going assignments during wartime be fully recognized as veterans and that full veterans' benefits be extended to them. The committee also recommended that a Book of Remembrance dedicated solely to merchant mariners who died in Canada's wars be placed in the Peace Tower.
Finally the committee recommended that the Department of Veterans Affairs encourage the construction of a suitable monument to honour the memory of Canada's
November 6, 1991

wartime merchant mariners. The committee suggested as well that Halifax would be a suitable site for such a monument.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs now has an opportunity, with the support of all other members of this House from all parties, to respond positively to the committee's recommendations. I hope he does so quickly. It is long past time for Canadians to seek out our forgotten heroes. We must do this to help realize some of our most profoundly held national ideals.
Not only must we never forget, we must strive to remember and ensure that veterans' benefits go to all veterans.

Madam Speaker, I would like to make a case respecting the need for an emergency debate on the situation in Yugoslavia.
Let me first say that no one in this House has any reservations about the problems there. We all know about the deteriorating situation. What we have to do to satisfy the requirement for an emergency debate is to meet the test of urgency.
I want to make the case to the Chair that we have had no opportunity in this House to have a full debate on the circumstances. There was some negotiation a week or so ago to have a general resolution. That has not been possible, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs has now left for an extended visit overseas. Therefore members of Parliament are deprived of the opportunity to make their views known and those of their constituents.
I would like to bring another important fact to the attention of the Chair. There were reports today in the European press, particularly in the London Financial Times, that proposals would be made tomorrow at the NATO summit, which the Prime Minister is attending, concerning the need for an oil embargo and the possible NATO blockade of the Adriatic. These are serious discussions that would have very important implications
for this country in terms of our commitment to those two orders.
It would be absolutely essential before a decision is made by the Prime Minister at that NATO summit meeting within the next 36 hours that this Parliament have the opportunity to debate the matter and to let the voice and concerns of Canadians be known.
It appears to me that the events taking place at the NATO summit are a primary cause for the need for an emergency debate and for this Parliament to speak with a voice so that we can represent the very serious concerns of many Canadians about the deplorable situation in Yugoslavia.

I can guarantee that this will be the one day for speeches but I would hate, particularly after going with one speaker on second reading, to deny members the right to speak. I know that my hon. friend shares my feeling on that. I think we have an understanding.

Madam Speaker, I would agree with what my two friends have said.
We would try with one of our 20-minute speakers to get two at 10 minutes. Perhaps the House will give us some leniency on that.
I hope and trust that we will continue our debate today. It was a rather remarkable debate that we had last night on amendments which flowed very well. It flowed late. Many people got on, through co-operation in the House, and we expedited a lot of work very quickly, very efficiently and very fairly. I think we can do that today. I will sit down so that the minister can get started.

Madam Speaker, I would like to know if I understand correctly, because we are rather far away.

Will we agree to go on a little later than scheduled and not to request a quorum at that time? Is that all there is in that motion or is there something else that I might not have heard from my seat?
