speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
that Bill C-17, an act to amend the Criminal Code and the Customs Tariff in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.
She said: Madam Speaker, I will try to keep my remarks at third reading reasonably brief because I did have the opportunity to speak at second reading and I want to give as many colleagues as possible a chance to put their views on the record in reasonable time.
I want to acknowledge the very hard work of members of this House who contributed to these proceedings. It really was an extraordinary effort. Members of all parties have taken an active interest in gun control legislation.
Their knowledge and concerns have helped bring forward many new ideas and possibilities, not only for this legislation but for future policy as well.

November 6, 1991
Government Orders

Gun control is a very difficult issue. During the past two years, members of this House have been made aware of the concerns of many Canadians. As this process has developed, we have heard that gun control is not just a justice issue, but also one of public health and accident prevention that touches everyone.

The progress of the proposed amendments from the special committee to the legislative committee was very important for developing reasonable, effective and practical legislation because it provided an opportunity for everyone with an interest in firearms or gun control to be heard and to be questioned by members of Parliament.
This is an important element of the democratic process. If we are to have workable legislation, we must have well informed legislators.
I think it is important just to say a few words about the process because much of the commentary of it seemed to suggest that the committee process was a delay and that it represented a lack of will on the government side of the House to see this legislation through. Nothing could have been further from the case.
As I think all of the people who participated in the process will be well aware, the differences in points of view on this particular issue are profound. The differences arise from the fact that this is such an enormous country with such an enormous diversity of life experience.
I can speak from my particular reality as an urban person. I am the member of Parliament for Vancouver Centre. My city is a major centre of the drug trade in Canada. It is a port. It is subject to pressures for crime. We are very close to the United States. That border is very close to our particular community and all the difficulties that that creates with the smuggling of firearms and drugs and other difficult sources of criminal activity.
The people in my part of the country, the people in my constituency, are largely preoccupied with the question of public safety and are concerned about the role that firearms play in destabilizing the comfort level that is so important and destabilizing their sense of security.
Not all of my constituents have that particular point of view. There are also among my constituents members of shooting organizations and people who like to hunt as a recreation. But the majority of them have what we might call that urban perspective. Yet at the same time many of the people of my own province-I do not even have to
go out of British Columbia-live a totally different reality where firearms are a daily part of their lives either because they are hunters, because they are ranchers, because they live far from urban centres, because there are predators in their midst, because they hunt as a natural part of supplementing their food supply, or because they enjoy shooting sports. They are responsible users of firearms. They feel that somehow those who wish to increase gun control are trying to solve the urban crime problem on their backs and they resent that.
The realities are profoundly different. What this bill represents is a really heroic and very mature attempt by members of Parliament from around this countiy to bring together those realities, to try to understand one another, to try to understand the need to create a framework of firearms legislation in this country that does provide security for people and that does provide a sense of safety.
In fact that good legislative framework is the best guarantee that those who wish to continue to use firearms for hunting or sporting purposes will be able to continue to do so, because the majority of Canadians will then be comfortable and secure in the knowledge that those who use firearms are competent to do so, that they are screened to do so, and that they are people who are using those firearms responsibly. Where they do not do so, society has the tools necessary to call them to account.
Even though I am from Vancouver Centre and represent that point of view, I think it is very important. I have learned a great deal from listening to other members of Parliament about the reality of their constituencies. That has been an extraordinary part of the sharing of attitudes that has gone on in the committee processes dealing with this legislation.

I am very pleased with the recommendation that the legislative committee has put forward. I am confident that these amendments will strengthen the legislation and make it more effective. All of us want a bill that will preserve the safety of the Canadian public and at the same time improve the administration of the gun control system.

I am especially happy to report that members from all parties who sat on this committee achieved substantial consensus on the amendments put forward. They were, like all members of this House, very much united behind the public safety goals of the legislation. But they also shared a desire to improve the administration of the gun
November 6, 1991

control system to ensure fairness to firearms owners and users.
This bill has measures to keep firearms out of the hands of those who should not have access to them, to limit access to the most dangerous types of firearms and to strengthen the sentencing and deterrence aspects of the law. The amendments put forward by the legislative committee not only preserve but enhance these goals. Some of the most positive and useful suggestions that have emerged during the hearing process have to do with specific areas of prevention. One of those has been the idea that court prohibition orders could be extended to apply to situations where there is a risk that a firearm could be misused even if this has not previously occurred. A prohibition order is of course an order which prohibits an individual from owning or being in possession of a firearm.
The sentencing measures were strengthened in Bill C-17 by adding drug trafficking to the list of offences for which a court can make a discretionary firearms prohibition order. The committee has proposed adding the offence of importing narcotics. This proposal will help to reduce a small but very dangerous area of firearms misuse, and I strongly support it.
As a result of evidence heard by the special committee on gun control chaired by the hon. member for Kitchener provisions were included in the bill which will allow courts to impose firearm prohibition orders in bail release and peace bond applications. This will help the authorities to remove firearms temporarily from potentially dangerous situations even before a trial takes place. I think it is important to point out that in many of these applications that result from domestic disputes there is a situation, a very volatile situation, where the presence of a firearm is an extraordinarily dangerous catalyst to perhaps further violence.
What this bill does is require the courts in considering those peace bond or bail applications to consider the presence of a firearm in that situation and, where appropriate, to issue a prohibition order even before the matter has gone to trial. I think most people would agree that that is an extremely important provision.
Government Orders
I would also like to comment very briefly on the debate on the amendments that took place at report stage, not on the specifics. I would like simply to say that I think Canadians who watched that debate were treated to a remarkably reasoned and intelligent discussion of the various aspects that have to go into consideration in drafting legislation in this area. Some of the amendments that were not supported by the government are amendments that were not supported because they are in fact in principle recognized in the legislation already.
I think, for example, of the provision that asked for a mandatory 30-day amnesty period. I appreciate the spirit behind that and I support it. I simply think that the bill does provide now through its blanket amnesty provision for new types of firearms that are declared prohibited weapons. The concern was that people not become instant criminals. It does provide the ability to create an amnesty. I am concerned that in fact in some cases 30 days may not be long enough. What it does is it enables the government to bring forward a set of regulations with respect to each prohibition that is properly tailored to the circumstances. The spirit I think is a good one. I accept it as I accept the spirit behind the proposed amendment to create mandatory prohibition orders for certain kinds of drug offences.
Where we differ, we being the government and members of the Liberal Party who supported that amendment, was in our concern that there would still be some discretion left in the court because that provision covers a huge array of offences. What our proposal does is require the court once again to consider prohibition orders.
One must look, for example, at a situation in the north, in Yukon, when an aboriginal person who relies on hunting is convicted of a charge of trafficking in a very small quantity of marijuana. I am not suggesting that is not a serious offence, but perhaps it is not an offence that would justify a mandatory 10-year prohibition order in those circumstances.
Where we differ is simply that we on this side of the House would believe that the judge should have some discretion, but we do agree very strongly that prohibition orders respecting firearms must be seen as part and parcel of the disposition and sentencing procedures that the courts enter into in dealing with these offences. They

Government Orders
must see the link between certain kinds of crime and the possible danger to be presented by firearms in that particular set of circumstances.

Many witnesses told the special committee of the seriousness of the problem of domestic violence in Canada. Members heard about the disturbing frequency of domestic homicides. They also heard that firearms are the single most common weapon used in those homicides. I was pleased to see that witnesses and committee members agreed that this proposal is a major step towards addressing the problem of firearms in domestic violence situations.
The presence of firearms in such situations is truly frightening. Our law should go as far as it can to empower and encourage those involved in the system to remove them whenever possible.

The development of this legislation has been a long process. It has been necessaiy to take the time to allow everyone to express his or her views. The interest and concerns have been carefully weighed in the development of fair and effective legislation. The process is nearly completed and it has proven to be a very productive process indeed.
During the committee hearings we have come to see the ways in which firearms and gun control affect us all. We have come to see that many Canadians have legitimate, reasonable and prudent uses for firearms and that they share the concerns about public safety expressed by all Canadians. We have come to see that firearms are not just an issue for sportsmen and enthusiasts but for our public health community as well. We have heard from doctors, lawyers, educators and firearms owners.
The process has at times been divisive but I am convinced that the end product has been the development of a consensus on many issues.

During the hearing process, the witnesses have educated on the issue of firearms not only the members who heard their testimony, but each one of us as well.
I think that this is something that those who participated in the process can be proud of and that all Canadians can be grateful for.

I would like to take this opportunity to express their gratitude along with my own. The contribution of the committee members and witnesses has proven a victory for the democratic process. It has resulted in better gun control legislation for everyone.
No one expects this or any other legislation to put an end to violence in society. That requires a much more concerted effort and one to which I think all members of this House are devoted and actively seek mechanisms to ameliorate and to resolve.
On the other hand we must give to the police, customs officers and the courts the tools that they need to do their jobs. Sometimes people say to me: "Well, you know, what is the point of having this legislation? People steal firearms and are going to break the law." That would be a justification simply for shredding the Criminal Code and saying: "We give up." It is very important that those who seek to secure our safety in society have the tools they need so that when we talk about law enforcement we have not undermined that ability by not providing our policemen, courts and customs officers with the statutory authority they need to act.
More importantly I believe that we must make a clear statement about the firearms culture in this country. I think it is important to underline the fact that we are unique. I had a discussion recently with the Home Secretary in Great Britain. In Great Britain firearms ownership is an upper class phenomenon. Hunting is the activity or the hobby of the rich. Similarly, the United States has a very different history from us. Their frontier was not opened up as our was in the presence of law and order and in the presence of the Northwest Mounted Police, later the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Theirs was opened up with a very much wilder and less constrained approach to resolving disputes that has created a different firearms culture.
Canada has its own firearms culture. It is one where many responsible, law-abiding Canadians own firearms, use them to hunt and for sporting activities. In fact this is a very important part of our cultural tradition. At the same time we also have a culture that is non-violent, that is concerned about public safety and respect for public security. Our culture believes it is appropriate to impose on those who own firearms a reasonable and well thought out legislated scheme to ensure public safety, to ask those people who have the privilege of owning firearms to respond to society's concern that these
November 6, 1991

firearms not be misused and that they be handled with care.
I believe that a very important role this legislation plays is to re-assert the uniquely Canadian cultural values with respect to firearms. Firearms are a part of our social activity but we also have very high expectations of those who possess them in terms of guaranteeing the security of all. As we become a more urbanized society we become more sensitive to questions of violence. As our own consciousness rises we want to ensure that we have in the system by which we govern ourselves, our collective aspirations, a system that can reflect that culture adequately.
I believe Canadians deserve effective gun control legislation and I would urge all members of this House to support this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the minister for her statement and her support of this legislation. I think the minister has fought hard for this legislation and I want her to know that members on this side of the House appreciate the fight that she has carried on in her government. It really indicates that here in Canada we are a very thoughtful people.
We are proud of our traditions, and we are very conscious of our heritage. The minister has made reference to the distinctive nature of Canada as opposed to Britain and the United States.
Our culture is not dependent on firearms the way it is south of the border. Without being demeaning to our American friends, I find it very much of a concern, frankly, the attitude that they have. A lot of it, of course, is based upon the fact that in the American Constitution the right to bear arms is enshrined.
That being said, I find it very alarming that the day after the tragedy in Killeen, Texas, the U.S. Congress voted 247 to 177 to defeat a gun control measure. The only one changing his vote was the member who represented the Killeen, Texas area.
To me, that is much of a concern. I know the minister has to go, but before she does, I want to say to her that
Government Orders
bearing this in mind, I hope that she will support the initiatives of the police at all levels, the provincial, the municipal and the federal police forces to work together and to have an integrated committee whereby they can plan and work toward the guardian against the importation of illegal firearms into this country.
I would hope the government would give support, be it financial or just moral support, to these police forces to allow them to continue to do this.
As the minister knows, and as the members, the parliamentary secretary and the member for Cariboo- Chilcotin know we have heard that there is this importation of illegal firearms in the country. We have to do, as members of Parliament and responsible people, what we can.
Certainly they are going to come in regardless of how many precautions. There is only a reasonable amount you can spend toward that, but I would hope that the government would do its best efforts in that regard.
I was also alarmed in the fact that three days after this tragedy in Texas that a reporter was able to go into a store in Houston, Texas and buy a dock 17 in 40 minutes, never having had a FAC or any comparable certificate. This includes having to go back a second time to buy the ammunition because the store's policy was that it would not sell the firearm and the ammunition at the same time.
The journalist had to buy the firearm, go out to the car, leave the firearm, go back in and buy the ammunition.
I think it is vital that we in Canada appreciate the fact that we have first of all a citizens' base in this country that is prepared to think on this question, to think about the fact the privilege of using firearms is just that, a privilege in Canada, and one which is very well adhered to by the firearms community. Also, we should appreciate the fact that we have not had the proliferation of firearms in this country.
I look to the recent ad put forward by the National Rifle Association. It advocates that the best way for a woman to protect herself is to carry a hand gun in her purse, or to keep one at home.

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
That, of course, is a proliferation of the use of firearms. Once that starts, how is that going to be controlled?
If the United States said today: "Elow are we going to control firearms? How would we roll it back?", it would be an extremely difficult thing to do. You have the attitude there now that you need firearms to be able to protect yourself.
If someone was to be asked to give up their firearms, the first question would be: "How am I going to protect myself with all those other firearms out there?" We could, in this country, get into that position.
Hopefully that will never happen. This bill is not a real strong gun control bill. It is a reasonable piece of legislation, but it is not really strict, strong gun control. I think those who say it are trying to alarm the Canadian public to an unreasonable degree. I wonder whether any kind of gun control would please some of these groups and some of these individuals and whether they are not just trying to say: "Look, we have this menace, we have this red menace at our door. The government is trying to disarm us and we have to fight back". It has been a heck of a good membership drive for a few of these organizations. I know of some that have lobbied on behalf of the pro-firearms groups and their memberships have gone up substantially. They were able to convince a great many firearms owners in this country that there was this threat. Their houses were going to be broken into and their firearms would be seized. I think that is irresponsible and counterproductive. I think it also very important that the people of Canada realize this is the sort of argument and propaganda that has gone on.
What we are doing in this legislation as far as the prohibition of firearms is concerned is to merely prohibit semi-automatic firearms that could be converted to the automatic mode. That is simply it. Automatic rifles are already prohibited. It creates the National Advisory Council which I will come to later. It will look at all military and paramilitary firearms to determine which ones are suitable for hunting and have an actual purpose.
Some automatics and semi-automatics are merely imitations and copies of already prohibited weapons and
are convertible to fully automatic mode. They too will be prohibited.
Where I ask is the loss in that? They are not even good hunting rifles. If you are hunting deer you want to shoot the deer, you do not want to cut it in half. The fact of the matter is that they are not as accurate as some very well made semi-automatics that are perfectly suitable and in fact desirable for hunting, which it is not the intention of this bill to touch in any way.
Most of the rifles in this country are not even registered or restricted. We do not even know the people who have them. It is not the intention of this bill to restrict those firearms.
This legislation will also restrict clip sizes. We are saying that in handguns the maximum clip size will be 10 and the maximum for a rifle will be five. That does not seem to cause a great deal of hardship to most hunters.
I have a lot of hunters in my riding. Most of them feel that is adequate and that a good hunter will not need to use any more than five in a rifle. There again we have made exceptions. We have looked to the possibilities that can occur.
This country has taken pride in the success of our competitive shooters in international competition. We have said that those involved in competitive shooting are exempt from this. They can have magazines with more than 10 rounds so that they will not be hurt in international competition.
We are not really insensitive to the exceptions that can occur. I believe the exceptions have been taken into consideration.
We also say that we want to have a firearms acquisition certificate to buy firearms. That of course is a common sense arrangement I would say. Before you actually acquire an FAC you have to go through a 28-day waiting period so that your application can be checked. There can be substantial checks made with those who the authorities feel would have pertinent knowledge about your ability and desirability to have a firearm. In effect a community check is done and I think that is suitable.
November 6, 1991

We are also advocating that before a person is granted an FAC he must pass a training course. All groups agree that it is desirable for those who own firearms and henceforth purchase firearms to complete a training program. The question of course is when will this training program be brought into existence? The training programs are under provincial jurisdiction and their actual implementation requires the federal government and the provinces to enter into an agreement. I want to say to the federal government that we see this as being very important.
Even though the amendment put forward by the member for Kenora-Rainy River was ruled out of order we hope that indicates the seriousness of this party in assuring that these training programs are put into place. We will be monitoring this and demanding that this be done as soon as possible if in fact it is not done.
We have also said that there has to be a photo on the FAC. Those who are going to renew a firearms acquisition certificate do not have to go through this waiting period. However they have to get an updated photo. They must have a security check and they have to be there to pick up the FAC in person.
Some say: "I have had a firearm for years. Why should I go through this training program? Why should I have to wait for 28 days? I am being treated unfairly. I am being treated as a person who has never had any experience in firearms and I think that is unfair". I would say to all members and to everyone frankly that there is a very obvious way around this. That is to get people to qualify for an FAC right now under the circumstances that exist before this bill comes into effect and this new program comes into effect.
If that is a concern anyone who knows that this bill is going to be providing these new requirements for an FAC and does not take advantage of it has no one to blame but themselves. We must have stricter FAC requirements and we have to ensure that these measures are enforced.
I know we have to start somewhere. Allowing those who do not have an FAC now to qualify before this bill and this program come into effect is being more than generous.
Government Orders
Those who have prohibited weapons do not have to give them up. If they want to keep them they must qualify as a genuine gun collector and therefore must have some knowledge of firearms. They have to show some responsibility in having adequate security provisions and must keep a log of their firearms. They have to allow someone to periodically come into their home or wherever they are storing their firearms and make an inspection to ensure that this storage is suitable.
That is not asking too much. That visit would be once a year at the most. With the work that the registrars will have to do they may be fortunate to visit each person every two years, although that is an excessively long period of time between visits. The fact of the matter is that the definition of a genuine gun collector is very broad. Perhaps it is too broad if anything.
What we have to do is ensure that this is effective. We have to ensure that the genuine gun collector is not somebody who just stores his prohibited weapon in the corner. We say there is a prohibition against these firearms and we mean there should be a prohibition against these firearms.
The fact of the matter is that there should be these safeguards. The advisory council will be looking into a lot of these questions and tightening the restrictions. One question which is of vital importance is that of safe storage. Safe storage is going to be tremendously important if we are to reduce the number of deaths from firearms.
In 1988 there were 1,400 deaths from firearms in this country. Eleven hundred were suicides. In the United States there were 34,000 deaths from firearms during that same year. We had 1,400, they had 34,000.
A lot of theirs were accidental deaths. The reason they had the accidental deaths was because the firearms were available. If somebody is morose and feels despondent and there is a firearm in the corner or in a closet that is not locked, with ammunition in it, it so easy on the spur of the moment to use that firearm to end one's life.
We are saying that there has to be a deterrent. The 28-day waiting period will be a deterrent. If someone does not have a firearm and needs one, they have to get an FAC, they have to go through the training course, and the 28-day period. For those who have firearms at home we are saying that there has to be a degree of safe storage. Not all of them are going to be genuine gun collectors protected by alarm systems and elaborate safety mechanisms. There are rifles that we do not even

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
know exist. They are there. We are saying that at the very least there should be precautions such as the storage of ammunition and perhaps the bolt from the rifle stored separately from the firearm itself.
We are also suggesting that trigger locks be placed on the firearm. This means that there will be a deterrent, the person who wants to use that firearm to shoot themselves would have to go through the motions of getting the ammunition and the bolt or getting the key to unlock the trigger lock. These are deterrents because it gives people time to think.
There are those who will say that it is not important. It is not important because you cannot enforce them. No, we are not going to send law enforcement officers into people's homes to check storage. That would be an invasion of privacy. That would be unreasonable. We are depending on people to obey the law and I think most people will. Elowever, should someone use their firearm to commit suicide or to commit an assault on another person then their storage will be examined by the enforcing officers and charges could be laid against them at that particular time. You run that risk if you are going to disobey any safe storage laws that are going to be put in this bill.
It is vital for the purposes of discouraging violence against women. In this country today 65 per cent of all murders or all deaths are a result-I see the member from Montreal is taking this all very seriously. He is playing cowboys and Indians in the aisle on the government side. It is a disgrace.
Sixty-five per cent of the deaths resulting from the use of firearms are as a result of crimes of passion and not of criminal acts involving robbery or the murder of people they have never met before.
In this country 30 per cent of the victims of firearms are women but only 5 per cent of the users are women. It is no wonder that women in this country are very concerned about whether this gun control legislation will succeed in this House. I think they have every reason to be concerned. With the increase in crime in Canada there are a lot of women who are concerned about just walking home from the bus stops in the evening. We have to be able to give them some assurance that this House and this Parliament is concerned about the safety concerns they have.
I am very disappointed that the government did not see fit to approve the amendments that were presented and voted upon here today. The minister referred to the period of one month suggested by the member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso upon the implementation of the bill to allow people a month to abide by the bill.
The minister says there will be an amnesty for a period of time, but we do not know how long that period of time is going to be. It is important for people who want to abide by this bill to know exactly where they stand in a definitive way, and not a very subjective period of time to be applied by the courts or subsequently by regulation. I think it should be in the act itself.
We likewise had an amendment suggested by the member for Haldimand-Norfolk. He suggested that not one month but three months was a reasonable period of time. I think two months is a reasonable period of time. We have to be able to allow people to know where they stand and what terms of reference they have to abide by this legislation.
It is also important that we be mindful. The government is putting through a lot of justice legislation this week because it is crime prevention week and it wants the public to believe that it is completely obsessed with doing something to increase safety in our communities. I take a rather jaundiced view of this. I am not convinced. While I do approve of this legislation some of the other legislation leaves something to be desired.
I think the government would admit that there is a major problem in our communities, particularly with respect to the use of drugs. The motions put forward by this party relate to the mandatory prohibition on the use of firearms. Right now Bill C-17 says that if a person is convicted of a crime involving violence that has a maximum penalty of 10 years or more they are prohibited from using a firearm for 10 years on the first offence and life on the second offence.
We are saying that anybody who is convicted of an indictable offence involving violence should be prohibited from using that firearm for 10 years on the first offence and for life on the second offence. We are also saying that these penalties should also be applicable to those who are convicted of indictable offences under the
November 6, 1991

Food and Drugs Act and the Narcotics Act. This would mean that somebody who is trafficking in narcotics, is in possession of narcotics for the purposes of trafficking, or is importing or exporting narcotics should be prohibited from using a firearm.
This is not an unreasonable request. Certainly you could say that some people might get into fisticuffs and would be charged with an indictable offence. I do not know about other areas but in my area fisticuffs results in a summary conviction which would leave the discretionary prohibition with the judge.
We have to do something to control drug related crime in our communities. We have to be able to say to people: "Look, if you are going to commit an indictable offence under the Food and Drugs Act and the Narcotics Act you are going to lose the right to use a firearm for 10 years on the first instance and life on the second". At the very least, we may prohibit those who are involved in or hooked on narcotics from using a firearm in the commission of a second offence while trying to raise money to feed their habit.
We have to do something. We cannot just sit back and allow this increase in crime to continue in our municipalities. These are two important amendments. They are related amendments and they deal with these issues. It is important to leave discretion with our judges but there comes a time in certain incidences when we want to send a message. We are losing the war against drugs in our municipalities and we have to acknowledge that. We cannot be blase. We have to admit that we are fighting a catch-up battle in this regard.
I am disappointed they were not accepted. I am prepared to remind the government that it turned this down on occasions when crimes are committed for drugs. These situations certainly could have been prevented, or at least dealt with responsibly, if these amendments had been brought forward. I might say that I will be a very bitter person if what happens is what I think is going to happen, and that is that drug related crime is going to increase and this Parliament has not put forward provisions necessary to deal with this.
Government Orders
The minister is from Vancouver. She mentioned that it was an entry point for drugs. Yet, this is not being accepted. I think it is unfortunate.
I do feel also that there are a lot of hand guns out there, albeit they are restricted and as such are registered. These registration certificates that are given to the owners of hand guns are good for life. I think that is a long period of time to give anyone a carte blanche right to have a hand gun, particularly since most of the crimes involving firearms are committed with hand guns. Therefore, I think it would have been wise for the government to have accepted a five-year limit on each registration certificate on a restricted weapon.
I do not want to go on too long because there are a lot of members here who want to speak. I see the member for Don Valley North. I want to thank her for her support and the member for Lethbridge who is chairman of the committee as well, and who did a marvellous job in Legislative Committee H on this.
I would be wrong if I did not also thank the critic for the NDP and the member for the Bloc Quebecois and others, particularly my two colleagues who worked with me in the legislative committee, the members for Stormont-Dundas and Bonavista-Trinity-Conception.
I know there are a lot whom I forgot to mention. This is a determination. Once again I see my friend from Cariboo-Chilcotin who represents, as I do, a constituency where there are a lot of gun owners. Ele worked extremely hard. I saw an awful lot of that hon. member in the last year working on these various committees. I developed a respect for him and many members in this House for their sincerity of not necessarily agreeing on every point of view, but wanting to bring together the points of view, the disparate points of view to develop a piece of legislation that would be a very important piece of legislation for this country and one which would bring us further in the area of gun control.
This is not everything everybody wanted. It is a lot farther than a lot of members wanted to go. Certainly there are lot of members in the public who feel that we did not go far enough.
I would like to say that it is a very meaningful piece of legislation and when you compare the inaction of our friends south of the border for whom we have a great

Government Orders
deal of respect, but we cannot really understand their position on this very question, I believe we are continuing to move forward.
The fact is we in Canada are saying the citizens are going to control this country, that firearms are not going to dictate the way of life to the Canadian public. We in Parliament are taking a position that Canadians are going to be in charge of their country, not firearms, and they are not going to be held ransom by firearms are we are not going to allow pressure groups to dictate that we take measures that are going to be counterproductive to our own well-being.
I want to thank everyone in the House and members of my party for the support they have given me, even though they may not have completely agreed with my point of view. I believe we have a very worth-while piece of legislation here and I hope it will be supported.

Mr. Speaker, we have waited a long time for this bill on gun control. It just passed into third reading a few hours ago in the House of Commons, overwhelmingly. It will pass tomorrow at ten o'clock to the Senate and then soon into legislation.
I just want to say that while we have passed the bill, the struggle for effective gun control in Canada has just really begin. It has just begun with this bill. There are a number of other issues that surfaced during our many hearings that we are going to have to face as a country and as a people. I say it has just begun with this bill because most of the bill, the guts of the bill, will be in the regulations. As hon. members know they will be passed later by the government through regulations, not here in the bill as specific law. The bill authorizes the regulations but the regulations are not in the bill and we have not seen the regulations.
For example, there is the size of magazines that will be permitted. The minister said 10 bullets for hand guns and five for rifles. We are going to have to wait to see that, and we are going to have to wait to see about the safe storage provisions of the bill. We are going to have to wait to see which, if any, military or paramilitary weapons will be prohibited.
I say to the various groups and the various people who worked for effective gun control that you have to keep the pressure on. We have to make sure that these regulations are drafted. We have to make sure they are not delayed. I am going to speak about those procedures later in my speech.
Let me say right off the top that this bill is a very modest bill, indeed a very modest bill. For example, the bill fails to clamp down on the possession of some 50,000 converted semi-automatic guns in Canada, many illegal, which, if obtained by criminals, can be changed back to automatic guns.
Even if we pass this bill tomorrow, as we will, Canadians will still be free to buy bullets without even having been approved or authorized to own a gun. More disturbing still, we have evidence from metropolitan Toronto police, and I will come back to this later in my speech, that there are some 50,000 registered hand guns in metro Toronto alone, not counting another 17,000 that belong to police security firms and gun club members, and this number is growing in spite of the fact they are restricted. This legislation of course does not deal with that at all.

November 6, 1991

The victim, Mr. Sharib, 15, of 715 Bay Ridge Avenue, was
pronounced dead at Victory Memorial Hospital at 11:15 p.m. Mr. Dalton was arrested and charged with second-degree murder and
criminal possession of a dangerous weapon.
One of the neighbours, the victim's aunt, Linda Sharib, said:
"He was just a baby. I don't understand the violence today between
children. They shoot to kill; they don't shoot to hurt."
That is a little story from Brooklyn. It is not Canada, but it is a little glimpse perhaps into the future of what may be Canada. Canada we think of as being different.
Unlike the Americans, the Canadian frontier was not opened with a gun. When Europeans went to the Canadian west, as well as the north, guns were checked with the RCMP, even at Dawson City. I spoke to Pierre Berton about this and asked him about guns. He told me that in Dawson City in Yukon at the height of the gold rush when you came across that border you checked your guns.
Even the police were under orders not to draw their weapons unless it was absolutely necessary. It was different in Canada.
You should see and hear some of the evidence we got before our committee. Listen to this. This is evidence presented before the committee. The member for Cariboo-Chilcotin was there and he will remember this.
Mr. John Bickerstaff said this: "Thank you for the opportunity to address you. Firearms storage and gun control came into my life and the lives of my family very recently. Although I am a gun owner I do not represent myself to be a gun expert. I am here to address you because I have first hand knowledge in dealing with the consequences of poor gun control. I have also had the opportunity to give the matter of safe gun storage a great deal of thought.
On August 13, 1991 my 18 year old son Lee was accidentally shot to death. He and five teenage friends were amusing themselves in the home of a deputy commissioner of the Ontario Provincial Police by playing with a service revolver.
The restraints on the gun if present were removed. A bullet was put in it and shortly thereafter Lee was dead. Criminal charges were brought against the son of an OPP officer and the families of those involved will never be the same again."
Government Orders
That was the evidence we got in front of our committee.
The aim of gun control is not to affect the hunters and the sports shooters. It is first of all aimed at criminals. It is also aimed at people who do not store guns safely, who do not look after their guns, whose teenager grabs the gun in a fit of depression and commits suicide. We heard evidence after evidence and witness after witness about this matter. There were 1,100 cases of that type in Canada last year alone. This is what gun control is aimed at.
We are trying to stop the Marc Lepines of the world, people who are deranged or unfit to have a gun. We are trying to implement some screening process. That is why this legislation asks for two witnesses and a photograph before issuing a firearms acquisition certificate. There is this need in Canada for gun control.
I want to deal with a number of matters. People have said: "Gun control does not work". The fact is that it does. It saves lives. It is a public health and safety issue in Canada.
They say that this bill is unfair, ineffective and an infringement on their sporting rights. It seems to me that this is a very modest provision in the law and I will come back to this.
People say the problem lies with criminals using illegal guns but as I said, 1,400 Canadians die each year from gun wounds. Over 60 per cent are killed with rifles and shotguns. A great number of them are legally owned. We are talking about 100 murder cases.
It is said that one-third of Canadian voters own guns so they better listen. In fact about 2.2 million Canadians own guns and few of these people will be adversely affected by this legislation. Canadians by and large support greater gun control.
We need to look at further measures. We need to register in this country rifles and shotguns so we know where they are, so we know what happens when they are stolen. That is possible to do. Why can we not do it? We need some controls on the sale of ammunition. Why can we not do that?
Legitimate owners, hunters and shooters need not be concerned about that. This would be a good regime. We need real courses in how to use a gun. We should consult

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
some of the gun people in the sporting clubs who could help the government on that matter.
Where are these courses? They were supposed to be here in 1978 but they are not here. The feds and this minister and her provincial counterparts better get their act together and get these courses going.
We should ban military assault weapons. There is no animal in the Canadian woods that you need a military assault weapon to kill. Canadian Eskimos, the Inuit, used to kill polar bears with bows and arrows and spears. Why do we need these kinds of guns? A good hunter will ask you this. These bans and so on are not in the bill.
I want to address just briefly the concerns of some of the gun clubs and rural Canadians. We tried to approach the bill to address some of these concerns as the member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys said. I will give you some examples of what we tried to do in the committee to address these concerns. We tried to get in a really good, safe handling of firearms course. We tried to show some flexibility so that if you were way up in the north the firearms officer would use his discretion to certify competence without a course or a test. We built in some flexibility for rural and northern areas.
We allowed Parliament to review the provisions of some of these regulations on magazine size and so on. If the bureaucracy got out of line parliamentarians could put them back into line.
Every firearms groups called for tougher penalties. My own group, the Port Coquitlam Hunting and Fishing Club called for tougher penalties for criminals. We put tougher penalties in the bill and Liberal and NDP amendments would have put even tougher penalties in the bill if the government would have accepted that.
We tried to clarify the regulations. One of the concerns was what the minister would put in. The people in my area were concerned with the Lee-Enfield weapon. Would that be prohibited? The government said no it would not be and people would still be able to possess it. We clarified that and we put that in the bill.
People who had firearm acquisition certificates had to renew them. We reduced the fee from $50 to $25. Is $25
really that much? It used to be $10 in 1978. We have had inflation since then. Hunters are paying $30,000 for a car or for a truck. They have to put licence plates on the truck and so on. Is it really too much to pay $25?
We allowed FACs to be renewed with an easier procedure for people who have them and there are one million who have them. We tried to deal with all that in the committee.
It seems to me and I said this to the gun club the other day when I spoke in Port Coquitlam: "You have nothing to fear from this bill". After we discussed it they agreed they had nothing to fear from this bill.
I want to conclude by looking at the future. What have we got to address? What are some of the matters that came out of the committee that we have to be concerned with? I do not want to repeat some of the things that were said by my hon. colleague who has gone over the bill. I will tell you one thing that really concerns me. I do not think the Minister of Justice understands this. Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the members who are speaking would speak outside. It would be helpful to me.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member does have the floor. If we could have a little more attention I would appreciate it. The hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam has the floor and I would like to listen to his speech too if I may.

Mr. Speaker, I am trying to deal with this matter. It is a technical one and came up in the course of our hearings. I think the House should be concerned about it. It is this. There is nothing in the bill that addresses the growing proliferation of handguns in our cities. The hon. member touched on this.
I proposed an amendment as suggested by numerous groups to limit the duration of a registration certificate for a restricted weapon, and that is basically a handgun, from a lifetime to five years. At least you would have to renew this certificate. That was rejected by the government.
What are restricted weapons? They are handguns, semi-automatic firearms with shorter barrels, automatic weapons grandfathered before 1977 and weapons declared by cabinet order to be restricted weapons. By far
November 6, 1991

the largest group is handguns. How many handgun certificates were given out?
The minister says: "Well, we do not have to worry because these are already restricted". However we received two disturbing pieces of evidence. One was from the customs people. They said that guns are flowing across the border and they cannot stop them. The second disturbing piece of evidence came from the police, like the metropolitan Toronto Police and other police forces. They are saying: "We are getting more and more applications, legal applications, for restricted weapons, namely handguns". There were 33,000 in 1986, 37,000 in 1987 and 46,000 in 1990. Metro police said that figure is growing by three times this year.
Who can get one of these handguns? You can get one if you say it is for the protection of your life, if you say it is for use in your lawful occupation, if it is for use in target practice, or if you are a genuine gun collector.
You can buy a "dirty Harry" gun in Toronto now, a magnum. You can say you are a gun collector, or you say you need it for your own protection and you can get a restriction. That is really going on. We are going to need new legislation to deal with this or we are going to need tougher laws to deal with this. What we are seeing in our cities is absolutely shocking.
Now I want to get back to the original story I told about the kid in Brooklyn and how Canada is different. We have to protect ourselves from becoming a gun culture. Once it gets into the minds of Canadians, especially in the big cities-and I say this to some of the rural people who have had some concerns-that they need a gun to protect themselves they are going to go out and apply to get legal guns. They are also going to get illegal guns to protect themselves. The general population, not just the criminals, is going to start turning Canada into a gun culture like the United States. They are going to have a gun to protect themselves, to settle an argument and so on. This is my great concern.
I want to also touch on something my colleague from Cape Breton said and it is that gun control is a woman's issue. Women by and large are proportionately the victims of guns. We had to fight this in committee and we
Government Orders
eventually came to understand that this was a real problem.

The massacre at the Ecole Polytechnique put the issue of firearms and violence against women at the forefront. This issue is far from new to Canadians. Sixty per cent of all murder victims are killed in a family setting. Most of the time, their attacker used a gun or rifle.

We have a lot of evidence, especially from the province of Quebec, that women were affected, specifically in family violence. This is in fact a real concern.
We have to thank-and I see the member here and I think he would agree with me-not only the politicians who did work but a group of people led by Miss Wendy Cukier. She took time out from her job and tried to organize, with very little money, Canadians across the country. She was joined as well by Ms. Heidi Rathjen, who went to great lengths to fight for effective gun control.
The member for Cariboo-Chilcotin entered into a dialogue with them, and it was really something to watch. He invited them to his constituency and so on. Today when the Constitution committee is having so many problems and the country seems to be falling apart, the people in Montreal who were especially affected by the massacre-we were all affected by the massacre at l'Ecole Polytechnique-were out talking to the people in Toronto, in Vancouver and in Cariboo-Chilcotin. Something wonderful was happening.
Canadians were all talking to each other and they were sharing something in common. Mr. Speaker, if you give me a chance I will end by saying that Canadians generally want effective gun control. This bill is the first step. The struggle goes on. We have a lot to do. I do not think that legitimate hunters and shooters have been injured by this bill at all and I think we can live with the bill. We should all work together in the future again to get more effective gun control and make Canada different and unique, as one of the most prosperous and most humanitarian, tolerant and safest countries in the world.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my friend from Port Moody-Coquitlam for the very good work he did on the committee and for the help he has been to all members in bringing forward this legislation.
I know he feels that he had some very good amendments that were not accepted. It is unfortunate but certainly he did everything he possibly could. I certainly join with him in paying tribute to those two ladies who, along with Mrs. Suzanne Laplante-Edward, worked tirelessly on behalf of gun control. They did a marvellous job and are to be commended. I do not know where we would be had they not made the effort they did.
On his visit to the gun club in Coquitlam he was able to see that once properly told about the provisions of the legislation the members were agreeable a lot that was in the legislation.
I wonder if he feels that a lot of the objection to the legislation is because many gun owners have not been told exactly what is in this bill or had the bill properly explained to them. They are getting this information from various groups.

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is right. I tried to lay out what the bill did. I did not hide my feelings. I am for strong gun control and I said that. The members were asking questions and they voiced their concerns.
As MPs we have an obligation in the future to gun clubs and hunters and so on to make them well aware of the regulations. There is a provision in this bill to get them referred to a committee. I wonder if that is a mechanism for delay but I am open and we will see how it works. We are going to see how it works. They say no. I think we have an obligation to make it work. We have to take the regulations and show the gun club people and take their concerns to the Firearms Advisory Board being set up to advise the minister or bring it to the appropriate House of Commons committee when the regulations come down. I think that is really important.
The member did pay tribute to numerous people. He added the name of Mrs. Edward. What can I say? I think we are all aware that Mrs. Edward appeared, with great courage. When we dealt with her there was a certain moral authority she has in this issue. We were all affected by that and it influenced all of us in dealing with the bill.
I would like to say again how courageous Mrs. Edward has been to come back from what must have been a horrible time after the death of her daughter in Montreal at l'Ecole Polytechnique de Montreal and work with the committees in the House of Commons and with the members. She was here this week. I think she is still here today and tomorrow. I know she will not give up until we get a bill. She would like a stronger bill, but at least we are going to get a bill and she has had a lot to do with that.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not an expert, but I think that for all practical purposes, firearms should not exist. In the United States and in many other countries where they are allowed, firearms simply generate violence. When it comes down to it, I am
November 6, 1991

not in favour of abolishing firearms in this country first thing tomorrow morning. Elowever, if we look at what is happening, especially in our big cities, if we look at what has been happening in Montreal in recent years, we see that violence is increasing. We also see reople involved in the drug trade using weapons for all kinds of reasons. In Montreal, armed robbery is the rule, and I am thinking of convenience stores and gas stations.
There has been an increase in armed robbery in all kinds of small businesses, and since the police can't be everywhere at once, owners of small shops decide to take justice into their own hands. In Montreal a few weeks ago, the owner of a jewelry store on Saint-Elubert was killed by a robber because he tried to resist.
If we give people too much freedom to possess firearms, violence will increase. I don't think firearms serve any purpose. I don't have guns, my wife and children don't either, and we can live quite happily without. If people were not entitled to possess firearms, policemen would not need them, no one would need them, and we could get along quite well without.
I am not saying we should go as far as that first thing tomorrow morning, but it should be one of our goals, so that some day there will be no more firearms except to defend our borders, for national defence and for special brigades in exceptional circumstances. Otherwise, I think firearms should not even exist in our society.

speakerposition: Speaker pro tempore
speechtext: I believe that was just a comment. Are there further questions or comments? Does the hon. member want to reply?

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the short speech by the hon. member for Quebec, and I would like to tell him there is still a difference between Canada and the United States. Canada is far less violent than the United States. As I said earlier, we heard from a number of mayors, including the mayors of Montreal, Lennox-ville, Vancouver, Edmonton, Hamilton, Winnipeg, Regina, Burnaby, Nepean and Ottawa in fact, from all over the country. These mayors favour stricter gun controls, and I agree, We have firearms in this country, but as I said earlier in my speech, we had to build Canada,

francophones and anglophones together, without firearms. That is why we live in a country that is less violent than other countries, and I hope we will be able to keep it that way.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in the debate this evening.
This week we are seeing a number of pieces of legislation in which my constituents have certainly had a very strong interest. The amendments to the Corrections Act, the Young Offenders Act, the Extradition Act and the firearm legislation are all issues of great concern to residents of my riding and of course other areas of Canada.
The firearms bill is one in which I have had a strong interest because my constituents and I believe that prevention is an important part of the package of reforms necessary to deal with crimes against the person.
I am supporting this bill not because I believe that it is perfect and cannot be improved but because I believe it is progress on this issue. The process has been a difficult one in producing this legislation. It has meant that many members of our caucus have had to compromise, including myself.
I would like therefore to thank those members of our caucus and indeed the members of the other parties who have participated, who have risen above parochial concerns and who have made an effort to understand the issue, to deal with it in a responsible way and to provide good and effective legislation in this area.
I also want to join in thanking the community and thanking Canadians for gun control, in particular Wendy Cukier, Heidi Rathjen and Suzanne Laplante-Edward who have made an enormous contribution of time and effort and indeed a personal financial contribution. I believe they have played a very key role in this issue by monitoring the committee, by going out to other Canadians and by informing members of Parliament. I think in particular of Suzanne Edward and her contribution in the calling of all the members of Parliament and the lobbying that she has done personally. In getting over her own personal tragedy, she has indeed made a tremen-

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
dous memorial to her daughter's death. I feel that she has made meaning out of that very tragic event.
I very firmly believe that people throughout Canada do not want a proliferation of powerful weapons capable of firing bullets in rapid succession for extended periods of time. They do want a system established which ensures that people who do own guns are competent, careful and respectful of the rights of others, and that is the issue.
Polling data overwhelmingly indicate the broad support of Canadians for stringent gun control. In my own party 72 per cent of the delegates at our convention this summer voted for stringent gun control. There is no significant split between urban and rural Canadians on this issue.
A Gallup poll sponsored by Safeguard attempted to confuse Canadians by asking them to choose between the alternative of severe penalties for criminal misuse of weapons and control over ownership. Canadians do not need to do that and have not really fallen for that at all. Canadians know that both are possible and both have been indicated as being good ideas that are supported by all Canadians. I think this week of legislation as well as this bill clearly illustrate that point.
Stricter sentencing, better enforcement of the laws and a more streamlined justice system are all important components and improvements that must be proceeded with as is clearly evident in these initiatives.
Tomorrow I am looking forward to the response of the government to the report which the subcommittee on the status of women produced entitled The War Against Women. There are many recommendations in that report which again address the issue of prevention of violence against women. Of course many of them also would apply to men.
There seems to be a supposition among many of the people opposed to this kind of legislation that all gun owners are legitimate gun owners simply because they have acquired their guns legitimately. I think that must be laid to rest.
In 1990, 197 or 30 per cent of the homicides committed in Canada were shootings. Some 243 or 37 per cent of the homicides that were committed by a spouse or
common law partner, and 50 per cent of those were with guns. Clearly those who are committing the worst crimes in our society are not necessarily by any means-in fact farm from it-people who are illegitimate gun owners. They also have a dismal safety record as has been mentioned many times: 1,100 suicides per year and several hundred accidents. If one compares the number of deaths produced by guns in this country with the number of deaths produced by automobiles, one-third the number of deaths are caused by guns. Gun owners are a far smaller proportion of the population, probably less than 10 per cent.
My particular community has had a tremendous experience in the last while with the use of guns. It has really made us all think very carefully about the use of guns in our community. In 1987 eight of the 60 homicides involved guns. In 1990 up until September, and the number is still growing, 28 of the 68 homicides so far have involved guns. In 1987 we had 367 robberies of small business with shotguns. In 1990 that number was 1,075. My sister's bank was held up, so it hits people personally. They know people who have experienced this kind of abuse of firearms.
In 1991 the police estimate that 1,400 robberies will take place, given the current rate. These are appalling numbers that strike fear into the hearts of many people, particularly when one lives a concentrated community. I think it is perhaps one of the differences between urban and rural people. We experience crimes as if they were next door to us because of the closeness of the community-
When one looks across Canada, Toronto is one of the safest places to live. We are a way down at number 15 in terms of the homicide rates in a census of metropolitan areas. Regina and Saskatoon clearly lead. Apparently the farther west we go those homicide rates rise.
I believe that is because people are spread out. They do not realize that the per capita figures are very poor. Because we are concentrated we are much more aware of it.
I also think that there is a mentality problem. The people in metropolitan Toronto-and I say this as someone who has experienced government in metropolitan Toronto since 1972-believe in the efficacy? of legislation and the efficacy of our police force. We believe very

November 6, 1991

strongly in law enforcement and in attempting to prevent problems in our society. There is a strong reliance on the educational system and a large amount of money spent on it and similarly on the police force. Our costs for policing are the highest in Canada, and I do not think anybody wants those costs cut. Many communities across Canada have similar beliefs.
I think that is one of the distinguishing characteristics between Canada and the United States. It is the belief that we can change behaviour, that we can have an effect. That is something that we recognize as very healthy in society.
We hear arguments that criminals will always be able to get guns. I do not think that is necessarily true. I believe we can limit them. Indeed right now they do not have to get illegal guns because they can go in and purchase guns themselves or they can steal them from other homes. Frequently the charge of illegal possession of a firearm is the only charge the police can make. The police want this legislation and they want even stronger legislation.
On magazine restrictions, this is an area in which there has been a great amount of compromise. I think people who oppose this legislation should feel that there has been a great attempt to accommodate the legitimate interests of hunters and of sporting enthusiasts.
Clearly the exemption around rim fire magazines is one that would allow people such as the hon. member for Crowfoot and hunters to continue to shoot rabbits and gophers as much as they would like. I know my own brother says if you shoot a deer with more than two bullets, it is not worth eating. My brother never puts more than two bullets into his gun. I think the real hunters out there are not going to be disturbed by this at all.
In addition there are not really serious problems with the gun club people. I agree with the comments made by the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam about the proliferation of these gun clubs and my family is certainly very familiar with these.
We have made great progress with this bill. I think that many of the people who started out with the "I am all
Government Orders
right Jack attitude" have learned and have compromised. We have come to something that I think is appropriate. I think that initial attitude has been overcome in many circumstances.
We as a society have a history and a culture of caring. We also have confidence in our law enforcement agencies and I think that Canadians care about their neighbours.
