First of all I want to compliment the hon. member for Don Valley North. I appreciated her speech. I believe that she and I have approached this issue from about as far apart as one could start. Through the parliamentary process and the party process, we have come up with a bill that is a national bill and in the interest of Canada.
She says she has compromised and has not received all that she would like to have in the bill. That is true for those who might represent a different part of Canada.
I want to say that there is another political party on the scene. Many gun owners are looking to them as a refuge. I speak of the Reform Party. Two aspects of its party policy are free votes and referenda. Anyone who thinks they would like to join the Reform Party to get what they want should note that if this issue was put to referendum most of the guns would be abolished from this country.
A referendum never looks after the minority. Referendum always gives winner take all and the majorities win. Those in western Canada had better recognize quickly that they are not the majority. On the question of a free vote in the Flouse of Commons, my hon. member for Don Valley East and ourselves who might have held a

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
different opinion have come together and have worked on a long, long, hard process. We made amendments and changes, worked on it and came to a national Canadian position.
I rose because I think we exemplify a divergence of views that have come together in the interests of Canada. But put this in its first stage to a free vote and those on either end of the issue would have lost, particularly the gun owners of Canada. They should be appreciative of this system. This is the system that respected it.
I want to thank the hon. member for Don Valley North for being a part of the system that helped all of Canada, including those for which she in the original stage may not.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Don Valley North, if she would like to rebut.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that comment. Certainly I appreciate the spirit with which the hon. member has addressed the issue. I think it clearly shows that we are people who will compromise. We are thinking of Canada not just our own little local area.
With respect to your comments about the Reform Party, yes, I find their position on this issue to be very, very un-Canadian, as I do on many issues. I know for example in my community all they need to get is about a thousand votes because we have very small margins and that would mean that a Liberal would win in my particular area.
Quite clearly we have a lot to fear from the Reform Party. But I find that when I really talk to these people about this issue and they really understand the complexity of the issue and the importance of prevention, they realize that what we have done as a government is produce something that is worth while. It is a good piece of legislation that accommodates and meets the needs of Canadians. That is what government is all about.
It is not about selecting one particular little viewpoint that a particular group has. It is about considering and accommodating minority views and producing legislation that is Canadian in total.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it was mentioned but we are sharing our 20-minute period in the interests of trying to get more people on the record.
Seeing as I have had the privilege or opportunity to have worked with this gun legislation for nearly a year now, I think I have said just about everything I would want to say. I think I have heard most of the things I want to hear about gun legislation.
We are all interested in seeing the results of this hopefully effective legislation. It will in fact increase the safety of Canadians from coast to coast, in rural as well as in urban areas.
It has been a very interesting experience for me. We have heard a number of people in the House today talk about the fact that although we came from different parties and diverse viewpoints when we began this debate, there has been a coming together of the people on the committee. As we came to understand the issues better and the points of view of other people, we started to find common ground. It has been fascinating.
We have watched the coalition for gun control-they have been mentioned several times, Wendy Cukier and Heidi Rathjen-and have seen them blossom if you wish. They became the focal point for the lobby groups interested in fighting for more effective gun control.
What was extremely interesting to me about these ladies and the people they represent is that they never tried to take extreme positions. They were always interested and tolerant of the points of view of others. As a result I found myself not only able to work with them, but I found them to be extremely beneficial to the process.
Although they did not tend to coalesce in the same way there were also many witnesses who came to us from the responsible gun users, people who were not used to making presentations on a national level, especially in Ottawa. Many people were very uncomfortable with it but they and their groups at local levels and at national levels did pull together their positions and did contribute significantly to the process.
I have mentioned members from the various parties who have spent so long with us and my colleague from British Columbia. I can assure you that when we started this process we did not see eye to eye on very many things. In fact when we finished the process we probably did not see eye to eye on a lot of things, but I can assure you that we do have a far better appreciation of why we believe what we do. I am actually confident that if given a
November 6, 1991

little more time we might even have the member for Port Moody-Coquitlam able to not only understand the gun users and their communities, but in fact able to probably find the common ground and compromises that are necessary.
In particular, I recall that late one evening in committee meetings when we were resolving some of the amendments that that member, my colleague from British Columbia, did in fact join the committee on one of my amendments. I did appreciate the fact that he took the effort to understand and to join together with us on what I consider was a major achievement to the bill.
The process ended up identifying the problems. Surprisingly, most people would agree. There was not too much difference from anybody as to the fact that the criminal use of firearms had to be and should be addressed.
There is the recognition of what I will call the "crazies", the mental disorders, the people who are performing these horrendous crimes that we read about not only in Canada but in other parts of the world, especially in the United States.
We heard from witnesses who brought home to us some of the tragic events of accidents. We heard about violence in the home which is an unfortunately increasing phenomenon. It is so depressing to me and to so many other Canadians, the increasing incidents of young people and the suicide situation.
Of course, the committee was charged with these issues. It did its best to try to address what it is that we can do in our gun control legislation that will in fact have an impact on some of these tragedies.
It is in trying to forge the solutions that I think we tended to have the greatest difficulty. I am going to try to explain why. Many people have said: "What is it about your constituents, this gun community that you represent that is so different? Why would they be opposed to this gun legislation?"
First off, I want to point out that they really are not that much different. I will try to briefly run through a questionnaire that I sent out to my constituents. My constituents, for those who are not aware, are from
Government Orders
Cariboo-Chilcotin, 60,000 square miles in central British Columbia who are guides, outfitters, ranchers from very remote areas.
They are people with a high percentage who are hunters, fishermen and gun users who are as comfortable with having guns in their day-to-day life as people in the city seem to be comfortable with what I consider to be a horrendous experience every day driving to work on freeways.
In that riding that I represent, the constituents responded, and I will give the results of only those who have guns. Those are the ones who you would expect would be opposed to this legislation.
On my question of should there be restrictions on military and paramilitary weapons, in Cariboo-Chilcotin the gun owners responded in excess of 70 per cent saying: "Yes, there should be restriction". When we talk about: "Should there be safe storage and safe transport", the gun owners in particular said: "Yes". I could go on with the question.
They will show that the people in the Cariboo are not really any different than the other parts of Canada in what they want to see achieved. In the methods that we use, that is where the difference comes in. It is in the sense that they have the feeling, as lawmakers especially here in Ottawa but representing in particular the majority of the people across the country who live in the major cities are prepared to impose heavy handed legislation that would affect them, their lives and their property.
I believe that much of their fear is unwarranted. It is a principle that I have been fighting for throughout the last 10 months to try to ensure that when we are coming up with what we think are solutions to this violence in society, we are always cognizant of the minority of the people in this country who are gun owners, but the vast majority of them are law-abiding and responsible and they want to play a positive role in this process, they do not want to be driven out.
I want to thank again the people who have worked with us so co-operatively, not only within the House but again the witnesses whom we heard from Nova Scotia through to British Columbia. I share with many members of the House that this is one of those pieces of legislation

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
where each one of us who worked on it can say we may not have made a dramatic difference in Canada but we have made a little bit of a difference and it will be seen in the years to come.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to put my question to the hon. member for Cariboo-Chilcotin.

I understand the member represents a gun community, to use his own words, where it is part of their livelihood, and this community represents what is good about owning guns, from the survey he has made. They are against, for example, paramilitary guns and so on, and they are for some form of gun control. I congratulate him and congratulate his community for this especially since they are in an area of the country where the use of guns is a way of life.
I know the member to be reasonable, and he suggests that there is a compromise that has found. My question is this. Given that there were in 1988 1,400 deaths through gun fatalities, in the United States alone 34,000, and given that the regulations we will be bringing in later, I have a concern that we seem to be missing the point here. It is sort of like the urban area versus the rural area, with people who think that anyone who owns a gun is not a correct or a proper person. I think perhaps we are missing the point by forgetting the incident at Ecole Polytechnique and the incident at l'Assemblee nationale, and you referred to crazies, or, to use your words, crazies or people with mental disorders. Following incidents or occurrences or great events that we see that make national and international news-people going into a comer market and shooting a great number of people, or into a school and shooting down a great number of students, or going to a hamburger joint and shooting everyone in sight-we discover that these people had mental problems.
Should there not be a registry of people who have done time in a mental institution. It is easy to make a check in a community, in most residential areas, but in downtown areas of big municipalities it is quite difficult because neighbours do not know each other. You may get cases of people who have been institutionalized and are possibly manic depressives. Are they not the type of
person who will go and buy a gun and will probably shoot themselves or go out and attack the world, as it were, because they feel the world is against them? Should there not be a registry of these people where the police would check into this and perhaps, just perhaps, we could prevent cases like Ecole Polytechnique or the sad event at l'Assemblee nationale?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
I would like to thank my colleague from Carleton-Gloucester.
The committees and the members working on them have spent a long time trying to wrestle with what to do about the people in society who are committing these atrocious crimes.
It is a terribly difficult one to address, but there is one thing that we all agree is necessary. Right now anybody can walk in to a gun store and, with a limited amount of time, very little screening compared to what we have put in the ground, is able to buy a very high-powered rifle. In fact, once they have the certificate, they can order them from a mail catalogue. They can get them half a dozen at a time.
It is what I call the proliferation of and far too easily obtainable high fire power weapons. That is something that we can address. Even in the gun communities a high percentage of the people will say yes, we do and we can address it. The first thing we have to do in that is to ensure that there are no more of these weapons coming into the country and being sold.
The more difficult problem is, how do you address those that are now there. In many cases many of these have been bought by responsible law-abiding people, hopefully for collections.
Are they registered?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
First off, we are talking about what we can do about them, and that is trying to reduce the proliferation of these kinds of weapons. In terms of trying to control the people themselves, we have done several things in that area. Anybody who is going to get a firearms acquisition certificate in the future will have to pass a competence test. They are going to have to go to a gun club in the community that they live and be able to demonstrate that they know how to handle their gun. The person responsible for that is going to have to sign
November 6, 1991

off that this is somebody they feel is responsible in having a gun.
In many cases, people with the kinds of problems the member is talking about will not pass that test. Further to that, the firearms acquisition officer will be meeting with these people and his responsibility is to check into the references and into the background of the individual.

Mr. Speaker, of the many debates I have heard in this House, of the many bills that are hotly controverted before finally passing, I do not think I have ever heard one where there has taken place in the House so much congratulations of one point of view of the other point of view about how accommodating they have been, how much they have come to see each other's point of view, how happy they are with the compromise that has been achieved.
I cannot comment on the process that led to this bill being before us today in its present state because I was not a part of it. I was not on the committee. I have been justice critic of our party in the past. I have been a minister responsible for gun control in the past, but as it happens, I took no part in the process that brought this bill before us tonight. So I cannot judge, as all those speakers before me have done in congratulating each other, what a wonderful process they enjoy together.
I can look at the bill, the bottom line, and say that I am very disappointed in this bill and that I think much more could have been done to save lives in this country with a stronger bill. I heard the leading speaker for the NDP say something in particular that disappointed me. He said that the process of gun control has just begun because now we have to make sure that this bill, as full of discretions and loopholes as it is, is applied in a wellmeaning way in favour and not against gun control.
I hope he is right. I hope more will be done within the framework of this bill to make it tougher to obtain guns, but I certainly disagree with his observation that we have just begun the battle for gun control in this country. I have news for him. Gun control in Canada began before Canada was formed in this part of British North America. Gun control occurred when the Klondike was opened, for example, where Mounties stood at the stations, at the entry points into the mining fields, took
Government Orders
rifles and guns away from the prospectors who were coming in, broke off the triggers, gave them back their weapons and sent them in to look for gold.
In the whole of the opening of the Klondike in the history of our country, not one murder occurred, not one person was shot. In California when the gold rush occurred and the opening occurred, there were a dozen murders some days. If my recollection is correct, there was never a day when someone was not murdered.
Let us not think that this is a country with a lower incidence of gun related crime because we are better people than the Americans are. That is not true. We are not better people. But we have had a commitment to gun control. We have over the years, going all the way back to then and even before, used the power of the government to reduce the amount of fire power in Canadian society.
I know that there are what one could honestly call two solitudes in this country on the subject of guns. Some people say it is rural-urban. That is a generalization which I think is right maybe in general but not at the fringes. Timing to these two solitudes, there is one very large group of people in our country who feel more comfortable when there is a gun around, loaded. It makes them feel that they are in a better position to make their livelihood, to protect their family, to protect their property and their households. There is another solitude of people who feel the opposite, who feel nervous when there is a gun in their house in a drawer up on the second floor, in a locked cupboard, in a locked safe, loaded or unloaded, and there are children around. They are more nervous than when that gun is not there.
They talked about a compromise. It is not a compromise. To be honest and blunt about it, it is zero sum gain. One side is winning because more gun controls are being put in, and the other side is losing because more restrictions are being put on a basic freedom.
The question is, and I will take it right out of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms: Are the restrictions that were proposed and rejected and are the restrictions that were proposed and appear in this bill reasonable in a free and democratic society? Was there a justification in real terms for taking away some of the freedom that would be enjoyed if this bill did not go

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
through or, if it had gone further as I would have like, could you justify taking away those freedoms?
I had a very close and intense experience with the gun control measures that were finally implemented in 1987 under the leadership of my colleague, the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace when he was Solicitor General of Canada. I know the bill that he presented to our caucus contained much less gun control than the bill that he brought to cabinet.
I can also tell the House that the bill which came from caucus to the floor of this Chamber in 1976 or early 1977 contained much less gun control than was presented to caucus because politics is the art of the possible. We live in a country that has these two solitudes. One side can make its arguments and the other side can make its arguments, but there has to be some recognition of a variety of points of view in a country as diverse as ours.
What I regret and what I condemn this minister for is not having recognized that she could have seized the opportunity and the events of the last two years to go further than she did. If she had gone further than she did we would have had a better bill. I feel I can categorically defend more gun control by making the very simple point that we have proof in the statistics that resulted from the implementation of the package of my colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace from 1978 that gun control works. The more we control them in rational, reasonable, effective and logical ways, the less people will be killed and the less accidents there will be related to gun use.
It is reasonable in a free and democratic society to do more. This minister had the opportunity because of a number of tragedies that occurred in this country-and I am going to talk about these tragedies because some of them happened in my own riding-to do more and she did not. Being the minister is a heavy responsibility and being the Minister of Justice is a heavy responsibility. There will be murders and there will be gun related crimes and accidents that will occur in the next two years or in the future that would not have occurred if the minister had brought in a stronger bill. It will be on her responsibility that those additional terrible crimes will
occur, because we know that more effective gun control reduces the amount of gun related crimes.
On December 8, 1989, after the murder of 14 women by a man using an automatic weapon, I was given the opportunity to ask questions in the House. I asked the then Minister of Justice if he would bring in I think four, five or six specific changes which if implemented in the law would in my opinion and based on statistics result in fewer gun related crimes in the future and fewer deaths of innocent people. I called for a compulsory waiting period for firearm certificates and a third party character reference. Those are in the bill so I am not saying that this bill does not do something. I am not saying that it should not be supported. Our party, as a matter of fact, is supporting this bill as has already been indicated.
We called for and have received a more secure screening process; the inclusion of a photograph of the permit holder on the firearms acquisition certificate, much like a driver's licence; and raising the fee for the firearms acquisition certificate to make the system selffinancing. I do not know if that low fee is really going to make it self-financing. If it is not, I hope there will be an effort by the government to see the fee raised to cover it. We have also called for the banning of semi-automatic versions of fully automatic weapons, the prohibition of large capacity magazines and the prohibition of military and paramilitary assault weapons.
As I indicated in my question, which had a lot of discussion in our caucus before I asked it, and as I am indicating today, we could go much further. I think the time would have been right to go further and we would have had enough national understanding. I am not saying national support because I know there are people who would prefer not to have any gun control, but I think at the moment we are in, in the history of our country, we would have had a national understanding of going further. The minister blew it in the sense of not taking advantage of that opportunity.
My leader called for prohibiting people who were convicted of violent crimes and sentenced to less than 10 years or indictable drug trafficking offences from being able to own a gun, giving judges discretionary power to prohibit gun ownership to anyone convicted of lesser drug trafficking offences involving violence. That type of measure which my leader has urged and which the

minister has rejected would have saved some lives if she had done it.
In my riding of York Centre in Toronto there have been more than 70 crimes committed involving guns just in the last 12 months. I am talking just about my own riding, one out of 300 in Canada. Most of these crimes relate to the activities of gangs and drug trafficking. In July the metro police seized 28 firearms including high handguns in a raid on drug dealers in my riding. In September gun-fire wounded six people at a dance for 500 people in my riding. These facts are compelling reasons for more action on gun control and compelling reasons which would have had a national understanding surely even among the other solitude that feels more comfortable and secure having guns around.
The bill and the policy have the support of our metro council. They have the support of the Toronto Police Association and the Toronto Board of Education. We have had tremendous efforts made by an association which I would like to acknowledge, the Coalition on Gun Control, Wendy Cukier, a Ryerson student from Toronto and Heidi Rathjen from the Ecole Polytechnique where that terrible tragedy occurred, which galvanized public opinion in this country. The government allowed it to go by without doing anything for months and months and then brought forward this veiy politically adjusted bill so satisfactory to so many of the participants in that process.
The bill is supported by the Canadian Police Association, by the Caucus of Big City Mayors representing Canada's largest cities, by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women and by the Canadian Criminal Justice Association, just to name a few. I know that tougher, more effective measures would also have had the approval and even more enthusiastic endorsement of the public of Canada that recognizes our history and the effectiveness of gun control in reducing the mass of weapons in our society and the amount of gun related crime.
I began by expressing my disappointment that the minister and the government of our country have blown an opportunity to move in a direction that history has brought the laws of our country at a time when more could have been done. I submit that more should have been done.
Government Orders
Therefore I support the bill because it takes a little step, but I cannot let the opportunity pass without expressing my regret that it does not take a big step.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to participate in the debate on third reading of Bill C-17. As the last speaker just said in the House, I think that we could go much further with regulations to control firearms in this country.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, a while ago, I was a victim in some sense of the Polytechnique tragedy, because while the killing was going on, I had two sons at that institution. I was here in this House on Parliament Hill and I had a very anxious time from 6 p.m. to 11.30 p.m. as I waited for news of my children. I can tell you that you really have to go through such an experience to understand how one can feel when a mad gunman decides to go on a rampage in a school or a shopping centre, as happened in the Polytechnique tragedy. Mr. Speaker, my wife and I lived through those terrible hours and I think that I will never forget them as long as I live.
There has been similar carnage on other occasions. When I see and hear those who oppose this bill that we are now debating, I think that they do not understand what it is trying to do.
This bill does not seek to take away the right or privileges of collectors or hunters to own firearms. On the contrary, this bill is to protect society. It provides that those who want to get firearms must register themselves and declare those firearms. The bill also prevents those who want to get firearms for purposes other than recreation or sports activities from doing so freely.
I heard several comments on ammunition. Some say that a permit should be necessary to buy ammunition. I fully agree with them. What difference does it make if I go to a store that sells ammunition for firearms and have to show a card confirming that I am an honest citizen who knows how to use firearms and does not want ammunition for evil purposes? I do not feel that this is a breach of my rights as a citizen.
We are discussing this bill today in the House because there is too much violence in the country and on the North American continent.

Government Orders
After the Polytechnique tragedy, I made a speech in the House and asked the then Minister of Justice to pass legislation for controlling firearms and violence on television and in the newspapers.
Mr. Speaker, if you watch TV programs, music programs or video clips closely these days, much of them is violent or incites violence.
So, you can imagine that a 10-, 12- or 15-year-old watching those programs gets ideas that are not too healthy. That young person is already rebelling against society; things are going badly at school; he does not get along with his parents; his girlfriend left him; he has taken drugs on occasion. That young person becomes so mixed up that a television scene can incite him to violence.
I asked the government back then to pass legislation and regulations to limit or eliminate completely this violence on television. I am not necessarily talking about pornographic movies, where violence is directed at women and children.
Some people think they are important and intelligent because they make movies showing violence against children and women, and sometimes men, and they sell those films and hope to become rich.
This is despicable. As civilized human beings and normal citizens, we cannot tolerate such a thing. We should eliminate all that violence. Some will say that here in Canada, it is quite difficult to control what comes from the United States, via satellite and television. I must admit that. But the fact remains that when we discuss a free trade agreement with the Americans or with the Mexicans, we should also put this issue on the table and say: "Listen, where are we going?" After all, the Americans also have a problem with violence.
Why could we not sit down and give this some thought? I am positive, that if only we tried and discuss or negotiate with our American partners and the Europeans as well-since we also pick up European broadcasts-there might be no need to put our picture on an application for a hunting permit. I have nothing against that, mind you, but, as a matter of principle, we are compelled to take drastic measures today in the hope that there will be less violence and fewer people killing
each other or dying at the hands of nitwits who use guns to put their ideas across.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to attempt to explain to my constituents and to all Canadians the situation we have before us tonight in Bill C-17.
This afternoon I had the opportunity to vote on Bill C-17 and I voted against this particular piece of legislation. I would like to explain why.
I think it is important that we try to focus on the facts and on what we want to achieve with this piece of legislation. One of the reasons why I believe very strongly that this particular legislation has the wrong focus and is ineffective legislation is because it focuses on the particular piece of equipment that we call firearms in this country rather than focusing on the crime which exists in the large urban centres and indeed in the rural areas of this country.
I want to deal with aspects of the bill that are missing because again what we have done with Bill C-17 is tinkered around. We have taken a piece of legislation and dealt just with the fringes of the issue.
After the next election I expect to see myself in some other seat, probably over there on the opposite side, dealing with this issue again.
The reason I say that is because we have done a very shoddy job. The NDP has said that this is just the beginning of gun control and we will have to visit it again. I have to agree with that. This is the wrong approach to gun control and that is why we will have to visit it again.
We have not dealt with the fundamental issue which is crime on the street, the individual who is not completely sane and decides to take a firearm or any kind of weapon, such as a bomb which they use very frequently in the British Isles to do carnage to their citizens .We have not dealt with that particular issue.
I thought when I first got involved in looking at gun control that maybe-my colleague who spoke before me in the Liberal Party touched on it very well-it was the wrong time in history to deal with this particular piece of legislation or this particular issue because it became such an emotional issue that we never did take a good look at the facts.
November 6, 1991

It is obvious that we did not take a good look at the facts because the parties made a decision very early in the legislative process to restrict the debate. At second reading we were restricted to having one member from each side talk very, very quickly about the legislation and then it was sent off to a committee.
Then as members of the public will say depending on what side of the issue they are on: "It was railroaded and sent to a special committee called C-80". Once the process was railroaded in this place, members were not allowed to speak and the media got hold of the issue, it took off on a life of its own.
The extremists on both sides came out suggesting that on the one hand for those who were in favour of guns, all the guns would be taken away. We all know that is not a fact. We know that is not what this bill will do, and those of us who tried to maintain some sort of rational process during this whole debate tried to explain that.
There is the other side of the issue where it is the opinion, to which there is a right, that society should have no firearms at all. Unfortunately living in a large rural country that has grown through the process of firearms from day one that is impossible and it will never happen in this country. At least that is my own firm belief.
What happened in the media when it took on a life of its own was that all of a sudden every single individual who ever was aware of an incident where people were killed or there was a suicide with a firearm, there were all sorts of tragedies out there, and out they came.
I never saw so many media reports about guns. I have never heard of so many in my whole life. This is something which appalled my constituents simply because legitimate gun owners do not run around with machine guns. First of all, automatics are already prohibited in this country.
I want to bring a little bit of sanity to this debate and a little bit of respect for what both sides are trying to deal with.
I understand what the urbanites and those who do not believe in firearms are talking about. Those individuals are talking about the unsafe feeling they have of living in
Government Orders
the city and the fact that there are statistics that will show that crime is much higher in the urban centres than in the rural areas. They do not feel comfortable because of the kinds of stories they see in the media every night.
I thought that what we would do when we got to Bill C-80 before it became C-17, as a member of that committee, we would deal with those particular issues. While it quickly became apparent that members were prepared to deal with the issue of Bill C-80, they were being told by the justice department that that was not the strategy they wanted.
For example I want to deal with the areas that we talked about very extensively at the very beginning of the whole issue of gun control. Let me just deal with the first paragraph of this particular committee's recommendations.
It is very important to realize that the committee had a different focus than the justice department. Let me read one quick quote:
The special committee believes that there must be established a mandatory competency and safety course the successful completion of which would be a condition to obtaining an FAC for the first time.
The committee recognizes the overwhelming support for the implementation of such an educational component and the acquisition process where virtually all witnesses who appeared before us.
Mr. Speaker, one of the things you notice is not in the bill is a mandatory training program. That was something agreed to by all sides. Everyone thought that if you wanted to have legitimate gun owners in this country, people who understood the law, who were going to understand how to deal with their firearms safely, the first thing to be done as Canadians would be to educate.
I suggested that all along. The first thing the minister should do is to tell her provincial counterparts who were also making presentations as the offices of the attorney generals were that they felt this was a good piece of legislation, that they simply allow us as Canadians, as members of Parliament, to pass the piece of legislation that puts in regulation, mandatory training, and allows the federal government through the advisory council to put in that particular training regime which will meet the needs of all Canadians.
That never got done. That is not in the bill, and that is something everyone felt strongly about under C-80.

Government Orders
We also talked about something that was very important and something that the committee felt it should deal with because the perception is that most Canadians believe, and rightfully so, that the courts are not doing justice to the criminals who are brought before them as it relates to firearms. The committee again said that it felt that the idea of plea bargaining was being used on most occasions instead of having mandatory sentencing for those who were using a firearm during a crime. The committee recommended that we increase to three years the minimum for a first offence and five years for subsequent offences.
Again, the minister decided under section 85 not to deal with that at all, that in essence it was working very well. Just about all the members who came forward who were involved in this particular issue in a large way felt very strongly that the process was letting them down, that the judicial system that we have in place now was not dealing with the issue the way it should.
There was another area that I thought we should deal with that I still think we will have to deal with very soon. That is the importation of firearms. You can prohibit whatever you want. Legitimate gun owners will follow that. They will respect the law as they have always respected the law.
One of the things that they will not do, or be able to help you with, is dealing with the criminal element which is buying illegal firearms that are being imported into Canada through the United States because of the difficulties at the border.
Let me read what the president of the customs union said to us on Bill C-80. Ele stated that the Department of National Revenue, Customs and Excise, suffers from staff shortages and inadequate training of customs officers. He suggested that at least 1,000 more customs officers were needed and that all customs officers require more training in regard to Canada's firearms laws.
It became very evident in talking to customs officers- and I happen to have a riding that is bordering on the United States and we have customs officers there-that one of the things they made very clear is that first of all they have no knowledge of the firearms legislation that we have now. Never mind the regulations that we are
going to be putting in under Bill C-17. They were also trying to tell us that they could not see themselves being able to justify dealing with the illegal importation of firearms because of the lack of staff.
If we are going to be serious about dealing with these kinds of things, and be able to feel comfortable in this place telling Canadians that yes, indeed we have put a good piece of legislation in, we should look at the obvious problems that are out there. I have just named a couple of problems. That is, one, the fact that we are going to start prohibiting and restricting certain firearms is not going to deal with the issue that is out there on the street now.
I want those who are listening to us tonight to realize that the situations that happen such as the one involving Marc Lepine in Montreal just in the last year or so are not going to disappear because of Bill C-17. I think everyone has to be very serious and straightforward enough to admit that. There is no possible way we have the ability to stop madmen like that from doing things that they are going to do.
If we remove the firearm that Mr. Lepine used which the government is proposing to do under this legislation, he would have used something else. I am not suggesting that because of that we should not have gun control. What I am suggesting is that we have effective gun control.
I am one of those who believe that this is all a smoke and mirrors game. This particular piece of legislation will not have the effects that the minister has suggested it will or that members opposite have suggested or the majority of the members in this place. I for one think that when we get the opportunity to deal with gun control again that we should look at it in its factual sense, not to let the emotions run wild the way they did in committee, where people were screaming and yelling at each other because they did not agree with their opinion and there was this myth created that there is this tremendous gun lobby out there that is pressuring people to allow guns to be worn on each hip.
That is not what Canadians are all about. Canadians in this country are very sensitive, very caring and very loving people. They are also very law abiding. They are also very carefree and very capable of honouring their commitments.
November 6, 1991

I sense the members are saying that if they continue to restrict the legitimate gun owner or the law abiding citizen that they are going to deal with the issue of crime on the street.
I would like to know from the minister how much money it is going to take to administer this piece of legislation. I would like to take that money and pump it into Toronto to help the people of Toronto fight crime. I imagine it will be in the millions to deal with that, not to mention the millions of dollars of firearms that are going to have to be destroyed under this piece of legislation through the amnesty provision.
All that personal property is all for naught because we simply have not dealt with the issue that is before the people of Canada today.
I was a very strong proponent of mandatory gun training and I still am. I believe if you want to change the views of Canadians, you have to educate them. We simply have done it the cheap way. We will continue to reduce, reduce and reduce the amount of fire power out there, hoping that will rectify the problem. Unfortunately, it will not.
I attempted to put an amendment before this House on mandatory training. The impression that is being left by the media, the Department of Justice and the minister is that we do have training now. We do not. The fact remains that the attorneys general of this country have to approve the whole process before it comes into existence. It is no different than in 1978.
What happened in 1978? We are still waiting for that infamous agreement that the minister suggested we were going to get.
The other day I mentioned a particular poll. I am not one for polls. A government should not be run by polls because it is just a reflection at a certain time of somebody's view. The poll seemed to suggest that Canadians were not looking to us as parliamentarians to restrict legitimate gun owners. They were looking for stronger laws that would deal with the criminal element.
If that is what the minister suggests this piece of legislation does, then I will have to say that I am wrong. I believe very strongly that I am not. Somewhere down the line there will be another situation that will happen such
Government Orders
as happened in Montreal. It is sad to have to say that in this place, but it is a belief I have. Then members in this place will be asked this very simple question by their constituents: "I thought you folks looked after that with Bill C-17". We have not. We have not looked after that one iota.
The other area I want to touch on is something we are still waiting for. I commend my colleague, the critic for justice from Cape Breton-The Sydneys, who asked the Minister of Justice in June if she would be willing to give us an explanation of what the regulations will be. This is a very unusual piece of legislation because most of the issues are dealt with in the regulations. We have no idea, for example, what the definition of a genuine gun collector is going to be. We have no idea what the definition of what safe storage will be. We have no idea what will be prohibited, military, paramilitary, what kind of semi-automatics. All of these are areas that are left to regulation under this particular scenario. We asked the minister quite a long time ago for that explanation. In June she said they were not prepared.
We are now into November and still no regulations and we as members are voting on something that we are not quite sure what the end result will be. The argument put before us is: "That it is perfectly acceptable, because you will get to take a look at those regulations and if you can find 20 members who are not in favour of it, within 30 days, then we will be able to send it to committee. During that whole process you will either vote yes or no and you will not have an opportunity to amend it because it is a yes or no. If it is not yes, you can amend the regulation somewhat". Those are all areas that really concern me as a member of Parliament. Many of my constituents come from rural areas and are avid hunters. They believe that they their use of guns is legitimate and legal in every sense of the word. They are quite prepared to be inconvenienced or restricted if they feel that they are getting legislation that will simply rectify the problem.
But we are not rectifying the problem here. I want to make that very clear to all those who are out there. Because of that I suggest to the government of the day that it take another look at what it has and try to deal with the issues that are so paramount in peoples' minds and that is the criminal element that is using illegal weapons and creating carnage in our society.

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
I thank you very much for the opportunity to bring my views forward. I wish the minister good luck with her bill. I am looking forward to seeing the regulations. That is the area that concerns me, more so than what is in the bill so far. Everything is in the regulation and not in the bill.

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to comment on the hon. member from Kenora-Rainy River's speech. I think it was a very good speech and a very thoughtful one. I want to make just a couple of comments with respect to the bill and the provisions in it.
The member talks about the consensus on the special committee for a training provision. As he well knows, such a provision has been in the Criminal Code since 1978. It is not in this bill because it is already in the Criminal Code. The problem is that it has never been implemented.
When I brought forward my package of firearms measures I made it very clear that there were three parts to it. The first part is the creation of a Canadian Advisory Council on Firearms to deal with such things as the question of how to have a training program. That had been in the legislation at that time for 12 years. I wanted to bring it into fruition and in fact I will be ready very shortly to table those regulations in the House of Commons.
There are other powers that are now in the Criminal Code such as the power to prohibit any kind of firearm. So in terms of defining military and paramilitary firearms governments have had that power for a very long time.
What I indicated when I brought my package forward was that I was going to get the very best advice that I could from a cross-section of Canadians. It is a regionally balanced, interest balanced advisory council consisting of many people who are in the shooting community, as well as people who are experts in the area of public health and law. They tried to bring together a reasoned range of outlooks to advise me on how to implement those provisions.
So a variety of those things require in fact no new powers.
I want to say to the hon. member that my provision for the House dealing with regulations allowed the House in
fact to veto regulations. At the suggestion of the government Whip that provision was changed to extend or perhaps formalize the consideration of regulations by a parliamentary committee. Even though there has been an amendment that my regulations would go to the justice committee, in fact because of the changes we made to the rules of the House after the McGrath committee report, any standing committee may deal with these regulations when I table them. If the agriculture committee wants to look at them, if the external affairs committee or the finance committee wants to look at them, they may. There is no way that I can or would want to prevent it. It simply means that as a matter of course they will go to the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General.
I will very much look forward to the input of my parliamentary colleagues on those regulations. I hope to be coming forward with a variety of regulations in the very near future.
I think it is important to point out that the criminal law is not the guarantee of no crimes. I think the hon. member makes a very important point but this is not a panacea. This is not going to do away with violence in society. What it does is give to the police, the customs officers and the courts the tools that they need. We have in fact very much increased criminal penalties. We have increased the length of mandatory prohibition orders and a variety of offences to which mandatory prohibition orders apply.
Where I differed with an amendment put forward by that member's party was where some of these orders would have been mandatory, even for relatively minor offences dealing with drug trafficking. I could envision a scene in Yukon or somewhere, where an aboriginal person is convicted of trafficking in a small amount of marijuana and a mandatory 10 year prohibition order I think would probably be considered in most cases overkill. Therefore, the discretion is still there in the courts.
I want to say that I very much respect the hon. member's comments because I think what has been frustrating about this subject is that there has been a polarity of views. I think it is frustrating for responsible firearm users to find that there are some people who think that anyone who owns a firearm is a latent homicidal maniac. That is not true. Similarly there are
November 6, 1991

many people who are firearm owners who do recognize the need for good legislation.
Just the other day I was speaking at the University of Ottawa and a young person spoke to me and said: "I belong to a shooting club. We use handguns. We are in competition shooting and we support your legislation. We know what you are trying to accomplish and we know that our ability to pursue our sport depends upon the confidence of the public in the firearms system".
I believe that we have to continue to evolve. My concern has been to create a legislative framework that is workable, to put into place the training provisions that have been in the statutes for so long, to reassure Canadians that those who have firearms are competent to have them, to create an atmosphere of tolerance, and to create a legislative framework which is truly national. We cannot legislate for downtown Vancouver alone. We cannot legislate for Kenora-Rainy River alone. We have to legislate for the country and that requires balance and co-operation.
I think we have come a long way. There has been an enormous sharing of points of view here. I hope the hon. member will continue to participate in the discussion and to be part of the process because I think it is very important. I just want to say that I think some of his comments were not well taken in criticisms of the bill because it is very easy to look at a piece of legislation and say it does not solve the social problem and therefore we should not have it. It is a contribution. The law and public safety are made up of a mosaic of tiles of legislation, policy and attitudes. This is a contribution, and I hope we will work together to fill in some of those other tiles with our attitudes and our policies that will eventually do away with some of the more outrageous scenarios which have been discussed in the course of this debate.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for her comments. Indeed it is a very difficult piece legislation to debate.
Again I suggest to the House that it is unfortunate that we have to debate it in these kinds of circumstances, as I mentioned, under second reading. I would have loved to have brought my views up at second reading so that they could have been used at the committee or that all members or all Canadians could have looked at the issue in a more factual way instead of allowing it to become so
Government Orders
emotional in that if you voted against a particular piece of legislation that dealt with gun control then as the minister said you were some sort of Rambo who wanted to run around with an AK-47 in the bush chasing a rabbit.
I recall when I saw that cartoon in The Globe and Mail. It really brought home to me just where this whole debate had gone. It had gone astray and it had caused a lot of members on both sides not to speak their mind. It is really quite sad to think that there are members over there and on this side who had a lot to give this whole debate on legislation this country so desperately needs and were not allowed to speak. I would say to the government and to all people who are listening that the next time we get into this issue we should allow everyone to speak their mind freely. Then we will get the kind of legislation that we so desperately need in this country.
I say to the minister that I wish her well with the regulations. I will be around to scrutinize them very carefully because there are some issues in those regulations that if done properly will make this legislation just a bit easier to live with.

Mr. Speaker, I want to tell the hon. member what I learned in the committee and at a lot of hearings. Most Canadians who are killed by guns are not killed by criminals but by people they know. The statistics are overwhelming.
We should focus on criminals, yes, and we do need legislation. I see the minister is in the House. In the future we are going to have to revisit restricted weapons, handguns, as I said in my speech tonight.
I am not quite sure what the member's position is or whether he represents the Liberal Party's position, because I heard from the member from York Centre saying totally the opposite. Does he represent the position of his party? Just in a very brief capsule, if he had a chance to do effective gun legislation, what would he do?

Mr. Speaker, I always welcome the member's foray into the House of Commons. I told him the other night that every time he speaks I gain about 100 votes. I have done real well by this member lately. I probably got re-elected because of his lack of understanding of the whole process of gun legislation and the

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
belief that anybody who happens to have a firearm is innately bad and is someone who cannot be trusted.
I go by the premise that law biding citizens who know their way around the bush of northern Ontario are capable of my respect and vice versa. I would not unduly legislate them to death based on that.
Just let me quickly finish. The member asked whether I represent my party. Obviously if he were in the House today he would have noticed that I was in the minority. My caucus believes that this legislation is better than no legislation at all. I simply think that this is not good enough for the circumstances that we are in right now as Canadians. Therefore I have walked away from following suit with my party even though it hurts me deeply to have to do so.
I think my constituents understand because of the fact that they believe that I am here to represent them first and foremost. That is what I have done here today.

Mr. Speaker, I too am pleased to have a chance to enter into the debate on Bill C-17.
I would just like to thank the member for Kenora- Rainy River as well for his productive comments and a very reasonable and rational approach to this whole idea which in effect is certainly an emotional issue.
Gun control generally makes its way to the top of the agenda due to rising incidents of armed violence, accidental shootings or suicides with guns. I think this is probably no exception to that. These types of extreme actions often evoke equally extreme reactions. We have certainly seen that in committee meetings with special interest groups coming forward. Neither side of the debate is immune to irrational and irresponsible lines of argument.
Too often these are the positions that are heightened through the media. We must seek to present a clear and undistorted picture of firearms control to the Canadian public. In so doing we must first define the general objectives that we believe are consistent in balancing peace, order and good government with the rights of the individual.
To my mind this encompasses three essential points. First, we must acknowledge the genuine concern especially in urban areas with respect to the easy availability
of firearms and their increasing use by unstable and criminal elements in the population. We must also acknowledge the desire of many Canadians to use and own firearms for hunting and for collecting purposes.
Second, I believe that the trust of firearms regulations should be toward more effective regulation of users rather than increased regulation of firearms themselves. There must be stronger enforcement of existing and future regulation with the cost of licensing being borne primarily by firearms users.
Third, there must be a higher priority on the right of Canadians to public safety than on the right to own and use firearms.
Having stated these general objectives we must now apply them to the legislation currently before us. We must ask ourselves: If we enact Bill C-17 will it be respected? Will it be obeyed? Most important, and I think the ultimate question that we need to ask here is: Will it curtail gun related crime?
In short I believe the answer is no. This bill does little in the way of protecting the average citizen. I believe it seriously undermines the freedom of the law biding individual.
Let me outline my misgivings about Bill C-17. As I have just stated, I believe Canadians are more concerned with public safety being the top priority for firearms control rather than the right to own and use firearms. However, this bill all but ignores public safety by way of focusing in on the legitimate users and failing to acknowledge the real threat posed by the criminal element in this country. My comrade beside me has just spoken very eloquently about that.
It would appear to me then that although well inten-tioned the committee has perhaps missed the source of the problem. I just want to congratulate the committee for the months and months of work that it has done. It interviewed countless witnesses.
The use of firearms during the commission of a criminal offence has not been addressed. If the reason for this bill is to combat firearms related crime then it has failed. The theft of firearms has not been adequately addressed. If preventing the theft of firearms by criminals was a significant issue, the Department of Justice would have been better off to make mandatory minimum sentences for this offence rather than penalize legiti-
November 6, 1991

mate gun owners with stringent, anti-theft storage requirements.
The new definition of safe storage is certainly a step in the right direction but we simply cannot put the onus on the owner for protection against theft while ignoring the thief. Weapons are not stolen simply because they are improperly stored. They are stolen because someone other than the owner has intentionally committed a felony. Criminals could not care less about how many locks they have to break in order to access a firearm. This exclusion in the legislation nullifies the impact this bill could have in preventing criminal acts which employ firearms.
The smuggling of firearms has not been addressed. Any criminal worthy of his or her profession is not going to register a firearm before he or she commits a crime. Let us think about this in a logical fashion. Mandatory minimums for smuggling firearms would be helpful in deterring this type of criminal activity, but again there is no provision.
The fact of the matter is that none of the increased penalties in the bill relate to criminals using firearms to commit crimes. Rather, penalties are only applied to those who have been recognized as qualified gun owners who have violated the law in terms of things like storage requirements. Thus there is little in the proposed bill which attempts to control crime committed with guns.
How is this legislation intended to insure public safety? I must submit that it contributes little or nothing in that area. In fact it is difficult to see how this bill will actually lessen the number of guns in Canada or prevent a future massacre and tragedy such as happened at l'Ecole Polytechnique.
The real problem with Bill C-17 is not with its contents but with what has been excluded in addressing criminal activity. That is the problem is not what is in the bill but what has been left out.
That being said, there are some significant steps taken in this legislation which should alleviate some of the fears of ordinary Canadians. I applaud the committee's work with regard to acquisition certificates. It is imperative that stronger enforcement of firearms regulations take place. The new FAC provision is a healthy contribution to that end.
Government Orders
The photograph which is to accompany the FAC, proposed by the justice minister and endorsed by the Canadian Police Association, is an important and logical step toward more effective control. I congratulate them for that.
However that is not to say that the proposed FAC is flawless. In fact there is a major gap in the logic of this bill in that it adds discretion for local firearms officers to certify competence without any course or test. Why would we think to place an unlimited number of restrictions on part of the firearm using population while at the same time allowing others virtually unlimited freedom? It would seem that there are two different standards to be employed in obtaining an FAC. Surely there must be one law applied to all of us.
The bill is therefore not devoid of good ideas. I want to reiterate that. However there are far too many holes in it to provide for effective firearms control while at the same time balancing the rights of individual Canadians. I must say however that some of the amendments proposed by the committee are in keeping with the objectives we should be pursuing. The new fee of $50 for an FAC is consistent with placing the cost of licensing with the firearms users themselves. Those who are not gun owners should not be forced or even asked to subsidize those who do exercise this freedom. In addition, deleting the provision that would have allowed individuals to rent restricted weapons seems a logical extension to effective gun control.
These are both reasonable and intelligent amendments. I think that everyone across the country will certainly recognize that.
However I must express my reservations about a provision which would allow firearms officers to question neighbours, social workers, spouse and family members of anyone who has applied for an acquisition certificate to determine if he or she has a history of violent behaviour. I can certainly understand the rationale behind such an amendment. However I wonder if anyone has put any thought into the consequences that such possible actions might bring.
In small rural communities, in fact where I live, these types of activities would almost certainly cause a great deal of strife and animosity between community members, neighbours and family. It is not inconceivable that such a process would create suspicion between family and neighbours thereby tearing apart the very fabric of that community. Imagine the distrust which would sweep

Government Orders
around a community knowing that some people may have been asked about a particular person.
All this may be done at the whim of the inspector and without any real guidelines for such an action. I hope the House will consider the extent to which individuals may be unduly persecuted in this respect.
These amendments contribute to some of the shortcomings of the legislation but Bill C-17 still remains fundamentally flawed. Many see this as a rural versus urban split. Of course this is a simplistic and stereotyped view.
I have received numerous letters from Canadians outside my rural riding of Beaver River asking me to defeat this bill on the grounds that it does not go far enough in achieving the three objectives I listed earlier.
These people are not uneducated, uninformed, trigger happy killers. They are doctors, lawyers, professional people, working Canadians, men and women. The spectrum is as wide and diverse as the Canadian people themselves. I have received a powerful statement from a female Ph.D at a very prestigious institution in downtown Toronto who writes: "This legislation would be seriously damaging to the legitimate shooting community and would offer absolutely no offsetting benefits to public safety."
This person is an established doctor of psychology, not an uninformed radical. We must therefore acknowledge that this issue concerns everyone and not just a particular set of interest groups whom we have all heard from be they on one side or the other of this issue.
We must strike a balance between the concerns of both rural and urban Canadians. It is my feeling from the correspondence which I have received and the studying that I have done that the bill satisfies virtually no one.
I submit that this bill is unsatisfactory in its present state. It is a patchwork of amendments intended to satisfy various interest groups on both sides of the issue. It therefore ends up falling short of doing what it should do and that is protect the average Canadian. It undermines the democratic process because there is no protection by members of Parliament against Orders in Council or regulations. We have seen that one of the amendments allows for regulations to be taken to committee
but when it cannot be debated openly on the floor of the Commons, then people certainly have a suspicion about that. I really doubt that much serious work could be done in committee as my colleague from Kenora-Rainy River mentioned earlier.
MPs have no vote against regulations and bringing in amendments and may not even be notified about these Orders in Council before they actually happen. It would be much nicer to know ahead of time what is coming rather than playing catch-up all the time.
Above all I believe this legislation is irresponsible because it presents the illusion that the government has done something to curb gun related crime when in fact there are no simultaneous measures directed at organized or unorganized crime.
Since Bill C-17 does not go far enough in achieving the objectives of public safety, upholding the rights of the individual Canadian, and putting a check on the unstable and criminal elements of the population, I am not able to support Bill C-17. As it looks as though this bill is going to go through probably on a vote tomorrow morning, I would certainly wish the government and the members of the committee well who have worked so hard on it. I think we certainly do not need to stop here. It will proceed but I think as Bob Nault just mentioned we need to keep moving ahead. This probably does not address the issues and answer the question, will this in fact prevent another tragedy such as the one all Canadians witnessed last year at Ecole Polytechnique. I am not convinced and I do not think anyone is convinced that would be the case. I hope that is what we will move towards in effective gun control.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I guess that is a pretty tough test that the hon. member has set for us here. It would have her support I take it if we could guarantee that this would prevent a tragedy or a massacre. Well I think the hon. member should admit even if she did not say so in her comments, that would be pretty difficult. If the hon. member has amendments or a draft bill that she would like to show us that she knows would prevent past tragedies from happening again I would be very interested in seeing it. I would love to see just what amendments would guaran-
November 6, 1991

tee that terrible tragedies like the one that was mentioned would never happen in Canada again.
When you have set up that kind of a test, I guess we are always going to be somewhat short because who can guarantee human behaviour? I mean it is a little bit like the arson bill. A year ago we were involved with that and somebody said to me that the arson bill which has not been amended in 100 years did not include setting fire to your car as an offence. If you set fire to a vegetable stack that was arson, but if you set fire to your car it was not. Somebody said to me well does this mean that people are not going to commit arson by setting fire to their cars? I said: "I do not know but I do know this, it will be an offence in Canada and we are setting a direction in the Canadian Parliament". We are saying what we believe is proper behaviour and what we believe is proscribed behaviour and I think that is what we are doing here. Just as I cannot guarantee that nobody will ever set fire to their car I can guarantee that people who want to engage in that kind of behaviour will find that there is a sanction of the Criminal Code against them. As I say it is a pretty tough test.
I want to direct the members' attention to a couple of things she said. Twice she said the issue of smuggling was not addressed. I heard it in a couple of speeches. I do not know if these speeches get passed around or if bad information travels but the hon. member should be aware that this bill raises the maximum sentence for smuggling from five to 10 years. That is in the bill. Again they always say: "You have not put a minimum sentence of five years". I think the hon. member would know what court decisions in this country are saying about minimum sentences. She should know what happens to the minimum sentence on importing narcotics. So we made it 10 years. It is a direction by the Canadian Parliament.
For anybody to say that we have done nothing in the area of smuggling is absolutely incorrect.
As well the other red herring put out is failing to mention that the wanton disregard for the safety of the public is also an offence for which we have increased the
Government Orders
penalty. I wish the hon. member would address herself to some of those concerns.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to address the concerns of this hon. member. I first must say, without being holier than thou, as I was delegated to be by my neighbour from Port Moody-Coquitlam that we have just witnessed in this House someone who made fun of an arson bill. Someone has come forward and made fun of setting a car on fire with a sanctimonious tone of voice and a defensive feeling. I think anyone who is watching this parliamentary channel right now would say we are dealing with an issue far more serious than getting up and making a scene like that.
I believe that if the government House leader is watching this and I am sure he will get this on demand video because he watches every word I say, I would say listen to that. If we are talking about decorum in this House let us address the issue of something so serious as gun control. I would dare say that if Mrs. Edward was watching this right now and heard that going on while we are talking about an issue so serious when somebody launches off about setting a car on fire, vis-a-vis arson, it is dreadful.
I do not want to appear sanctimonious but I will say that is why we get ourselves off the issue far too often.
Thirty-two recommendations were brought forward by the special committee on Bill C-80.1 dare say that if half of those regulations and recommendations would have been put forward in this bill, people would have been far happier to accept it. People would have been far more pleased to say that we realize that a special committee has been brought forward and that people worked very hard on these issues and that 32 recommendations were brought forward. How many of them have been acted on in C-17? How many have been acted on? Not very many.
I would draw the member's attention to the Canadian Police Association and some of the recommendations they brought forward. They said that over 90 per cent of our respondents believe that guns of all kinds should be registered. I agree with that and I think every Canadian would agree with that. There should be a minimum age. I think that is perfectly acceptable as well and that compulsory training requirement should be in effect to

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
obtain a gun of any kind. Those are things that we think are extremely important.
I would also like to say that the maximum sentencing for smuggling of 10 years was addressed. What are we going to do about the minimum? We know how the courts work in this country. What is the sentencing going to be? What about a mandatory sentence, that my neighbour here from Kenora-Rainy River spoke about? What about people who are involved in policing across the country who are saying: "What do we do when we catch these people"? Are we going to make sure there is a mandatory sentence and that they will not be able to plea bargain themselves out of it.
In terms of existing legislation, I would like to record something that the Lac-la-Biche Shooting Association, a very prestigious and renowned group in my riding of Beaver River, hundreds of miles away from central Canada said to me. These people are very responsible citizens. They said to me and they have said it since Bill C-80 was first introduced in June 1989: "Although violent crime is on the increase in Canada, firearms related crime is decreasing and is not a major sector for concern. Current legislation, although in no way perfect, is adequate". That is what I have been hearing from right across the country. Current gun control legislation is not perfect, neither is Bill C-17.
The issue that I think every Canadian looks at is whether it will be enforced. Whatever legislation is in place let us make sure it is enforced. I fear that many people, such as fish and wildlife officers and policemen to whom I have spoken, are saying we are going to have a very difficult time enforcing this legislation.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Beaver River very appropriately and correctly states that both sides of this issue at the extremes were irrational. It is a highly emotionally charged debate. Concerns of urban areas often were distinctly different from that of rural areas.
She belongs to a political party that would like to put these things to free votes in the House. Free votes lead to purist attitudes. They do not bring out party compromise which provide balance on issues.
Her party also believes in referenda where the winner takes all, except in the case of Ernest Manning who had
a referendum on Sunday sport in Edmonton. He did not like the results and therefore rejected them.
I would like to ask the hon. member how she would resolve an issue that requires balance and work to bring sides of a country into some sort of compromise for a national Canadian perspective when she belongs to a party that would let the purist attitudes and the winner take all, either through free votes or referenda.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to address the question of my neighbour from Crowfoot in Alberta.
The whole idea of compromise, in bringing things together so we do not run rampant, is a very important issue. We have seen that members on opposite sides of the spectrum on this whole issue have, as the member for Cariboo-Chilcotin said, come together on this issue somewhat. It probably is a long way down the road from where this issue started in 1989.
My question would be why was this thing, if it is so good and is coming along so well, immediately sent, quietly, to committee? Why did only one speaker from each party address it? Why was it passed quickly and silently at five minutes to six one night? Is this compromise? Is this what we look at when saying that we are all free to speak our minds? No it is not.
We saw today whether it was a free vote. That is the question we need to ask ourselves. No it was not, because of party discipline.
I want to congratulate the eight members, I believe, on the government side who had the nerve to stand up and say that constituents are important, that they saw weaknesses with this piece of legislation and that they would continue to move ahead.
I do not know what is going to happen to them, if they are going to come and join me here in the independent ranks as others from the government side have done. We believe it is important for people to stand up in the House of Commons, as we witnessed here today. It would be advisable for the member for Crowfoot to be very careful about what he says when throwing stones at this side of the House.
