Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to join in this debate. I do that not for the purpose of adding to some of the fireworks which we have seen in the last several exchanges but rather to explain to people who have expressed their personal concerns to me as a member of Parliament why I cast a vote in support of the principle of this legislation, as I did today.
Among the responses I received, probably similar to those that many other members received, there were basically three categories of interventions that the people of Canada made to us. The first of those categories of interventions or opinions were from people who opposed gun control on principle, who do not want to see any gun control of any sort in this country.
I had the opportunity to pursue studies in the United States for four years. I lived there for four years. I have had the opportunity to visit many American communities during that time and since then. As a result of that experience I have to categorically reject the whole notion of not having gun control.
I do not want to see our communities turn into the kind of free fire zones that so many American communities have turned into. I do not want people to get the idea that going to bed with a handgun under their pillow is any kind of solution to their feelings of personal insecurity and fears for their personal safety.
Government Orders
A second group of people that intervened in this debate wanted a much tougher approach to gun control. In fact a lot of these people did not really see any reason why there should be any guns in the country at all, why people would want to own firearms in the first place. I also could not support that particular point of view.
Certainly in my own constituency in northern Saskatchewan there are a lot of hunters who hunt for sport and hunt for food. I would not be representing my constituents if I subscribed to that point of view. Personally I do not subscribe to it either. As I mentioned, food hunting is a necessity of life for a lot of people in northern Saskatchewan and a lot of other northern and native communities in this country.
The figures indicate, as I have presented to the House before, that in a community such as Black Lake the cost of food to feed a family of four by the Canada food rules is $955 a month. Ninety per cent of the people in that community are unemployed and thus living on welfare. Welfare payments amount to $555 a month. That means they are $400 short of being able to feed their families in accordance with the Canada food rules. Obviously, although those people are hungry and unhealthy as was shown on The Journal just the other night, they are not starving. That is a result of the fact that many of them hunt and fish and pursue traditional livelihoods for a living. It is not just a tradition. It is an absolute necessity for a lot of people. Firearms are a necessity in providing food for many of the families in my constituency.
Second, there are a lot of rural users of firearms who require them for things like pest control or a humane method of doing away with animals that are sick. I grew up on a farm myself. I still pursue farming from time to time. There was always a necessity for a .22 on the farm for shooting skunks under granaries or putting down animals that are in pain. This is a legitimate use which certainly has nothing to do with criminal or frivolous uses. It is a necessity in those kinds of circumstances. That is a legitimate use for firearms.
As well, I am not going to say that people who hunt for sport are not legitimately using firearms because I believe they are. I think it is a legitimate sport. Certainly a lot of the tourism in my constituency is based on the sport of hunting. Many of our tourist operators, many of our communities would be much poorer if it were not for that possibility. Therefore I also rejected the arguments

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
of people who said there is no need for firearms, no legitimate use for firearms in our communities.
The people I had the hardest time responding to were those who were concerned about specific aspects of this legislation, particularly some of the technical aspects of the legislation. A lot of these people intervened to say that while they did not take one extreme view or the other they felt that we had to be a lot tougher on crimes involving weapons and firearms and much tougher in general with people who own firearms and are known to be violent offenders because of the records they have had in the past.
There were a number of amendments before us that addressed the whole question of violent crime and keeping weapons out of the hands of violent people. I supported those amendments, and I am very disappointed that more of them did not pass and become incorporated into this legislation.
I am also concerned that this legislation probably in no way deals with the situation in my home community of Prince Albert which had to do with the shooting of an Indian gentleman by the name of Leo Lachance, I believe it was last January, by the leader of the Aryan Nations in Saskatchewan, a man by the name of Carney Nerland. What appalled me in that case as much as anything was the fact that Carney Nerland had been allowed to operate a firearms shop, a gun shop, quite openly in spite of the fact that he was openly identified and known to the authorities, to police forces and so on, as being involved with the Aryan Nations, a group which preached hatred and violence toward particular minority groups. This gentleman was allowed to run a gun shop in our country. He shot an Indian gentleman in that gun shop and this whole issue has never been properly dealt with. I fear that there is nothing in this legislation that would help deal with it either.
As well, there were a considerable number of concerns expressed about technical aspects of this bill. I guess the reason I ended up supporting the bill is because although there are still a lot of technical problems left in the bill, I do believe that a fair number of those have been addressed. I would like to outline a few of them.
First of all, when it comes to the FAC certificate, there is a requirement that there needs to be a course or a test. However, it is possible to waive that test in specific
circumstances, especially in northern isolated areas when for logistical reasons it is not possible for an individual to take that test for reason of language or distance, or whatever, which makes it possible for a lot of those hunters to have their competence vouched for rather than have to take a particular test. I think that is an improvement.
A second improvement was that people were concerned that it was strictly a regulatory decision-making process that would deal with the final aspects of this bill. I think there have been some parliamentary controls built into this bill that improve it somewhat in that area. Although I am not entirely satisfied with that, I think we have made some improvements.
There has also been an exemption from the proposal to ban large capacity magazines for competition shooters. I think that is only fair.
As well, there were a lot of concerns expressed about a designation of prohibited devices when it came to magazines. A lot of people said that was too broadly defined. Under the revised legislation it says "parts components, accessories and ammunition". I think that is an improvement.
At the committee stage, as well, there was a proposal made which was accepted, to have the fee for FAC renewals reduced from $50 to $25. For a lot of these people who hunt for food and do not have very much money, that is an improvement. As well, the 28-day cooling off period is not going to apply to renewals.
The seventh improvement was that there is an option to waive the photograph requirement on the FACs. Again that posed a lot of practical difficulties for people who might have to fly a thousand miles in order to find a photographer to take their picture.
So we end up in a situation where the kind of weapons that are principally used by hunters in my constituency. There is no magazine limit on 22 rim fire rifles. There is no magazine limit for bolt pump or lever action firearms and the old faithful, the Empire, is still a legal weapon.
Because of some of these changes that were made, I ended up supporting this bill. Certainly, I still have some qualms about it, some reservations. I think we should have dealt with the question of violent crime more directly. However, a lot of people put a lot of hard work into this. I think it is an improved bill as a result of that,
November 6, 1991

and I think those improvements are good enough that people like myself who represent a lot of hunters and people in rural areas can still vote for this bill in good conscience, knowing that we represented our constituents effectively because there were significant changes made in the bill to reflect their concerns.

Mr. Speaker, this debate on Bill C-17 is finally drawing to an end. I think it is about time, because we are all, if not tired of hearing about it, at least all talked out.
I want to say, first of all, that I sat on the legislative committee considering Bill C-80, the predecessor of Bill C-17, which also dealt with firearms. I was the vice-chair of that committee. I think that fact was not well known because some were not too pleased to see me there in that capacity, in view of the fact that-there were surely many reasons, but this was certainly one of them-I am a woman, and normally women do not meddle in firearms. In any case, we are not used to see women involved in such issues. I was there because of my background or, so to speak, of my legal expertise. Having studied law, I could determine whether the amendments were in order and could correct, if I may use the terms, the Criminal Code. So, I had two valid reasons for being there.
But I do not think that my presence was appreciated, as evidenced by the fact that the first time the chairman, had to leave the chair, he refused to let me take his place. He actually asked one of his male colleagues to fill in for him. I was shocked and appalled to see that although I was the vice-chair, I was not called upon to substitute for him in his absence. I made it quite clear to him, in my own feminine way, that this was not the thing to do, at least as I saw it, when there was a vice-chair present.
I was interested in the issue because I go hunting. So, I am of course interested in firearms. As I said, I has many reasons to be there. Now, I would like to come to the reasons that are more peculiar to women. I think this was kind of brushed to the side, because women are often called sentimental and emotional and because there was no reason to make this debate passionate. Quite the contrary, I think this aspect should have been emphasized. Unfortunately we have once again stuck to the
Government Orders
rules made by males, who were in the majority on this committee.
I would like to quote a few statistics regarding firearms. I know that statistics are always a little boring, but I think that they are necessary in this context. Let us begin with conjugal violence and firearms: between 1979 and 1988, 42 per cent of the women killed by their partners were shot; in 1989, it was 46 per cent. Firearms are used in 35 per cent of the murders committed within the family; on average, a woman is killed every five days in Canada.
In 1989, 74 women, or 30 per cent of all women who were murdered, were shot to death. Most women who are killed are shot with unrestricted weapons like hunting rifles. Between 1980 and 1989, 464 women were killed by gunfire; this is 72 per cent of all women murdered. I think that all those statistics are quite disturbing.
I would like to go on but not give you statistics, because as I said, I know that it is boring, but these things should still be mentioned. It must also be said that we received quite a bit of mail from people who were for stricter gun control. For example, the Community Health Department of the Montreal General Hospital, in co-operation with the Community Health Department of the Centre hospitalier de Rimouski, sent us some documentation and asked us to remove subsection 106(10) of the Criminal Code, which reads as follows:
No local registrar of firearms, firearms officer or other person shall require as information, to be submitted by an applicant for a firearms acquisition certificate or permit, details concerning the makes or serial numbers of shotguns or rifles of a type, kind or design commonly used in Canada for hunting or sporting purposes.
On that point, the doctors at these community health departments remark that 85 per cent of the deaths due to firearms in Canada are caused by shotguns or hunting rifles. We ask whose interest is at stake and who is being protected. It is certainly not in the interest of public health.
I would mention that people wrote to us, asking us to support them and, in many cases, to improve Bill C-17. Among other things, they suggested a motion, which I put forward but which was ruled out of order by the chairman. This motion asked that a firearms acquisition certificate be required for buying ammunition. In other words, this famous firearms acqusition certificate would

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
always have to be shown when buying ammunition. Unfortunately the motion was ruled out of order.
We also called for the registration of all firearms. Several people have spoken about it. Here again, this motion was ruled out of order by the chairman because it was said to go beyond the scope of the bill.
Another motion that was rejected would have required those whose firearms were lost or stolen to report it to the local police. This amendment was also rejected by the chair.
All this to say that all along, we tried to improve Bill C-17. We have not succeeded completely, but I think that our efforts were not totally in vain. One only has to see where we started from. Bill C-80, the present Criminal Code, allows a 16-year-old to obtain a firearms acquisition certificate. In Bill C-17 we first improved that provision by saying that, from now on, the minimum age would still be 16 years but that parental consent would be required. Now, the minimum age is 18. That is certainly a real improvement. There have been several others but, as I said, we were not always successful.
I would like to conclude by saying that we will certainly vote in favour of this bill because we feel it is a step in the right direction.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have a few minutes, as the member representing the riding of Outremont where this terrible tragedy occurred, to participate in this debate.
As I just said, this tragedy occurred in the riding of Outremont. I taught at the Ecole Polytechnique where I gave courses on human relations and psychology. It may have seemed, on the surface, that I was not immediately involved in the debate. I thought that so far, this issue belonged to those who had been directly involved. Today marks the end of a long process.
We all know that perfection does not exist in this world, and as the famous French writer La Fontaine said, we cannot please everybody at the same time. This is not an excuse or an attempt to dodge the issue. And I fully intend to get into the specifics of this bill. However, I
think that first of all, we should realize that we cannot achieve perfection immediately.
Very briefly, the sequence of events was as follows: On December 6, 1989, Marc Lepine took a gun and went to the Ecole Polytechnique. Twenty-eight people were hit. Twenty-eight people were shot within a matter of minutes. Fourteen were killed. Ever since that day, students, staff and graduates of the school have made an extraordinary contribution to the debate on gun control in Canada.
And it is a pleasure and a privilege to have this opportunity to thank all these people who made Canadians take a long hard look at this fundamental issue, in a society that is seeking a new identity. Again, on behalf of my colleagues, I wish to thank the students, teaching staff and graduates of the Ecole Polytechnique who supported this action and made a truly outstanding contribution. They came here to testify before the committee and they read their briefs. They met members of Parliament. They met owners of firearms. They organized petitions, and their contribution, in a difficult climate, has enriched the legislation before the House and contributed to the awareness of all Canadians.
This legislation will not undo what happened at the Ecole Polytechnique, but it will substantially and indubitably limit the recurrence of such tragic incidents in the kind of society we have today. It will make it far more difficult to acquire firearms. It will help the police, the constabulary, by allowing them to screen prospective owners of firearms. It will make it possible to prohibit persons with a tendency towards violent behaviour from having access to these weapons which are not evil as such but can easily become dangerous in the hands of a person whose personality tends towards extreme violent behaviour. It will also give police more authority and more opportunities to confiscate firearms found in homes where there are instances of family violence or violence among groups of people.
What is even more important, is that there will be strict controls on high-performance firearms of the type used at the Ecole Polytechnique. The bill will restrict access to many weapons that Canadians might wish to
November 6, 1991

own. It will also allow the government to limit the use of firearms by restricting the use of cartridge magazines. There is a great deal to say but I only have two minutes left.
Finally, whose recommendations will we follow? Will the government listen to the gun lobby, which says that gun control does not work, that Bill C-17 is unfair, and so forth? The answer is clear. We say that gun control saves lives and that Bill C-17 is a great improvement on the existing law.
A few more points in conclusion: this bill, although not perfect, is more than a step in the right direction. Such important people in the community as the director of the Montreal Urban Community Police Department, the rector of the University of Quebec, the president of Concordia University, the president of the Ecole Polytechnique and a mother who is still going through a difficult period of mourning have supported this bill. They know that it is not perfect as they, and all of us, would like it to be. But it is a definite step in the right direction. Once the bill is passed, it will be possible to move forward on that basis to continue to protect our society.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Five minutes for questions and comments. The hon. member for Lon-gueuil.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to know whether the hon. member for Outremont, who just made an excellent speech, would agree that firearms registration should be mandatory. He did not mention it in his speech.
I think that registering firearms would be the least one could do and it would cost the government absolutely nothing, since the people who want to register their weapons would have to pay for it. In that way, even the government could make some money and at the same time keep track of exactly where firearms are located throughout the country.
Another point that I would like to raise is whether he would agree to register firearms for all applicants who know how to operate and handle them. We know that firearms are dangerous. Many people who own firearms do not even know how to use them. Why did the government not go a little further in its bill, knowing that
Government Orders
it would not have cost it a penny more? On the contrary, it could even have made some money on it. That is my first question for him.
Second, as far as I am concerned, we should go quite a bit further. I think that in principle, individual citizens do not need firearms. Citizens should be completely forbidden to own firearms. I do not believe that it is really necessary in our society to have firearms. I do not have firearms, my family does not have firearms and one can live very happily without firearms. There are many other things one can do for fun and for sport.
That is only a brief comment, but I would like the hon. member to answer the two questions I asked him at the beginning.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague, or shall I say my former colleague and nevertheless friend from Longueuil, for his two interesting questions. He is still my friend, but he certainly is no longer my colleague. One day, he will see the light and, as silently and discreetly as some weapons, he will get back on the right track. I am telling him this tongue in cheek, but I am very serious.
This being said, I do not know whether if I should answer him as a psychologist or as a colleague but one thing is sure: I would hate, I just could not stand that the notion of profit be associated in any way with a bill as important as this one. It is about human lives, not about making money through controls and regulations.
I think I can appreciate the concern of the hon. member for Longueuil when he asked whether the government could make money with the registration of guns and rifles. I think this is too important an issue- It is a social concern. The whole of society is taken to task, not just individuals. I do not want to associate in any way financial gains or whatever economic consideration with such basic ones as psychological and social concerns.
As regards tests, I think they are really useful, but framework legislation cannot go into the smallest detail. We are faced with a social problem which is reflected in this bill. It is symptomatic of another problem that society must decide to tackle. Society must take a stand on this issue.
In his second question, our friend from Longueuil said that he does not own a gun and can get enjoyment from many other things besides guns.

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
I do not shoot either since I am not interested in firearms, but I would suggest that the hon. member for Longueuil have a talk with his colleague from Saint-Hubert, who told us about 15 minutes ago that she was a highly-skilled hunter and that she loved firearms. I will leave it up to the Bloc Quebecois members to try to get along with each other. Once again, there is total dissension among them, and once our colleague from Longueuil will-

speechtext: Order. Resuming debate, the hon. member for Calgary West has the floor for ten minutes.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure this evening to speak after the hon. member for Outremont. There are two psychologists in this House. In French, the word psychologue is difficult to pronounce for an English speaking person. Those two psychologists are the hon. member for Outremont and myself. It is a treat to have the opportunity to make a speech immediately after the other psychologist.

I am going to say it in English in part because it is a whole lot easier for me and hopefully a whole lot more expressive and a whole lot more precise. It is appropriate perhaps to start in French and move to English because I got sort of submarined and sabotaged by some people from central Canada, some from Montreal and some from Toronto, who have a kind of stereotype of western Canadians and in particular people from Calgary. I would like the House and people watching to know that all six members of Parliament from the city of Calgary, Alberta have post-graduate education and three out of the six have doctorates. We do not have pointy heads and long tails. We are quite used to talking to each other and listening.
One of the things you can count on with a western Canadian is if he says you have a deal and he shakes your hand, you have got a deal. You can do the paperwork later and nobody is going to go back on it. That is not true of all the people in this Chamber. It is not true of all the people in Canada. It is not true of all the cultures in this country, but that is part of our culture: when you shake hands and you have a deal, you have got a deal.
I made a deal with myself not too long ago to use every opportunity in this Chamber that I thought was appropriate to talk for a minute or two about the press in very specific terms. I want to talk about the Calgary Herald, a nice local newspaper that has been around a long time. It wrote an editorial about me and what I was going to do in relationship to this piece of legislation based on a Toronto Star story, and it should know better.
I would like my constituents and everyone in the Chamber to know that those people never talked to me. They never asked me. Obviously they never read the committee hearings or anything I said about the subject matter at the committee hearings which are a matter of public record. Of course after 12 years in this Chamber that does not surprise me. That is the press in this country.
I spoke to a report yesterday about the constitutional committee. I said that if members of the committee did one thing wrong then tomorrow's newspapers and tonight's TV news would be totally on the thing they did wrong. If they did 99 things right we would never know it because they will not have a single word about anything they did right. Of course that is what happened this morning. There is another editorial in the Ottawa Sun.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if we are now debating a bill about the press and the freedom of the press in this country or if we talking about a serious matter. I know the hon. member is on the defensive, but I would like order to be brought back to this House so that we could discuss the topic that is before us.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can guarantee you one thing, nobody in the press world of this country has read that bill with 39 amendments. I make that statement and challenge the entire press gallery to prove me wrong.
I will bet you are right.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Okay, you will bet I am right. The stories about this bill, the way it came into being, the way it was amended and the thrust of those amendments, are so terrible that Canadians out there have really very little idea of what this piece of legislation is about or most pieces of legislation that come through this Chamber.
November 6, 1991

I do not have a whole lot of time to speak. I would like to get a few thoughts about this bill out into the public domain and into the record of Hansard so that at least I can send it to my constituents.
The first myth that exists in the Press Gallery and in the minds of a lot of people in this country is that gun owners, those who belong to shooting clubs and those who hunt have no concern about gun safety. That is one of the biggest myths in this country. They have more concern about gun safety because their lives are at risk the minute they decide to store a gun in their home, the minute they go to a shooting range, the minute they go out and hunt. Clearly they are, if you listen to all the witnesses, absolutely the most knowledgeable group and the most concerned about gun safety.
That should never be mistaken by anybody. That is the group that we as parliamentarians and law makers must depend upon for help and advice if we get past the first part. If we were to say that guns will exist and people will have them then under what terms and conditions? The best piece of advise for safety will come from those with experience and knowledge about the subject matter. We should never forget that 10 years from now or 20 years from now.
They helped us a lot in making up those 39 amendments and I think there were two more or 41 amendments in total. All those amendments met one test by all members of the committee if they decided to vote for them-and I voted for every single one-they produce a somewhat safer world. They reduce to some extent, in some cases, the hassle for individuals that would not have been upheld by courts and should not be upheld by courts.
The notion of a warrantless search and seizure without cause is an absurd notion under our legal traditions. No court would uphold that kind of behaviour in the first place, but the bill in its drafting was not clear and now it is more clear than it was before. That is in there.
What did we have as an assignment? We had to have a piece of legislation that dealt with the issue of crooks. Drug dealers and robbers are perhaps the best words to describe the crooks. We had to have a piece of legislation at the same time that dealt with disturbed people, two kinds of disturbed people primarily: those who are
Government Orders
suicidal or attempt suicide at some point and those who are into violence and in particular family violence, particular crimes of disturbances.
We had to deal with this piece of legislation as best we could with the notion of trying to reduce accidents. The kinds of accidents that occur are in hunting areas and in peoples' homes. Children get hold of a firearm and use it inappropriately. They do not understand it and there are accidents in the home. There are accidents from time to time in other kinds of shooting areas and in particular in the hands of those who use a firearm as a tool. Policemen use the firearm as a tool and are frequently involved in accidental use of those firearms. Perhaps one of the things we learned is that there may not be enough training for policemen.
The third thing we had to be concerned about is those who use a firearm as a tool. We had crooks, disturbed people, accident situations, and those who use a firearm as a tool. To design a piece of legislation under the Criminal Code that would do all of those things with the kind of sensitivity that was required was a challenge in itself immediately, but as we listened to witnesses it just grew.
The crack dealer in downtown Toronto has so little in common with the aboriginal person in northern Saskatchewan who has a gun in the home. How do we do that under the Criminal Code? The only possible answer in our system is in the utilization of a regulatory power. We looked at that. We have had that. There has been not some very sensitive uses of regulatory powers in lots of statutes.
What is the antidote to sensitivity and common sense? It has to be the notion that a regulation proposed by the bureaucracy would be reviewable by the elected people of the country. They could call knowledgeable witnesses to look at a regulation before cabinet could proceed to gazette it and it could start down the process to become law.
For the second time in Canadian history and perhaps in the clearest way ever the members of the committee invented a set of words to put that principle in this particular amendment to the Criminal Code. All the regulator power that exists currently in the Criminal Code without the amendment, all of the new powers, forever after will have to come to Parliament first, to

Government Orders
both Houses, the Senate and the House of Commons, with whatever set of words people dream up for review.
If the whole examination of Bill C-80 and Bill C-17 has taught us something, it is that if you show the exact wording to knowledgeable people in Canada they will comment about it. You are well advised to listen to those comments because there is an awful lot of common sense in an awful lot of what they have to say.
The protection for firearms' owners and users of the future in terms of this statute lies primarily in that provision, which allows them to come before Parliament in the future and argue about whether a particular proposition is right or not.
The long-term solution lies in training. In five or ten years we can get a complete licensing system. It makes sense to those who own and use firearms that training courses be rigid and that safety aspects be very well vetted and very firm.
People out there who are listening tonight need to write their provincial attorneys general and their provincial members and tell people to enforce the criminal law. That is an administration of justice. The power is there. However if they plea bargain their way in the prosecutor's office it does not do anybody any good.
I would like to encourage everybody listening who cares about this issue to write their provincial attorneys general who are involved in the administration of the law, pound on their heads and get them to exercise those provisions which already exist.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not find the speech by the hon. member who was assigned an arm-twisting role throughout the process very edifying, and when I hear the government Whip say that the committees had plenty of leeway and freedom, I think we know that the main artisan of the arm-twisting that took place before this committee, the bully acting on behalf of the government, was the hon. member who just spoke.
My question is very simple: The hon. member referred to the principles that guided the committee's proceedings. With respect, I doubt any principles were involved. I think the committee's proceedings were guided by the
lobbying that went on, and especially by the government's attitude. I would like to ask the hon. member why the government did not decide to establish a general rule and subsequently make exceptions, instead of doing it the other way round? It looks like the government's position on gun control was determined by events, and we could say that they very reluctantly came up with a bill, but instead of defining the general principle, it seems they preferred the American approach. In fact, in this government, they are Americans at heart but do not know it.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of Legislative Committee H which studied Bill C-17, I welcome this opportunity to participate in the debate on third reading of this legislation.
Our committee heard testimony from some 25 witnesses, including the Minister of Justice. We received numerous briefs and letters from various groups, organizations and individual Canadians. As well, like every member of this House, I have personally received countless correspondence from across the country concerning both Bill C-17 and the entire issue of gun control.
From my experience on the committee and from what I have heard and read a common conclusion can be drawn. That is whether or not one supports separate gun control measures or conversely that the criminal justice system has to make the effort to deal more severely with those who commit violent acts involving firearms, the underlying issue remains one of public safety.
Certainly the argument that guns do not kill people, people kill people is far too simplistic. Obviously as a society we have to examine all the aspects of the problem before us and proceed to find acceptable and practical solutions.
As I did not sit on the special committee that examined Bill C-80, the precursor of Bill C-17,1 went into our committee's deliberations with an open and unbiased mind. Obviously, like every Canadian, I was not entirely unfamiliar with the issue of gun control. However I did not wish to examine the issue on the basis of personally supporting one viewpoint about gun control over another. I did however remain conscious of two fundamental aspects in our society, aspects which I believe every Canadian is interested in. The first is one's own personal safety, Canadians want to live in a country that is safe for themselves, their loved ones, friends and neighbours.
The safety and protection of any society is a paramount concern for the members of that society.
The other item concerns individual freedom which includes, among other things, the ability to carry out one's personal life without undue intrusion by the state or other authority. Therefore, with Bill C-17, two considerations have to be given. Does the bill offer protection for the public and would it provide gun control measures to be implemented that still permit legitimate firearm users to pursue their livelihoods, recreational activities or any other legitimate pursuit without undue restrictions being placed upon them? I

Government Orders
believe this legislation is a positive step in meeting these two considerations.
This of course does not mean that I can stand in my place today and state that Bill C-17 is the panacea for the problems improper use of firearms create. The bill will not stop violent gun related crimes and the taking of human life. Bill C-17, in reality, is a beginning. Some say the bill is not strong enough to tackle the serious problem it tries to address. Others say it is too strong, that it is an infringement on legitimate gun users.
I wish to believe that the bill should be viewed as a positive step in the right direction.
No one should be under the impression that Bill C-17 will prevent a future massacre as Canadians witnessed in horror on that fateful night of December 6, 1989. It will not. However, I believe the bill will put in place a series of obstacles that may well prevent future tragedies from occurring. These obstacles may go a long way to reduce the lethal potential which firearms in the wrong hands have.
Bill C-17 should be viewed as having measures directed toward controlling the escalation of firearm related violence. It will not eliminate the all too many acts of violence and death we see occurring throughout our country. Statistics show that in Canada today, approximately 1,400 people are killed by firearms, 1,100 of these deaths involve suicide. The remaining 300 were homicides, usually the result of arguments and normally involving hunting rifles and shotguns.
One may suggest that the number of fatalities could have been reduced if firearms were not so easily obtainable. Others may argue that alternative means would have been found to make up for the lack of a gun. Nonetheless, if we permit the continued proliferation of firearms and the ease by which they can be obtained and choose to simply stand idly by, then we will never know just how many lives could have been saved.
Almost one million Canadians have permits to own guns. These permits or firearm acquisition certificates enable the holder to purchase an unlimited number of firearms. In 1990, some 40,000 FACs were issued in Canada. Statistics indicate that the known total of restricted weapons, such as hand guns was 981,000.
Another 5,000 fully automatic guns are owned by gun collectors and roughly 6 million shotguns and rifles are out there. The shotguns and rifles do not have to be registered. This is quite an amount of fire power for a country of 26 million people.
In addition, what about the number of illegal weapons in circulation and the countless other weapons that are unregistered that we do not know about. I believe many Canadians are wondering why our society needs so many firearms.
Given the number of firearms in Canada, I hope that the Minister of Justice accomplishes what she first set out to do with Bill C-80. On June 26, 1990, the Minister of Justice presented her gun control proposals to Parliament in the form of Bill C-80. At the time she stated that the bill would, in her own words, and I quote: "Reduce accidental and criminal misuse of guns. That it will keep guns out of the hands of dangerous persons and encourage and ensure responsible gun ownership and use".
While I am sure that the minister shares the same sentiments with regard to the proposals contained in Bill C-17, I sincerely hope, as I believe a majority of Canadians do likewise, that this bill is able to reach such desirable goals.
When the Minister of Justice appeared before our committee, she alluded to the point that there were concerns in Canada today about the proliferation of high-powered firearms. She said that Bill C-17 would address this concern by making three basic changes to the existing law.
The first change is firearms which have been converted from fully automatic to semi-automatic would become prohibited.
Second, certain paramilitary firearms will either become prohibited or restricted weapons by way of Orders in Council.
Finally, the minister said that Bill C-17 will place absolute limits on the fixe power of semi-automatic firearms by limiting the capacity of cartridge magazines. This would be accomplished through regulations introduced after Bill C-17 is passed.
November 6, 1991

There are other positive elements in Bill C-17 that I would like to comment upon at this time. For example the bill will tighten up the screening process of FAC applicants. The minimum age for obtaining a FAC will be raised from 16 to 18 years of age. There will however be an exemption for youths who require a firearm for sustenance purposes.
A mandatory 28-day waiting period will come into being which will cover the time an applicant applies for an FAC to when it is granted. It is hoped that this so-called cooling off period will prevent individuals from obtaining a firearm on the spur of the moment. In addition, every application for an FAC must have a guarantee from two references who have known the applicant for three years. The references would be protected from civil liability but would be criminally liable if they knowingly made a false statement.
A photograph of the FAC holder will now appear on the FAC. This would permit only the individual whose photograph appears on the FAC to purchase a firearm. There is also a fundamental change in existing rules whereby applicants who are refused an FAC by a firearms officer will now have the onus placed upon them to prove wrongful refusal. Currently the firearms officer has to justify why the FAC application was refused.
One of the amendments I put forward at the committee stage of this bill that was adopted and appears in the bill before us concerns the issue of community checks. I am grateful to members of the committee for their support on this amendment which will enable a firearms officer who has received an application for an FAC to conduct an investigation. This may consist of interviews with the applicant's neighbours, community, social worker, spouse, dependents or whoever in the opinion of the firearms officer may provide information pertaining to whether the applicant has a history of violent behaviour including violence in the home.
I believe this provision will further assist the firearms officer in his investigations. It will also complement the other proposals relating to the screening process. I also hope it will have some impact on the very serious issue of family violence and the often tragic consequences that occur when domestic disputes and firearms come together.
Government Orders
As is currently provided for in statute, FAC applicants will still be required to pass a course or test in the safe handling and use of firearms or be certified as competent by a local firearms officer.
Bill C-17 however will add a component on firearms law and responsibility to the course curriculum. There will be a provision that will allow a local firearms officer to certify an applicant by an alternative means. Obviously there may be instances where it is either unnecessary or not practical for an FAC applicant to write a formal exam and this is understandable. The criteria for direct certification would be limited by regulation.
I would like to stress at this point that there was considerable support indicated during our committee's hearings for mandatory firearms training and competency tests. A number of witnesses both supportive and opposed to Bill C-17 found common ground in the desire that steps be taken by the federal and provincial governments to create some form of national firearms training system.
At the very least it was hoped that training and course requirements would be sufficiently designed at a national level to ensure the safe use and handling of firearms and knowledge of all facets of firearms legislation. I believe this is a credible recommendation. I hope to see the federal and provincial governments take steps in the immediate future to bring such a system about.
We all of course recognize once again the administrative problems as well as the financial implications involved in trying to establish such a system. Nonetheless, there can be no doubt of the benefits that would be gained from its creation.
In order to finance the new FAC system, fees for FACs will be raised. This will help offset the current $3 million deficit of the FAC system. A fee of $50 for first time applicants and $25 for renewals is being considered. The current fee for an FAC is $10.
Given that an attempt is being made to have the FAC system pay for itself the provincial and federal governments in consultation with the firearms community and other interested parties may wish to enter into consultations on ways revenues could be generated to help cover the cost of implementing a national firearms training system.

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
Discussions should also be held with the parties I have just mentioned in relation to the type of training curriculum that could be implemented in order to meet the objectives of a viable and acceptable national firearms training program.
Aside from the new rules pertaining to the FAC, Bill C-17 also addresses by way of the regulation process the strengthening of safe storage requirements for firearms. As in the case of other regulatory matters, the measures concerning safe storage are not as yet known. I might add that our committee was hampered somewhat by the lack of information we had concerning the nature of future regulations. This was indeed unfortunate as a number of these regulations deal with very important subjects. One could argue that if more information on the regulations was provided perhaps some of the fears and uncertainties from the firearms community and supporters of tougher gun control laws could have been avoided. I hope the Minister of Justice and the Advisory Council on Firearms, which is the body mandated with providing regulation recommendations to the minister, will soon announce the nature of these important regulations both to Parliament and to all Canadians.
Another issue of concern is the so-called grandfathering clause. The clause allows anyone who currently owns a weapon that would become banned under this legislation, such as a converted fully automatic weapon, military or paramilitary, to retain possession if it is registered by October 1, 1992 and the owner becomes a genuine gun collector. While it is uncertain as to how many firearms this involves, the Canadian Bar Association has suggested that it may include some 50,000 firearms. The government may have to give this issue more consideration. Perhaps they may wish to implement some form of compensatory program which would give an incentive to owners of these weapons to turn them in rather than keep them in their possession.
While Bill C-17 does provide a definition of genuine gun collectors, these collectors will however be permitted to keep firearms that the bill proposes to ban.
In relation to safe storage requirements, I have alluded earlier to the fact that regulations will be devised for the safe storage of firearms unaccounted for in Canada today. Therefore the government must ensure that regulations for safe storage are indeed adequate.
We must curtail the opportunities presented to unauthorized individuals receiving firearms that were not properly secured by the owners. As well, an element of safety is involved here inasmuch as tragic accidental deaths have occurred from improper storage procedures of firearms. This also includes police firearms as tragically portrayed to the committee by Mr. John Bickerstaff who lost his 18 year old son, Lee, to an accident that involved a police officer's sidearm.
There are other tragic cases we hear about too often and many involve young children. There must be proper safe storage regulations implemented as soon as possible.
The definition of a genuine gun collector in Bill C-17 is another issue that has caused some concern. A genuine gun collector is not presently defined by statute, however only genuine gun collectors may register firearms under a grandfather clause where restricted weapons are part of a collection.
Bill C-17 will provide a definition for genuine gun collector. It will be anyone who has or seeks to acquire one or more related firearms and can demonstrate knowledge of the firearm involved while satisfying any regulatory requirement for safe storage or record keeping. Regulations concerning safe storage and the record keeping requirements will be forthcoming.
Much has also been said about the need for a national firearm registration system for Canada. I agree that a concerted effort must be made to establish such a system. Obviously the logistical and financial implications are considerable. There may also be federal-provincial considerations to be ironed out so that the most viable system possible can be developed. My colleague, the member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys proposed an amendment to Bill C-17 which I believe was certainly worthy of serious consideration. I would hope that the government would re-examine this important issue and work toward the creation of a national registry for firearms. The system would obviously start by registering firearms from the inception onwards. This would be the most practical. I believe a national firearms registry is feasible if the right course of action is followed. This system would be of considerable benefit to our police forces and would add another measure of security for the entire population.
November 6, 1991

Another issue which I believe could be improved upon concerns the sale of ammunition. There are certain types of ammunition available that have more than the average lethal capability such as the so-called KWT "super slug". This bullet, according to the testimony provided to our committee by the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police, fits conveniently into most standard handguns. Its teflon coating and composition is such that it can penetrate automobile engines and bulletproof vests. This type of ammunition, if not banned for sale in Canada altogether should, as the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police suggests, be included in the definition of prohibited weapons. As well a number of witnesses called for controls to be implemented on the sale of ammunition. One often heard suggestion was that an FAC be required for the purchase of ammunition. I hope the government will give consideration to implementing such a provision in the regulations.
Another point I would like to comment upon concerns the mandatory reporting of all lost or stolen firearms to the police. I believe such a requirement would be beneficial to the efforts being undertaken by our police forces. It would assist them in knowing what is out on the streets and also indicate how successful safe storage requirements are and where improvements can be made. According to Police Chief Flanagan of the Ottawa Police Force, guns used in the commission of crimes are for the most part stolen. These guns were originally legal guns or were in legal hands. For various reasons these firearms, whether because of unsafe storage or otherwise, fell into the hands of criminals. Chief Flanagan went on to say that there have been large scale thefts where up to 100 firearms have been stolen with the potential end result being that 100 criminals have firearms. His experience has shown that the problem is stolen firearms rather than illegally imported ones.
During his 40 year career in criminal investigations he could not remember a case where an illegally imported firearm was seized. The firearm is usually stolen from some place. If thefts are required to be reported, the police may find something to go on to locate the thief and recover the firearm. There are obviously numerous cases where stolen or mislaid firearms go completely unreported and this has to be corrected.
Government Orders
A number of individuals and organizations who have been before our committee and those who wrote to me personally on the subject of gun control, raised the need for stronger legal deterrents for those who use firearms in the commission of criminal acts. Without getting into a lengthy discourse on the merits or failings within our criminal justice system or the adequacy of legal sanctions I would like to make a few comments.
Bill C-17 introduces changes to the current sentences for part III Criminal Code offences which concern firearms. Presently maximum sentences are set at five years. Bill C-17 will increase the maximum sentences for certain offences to 10 years. These include the possession of a prohibited weapon, possession of a firearm while prohibited and the importation, purchasing or selling of a prohibited weapon. While I would like to leave the debate over harsher penalties to judicial experts, criminologists and the government to re-evaluate, many Canadians feel that the legal community and the government have to seriously examine the issue of firearm offences and sentencing and determine if sufficient deterrents are indeed in place to reduce firearm related criminal acts.
I wish to take this opportunity to thank the members of the committee of which I had the privilege to be a part. I particularly want to thank the chairman and the member from Lethbridge. I believe the amendments our committee put forward strengthened Bill C-17. I hope the government will take additional steps to further enhance this bill and thereby improve the safety and security of all Canadians.
The issue of gun control is a very controversial one. I hope that this bill and the regulations which are to follow will provide a beginning to provide Canadians with gun control legislation that is both reasonable and effective. More important, I hope that this bill will indeed reduce the tragic loss of life that firearms have caused and that it will improve the safe use of firearms.
In conclusion, I believe responsible gun owners and all Canadians realize the value gained in the past with the introduction of gun control measures. The creation of the FAC system and the banning of fully automatic weapons contribute to a safer Canada. In the final analysis both the firearms community and advocates for

November 6, 1991

tougher gun laws want nothing less for our country and its citizens.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Stormont- Dundas. I would prefer to speak French exclusively, but I do not speak it very well.

But I would like to thank him for a very thoughtful and worth-while contribution to this debate. I would like to make a brief comment and raise a question. I will do it as quickly as I possibly can. I just received a letter from Mr. Bill Snowden of Hannon, Ontario in the Mount Hope area of my riding. The letter reads: "I am writing to you as a member of your riding and someone who has voted Conservative for the last 20 years. I have been a hunter and a gun owner for 27 years. As such I feel that recent legislation introduced by Justice Minister Kim Campbell, namely Bill C-17 does not represent my best interests. Although there are some genuine improvements in this bill, it retains many of the flaws which caused its predecessor, Bill C-80, to be rejected by your own Conservative caucus. If you choose to support this bill I will have no choice but to withdraw my support of your party in the next election and I am sure many of the seven to eight million law-abiding firearm owners in the country will'.
The letter goes on: "It is the kind of thing that we are getting from the rural areas and, as the Whip of our party says, we get killed by the city folks if we talk about anything less than what Bill C-17 proposes. In fact the city folks want something much, much stronger".
I am confronted by an conundrum here. It is a lose, lose situation for me. I do not know in my 13 and a half going on 14 years in the House of Commons how on earth I am going to vote on this one. I am alerting the Whip that I may not be able to vote for Bill C-17.
How do you reconcile the profound differences among the gun club owners, the gun owners, the responsible people and those in the cities, towns and villages who are fearful of those who own guns and use them illegally and in an horrific way against Canadian society? That is the question I put to the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth for his comments, and I must say that the problem he raised has been shared by many members in this House ever since the tabling of a bill dealing with this very controversial subject which affects all Canadians.

I would say to the member that in committee particularly I was obviously struck by the testimony of individuals and organizations from across the country that related to the situation. I think in some cases they were raising the issue of urban-rural, but I agree in this instance to a great extent with the minister that there has to be some consistency in implementing federal gun legislation.
I do not know how we could ever devise a piece of legislation that would address specifically just the concerns of large metropolitan areas and then a separate bill that would address the rural concerns.
What is creating a lot of the anxieties at this point are the regulations. Not knowing what those regulations are going to be is creating a great deal of anxiety for the groups at both ends of this debate.
I know in my riding there is a large rural area and a small urban area of approximately 50,000 people in Cornwall. I have had to wrestle with the same concerns the member for Hamilton-Wentworth has to deal with, as have all other members on both sides of the House. This is not an issue that has been easy for any member. I think we have all been the recipients of the type of correspondence which was just related to the House.
However, by the same token we are called upon in this instance as we are in any other to make a final decision, having examined all of the evidence, weighing all the evidence, and taking into consideration all the interests in presenting what is in my estimation a bill, a beginning or a part of the solution of a far larger problem.
The responsible gun owners will remain the responsible gun owners. We count on their sense of responsibility. They want to continue to enjoy their sport. I do not think we are going to impede their ability to enjoy that

sport, whether it is hunting, marksmanship or what it might be.
In the end the bill does not please anyone on one hand, but on the other hand it is a step in the right direction. For that reason I will support it tomorrow.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier today there were 13 individuals, 12 plus myself, who felt it was their duty to stand in this House and vote against a bill.
I want to make it clear at the start of my comments that not one of those individuals, including myself, is against gun control or law and order. We are against this proposed legislation.
If you listen to some in this Chamber or some across the country, you would think that the 13 of us probably either have horns, are rednecks, or live in the stone age.
Let us make it clear that none of that, not one bit, is true.
We are talking about a bill that is going to be voted through this House tomorrow and will become law and in it there are quite frankly no regulations. As a member of Parliament from rural Canada, the riding of Timis-kaming in northern Ontario, I am not prepared tonight or tomorrow to sign a blank cheque without knowing what the regulations are.
I say that for a very good reason. I have heard on numerous occasions the critic for the NDP who has said that this bill does not go far enough. That troubles me. It indicates to me that the member from Vancouver is really not concerned about fairness. He wants to take

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
away opportunity from individuals across this country, in fact the people in the regions who have developed this country. He is prepared to take away a right of these people. I am not prepared tonight or tomorrow morning to allow that to happen.
When reviewing this piece of legislation earlier we heard about some increase in sentencing on the criminal side. It has not gone far enough. Why are we punishing law abiding citizens with this piece of legislation when we are not sentencing in terms of violent crimes involving guns? What about the incidents of violence and the cross-border black market? What about the efficiency with which we are dealing with this bill and stiffer penalties?
It is fine for us to say that we will be looking at a maximum of 10 years. Who is to say within the justice system today that someone will end up getting two years on a plea bargain? Yet a law abiding citizen has to go by this. Violent crimes have not been dealt with in this bill in the manner they should have been.
I want to deal with a couple of other areas. It is fine for us to say that $50 is not too much. With the salaries around this place and this being central Canada, $50 may not sound like a lot of money. However, let me tell the House that in my constituency and many other constituencies across this country $50 means putting food on the table.
People ask: "How much is a gun?" There are a lot of people out there who have not bought a gun for many years and have no plans to buy a gun. Under this legislation, before they can buy a gun to go out on a trap line to hunt for food for their family, they are going to have to pay $50. There is nothing to say that in five years from now that is not going to be $75, $100 or $150.
It should be.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is fine for the member for Ottawa Centre to say that it should be, because he lives under the dome. He does not deal with the reality that those of us who come from the rural part of Canada deal with on an ongoing basis.
Regulations on types of guns, storage and clips should be determined and printed to be passed into legislation. To limit semi-automatic firearms and prohibit the same styles of guns which are now being used for recreational
and hunting purposes in the north affects those individuals who purchased guns many years ago. The 303 Lee-Enfield rifle with a clip of 10 which many of my constituents own today will no longer be lawful when this piece of legislation is passed.
I just want to give a few numbers here that make it veiy interesting in terms of deciding what we are really talking about in Bill C-17. Private insurance companies paid out $6.4 billion in 1989 as a result of automobile accidents. Out of that 284,234 people were injured and 4,246 were killed. Some 495 people including 81 children and 7 firefighters died in fires in 1988. Of 656 homicides in Canada in 1989, 218 were effected by firearms.
We are trying to say that this legislation has been driven more by emotion than by facts. I have received letters not just from rural parts of Canada but from from concerned citizens all across Canada. I have one here from Victoria, B.C.: "Hunting, target shooting and collecting are traditional sports and should be preserved for future generations. If saving my way of life means that I have to become politically active I plan on doing so".
A corporation in my riding has received information on Bill C-17, the new gun control legislation. The council objects to Bill C-17 for the following reasons: "The real purpose of gun control use is to reduce violent use of firearms. However, Bill C-17 will effect the average northern hunter and their traditional values. A $50 FAC fee is unacceptable to most rural Canadians. Stiffer penalties should be imposed for criminals for the violent use of guns. There should not be a requirement for further safety courses over and above those already in place, and this is completely unnecessary. And this council hereby petitions the legislative committee studying Bill C-17 to completely review the entire part of this bill".
I could go on, as you can see from the numerous pieces of information that I have received. My greatest concern is not only the fact that we are dealing with this one piece of legislation here tonight but it seems to be an ongoing effort in the real rural parts of Canada. The livelihood and the way of life of those of us who come from those regions are, on an ongoing basis, being jeopardized by the fact that none of us believe that criminals should be loose.
November 6, 1991

None of us can say how sorry we are about what happened in Montreal. However the fact is that the history of northern Ontario and the history of rural Canada is that we have grown up and learned how to hold firearms and learned how to use firearms. Who can say today without regulations in place that trigger locks, cabinet locks, room locks and who knows what else will be put in place.
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity to speak here tonight. I know that there is a voice out there that wants to be heard. I hope they have been able to hear what I have tried to say on their behalf.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for his remarks and just say how much I admire him for speaking against this legislation. One of his colleagues, the hon. member for Crowfoot mentioned earlier that the Tory party comes up with consensus. I just want to congratulate him and others who I see here tonight who had the nerve to say that there are concerns about this legislation.
I would like to just make one quick comment in reference to a member of my riding, Lionel Tersier from Bonneville. I was wondering if the member would concur with what Mr. Tersier said in light of the remarks he made. He says: "Unfortunately it seems that a series of ill-considered regulations and unenforceable laws will be put on the shoulders of law-abiding gun owners who, in the past, have tried to follow earlier regulations that have not had the desired effects, and that is reduce criminal activities".
Could the member enlighten the House further on his views?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, back in January 1978 legislation was put into place to protect life, it was put into place for bona fide gun collectors.
This is something that has been going on for many, many years. In fact I have other legislation here that goes back to 1961. My greatest concern is that we are getting carried away, we are not dealing with the real problem and which is the criminal.
That is what we have to deal with here. It is not the law-abiding citizen. I hope we will see more changes to
Government Orders
this, but there is still a great concern that not enough has been done to make changes that will affect the criminal.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say to the member for Timis-kaming that I have deep respect for him, and I listened to him carefully. He should not think that members from urban ridings are not suffering with him tonight over this legislation.
He mentioned the fact that there is a lot of emotion in this debate and I share his view. There is a lot of emotion in this debate. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
It is very simple and I want to thank the hon. member for his question.
The law side of it is what we have to deal with, the punishment side dealing with criminals. I am still very concerned about plea bargaining. I am very concerned that we have said we have increased the sentencing to 10 years. I do not think that is strong enough. I believe we have come to a point in this country that we have to make those that break the law pay. We can no longer have a society out there where people just have their fingers slapped when they commit a crime. That is what we are looking for in this legislation. When you err, when you break the law, when you end up taking a life you should pay for it, not the honest, law-abiding citizen.
