speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is agreed that we are allowing the pages to go home.
Earlier today I voted against this legislation. It is very difficult to vote against legislation that members in my caucus have worked so hard to reach a compromise on, to reach a position that they feel, and justifiably so, has found a balance.
I refer particularly to my colleague, the member for Lethbridge, who worked very hard on this legislation.
I want to read you a couple of quotes tonight if I may. I think they outline very carefully the feelings that I have and the feelings that my constituents in Alberta have. This is a letter I received from the office of the Farmer's Advocate of Alberta. I will not read it all but it is regarding Bill C-17, the firearms legislation.
It says: "I was recently speaking to a law professor from Osgoode Hall and he tells me that in Canada there are about 350 different charges that can be lodged under the Criminal Code of Canada but that there are approximately 40,000 other legal restrictions under which charges can involve our citizens."
I would assume reference is to laws and regulations enacted by our three levels of government. His main concern is not with the Criminal Code since, "if charged under this a citizen is innocent until proven guilty, sometimes a difficult task, but the principles of English common law prevail.
The concern is with the laws and regulations of the associated charges that can be laid under a large portion of those other 40,000 laws and regulations applicable to
Canadians." In reference to the latter he indicates that in many cases, penalties can be as severe as those of the Criminal Code but a citizen, if charged by an inspector or other official carrying out the intent of the act, is faced with having to prove his innocence. That is quite another case.
"Further, a good many of our citizens can no longer bear the cost of seeking justice in the court system."
I would like to move to another one. Of course, he is against the enacting of Bill C-17. I will quote another paragraph: "I do not believe anyone would quarrel too much with the removal from sale of military type assault weapons but most of the other provisions of the bill will only serve to penalize honest people". That is what I feel is happening with Bill C-17.
Then he goes on to say: "My constituency happens to be one comprised of farmers living in western Canada". Indeed, that is much of my constituency. "The moment the firearm bill is passed you will have created thousands of law breakers on our farms for I cannot imagine that they will take the rifle from the back porch, from behind the basement door or from behind the seat in a half-ton truck and lock it away someplace officially regarded as safe."
Then there are the changes concerning magazines, capacity and the measurement of a barrel length which will sweep even more into the net.
I think a very significant paragraph is the last one: "If the realities of life and politics regarding guns are that much different in the Golden Triangle than they are in farms in western Canada at this moment in history in which we live, then consideration should be given to other solutions. Obviously the U.S. recognized this since gun laws differ from state to state and tend to be more stringent in the densely populated areas".
I would like to go on record as saying that I truly understand and feel real empathy for those living in urban centres like Montreal where the tragedy that we are all aware of took place.
Bill C-17 will put the individual honest Canadian who takes up a legitimate activity, the gun club members across Canada and farmers who use their weapons consistently in their daily activities in a position of breaking the law as they carry on in the normal, safe manner that they have always carried on.

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
To me that is wrong. There has to be another way and I think the way is to make it very strict and very tough on the criminal element who by the way acquire their guns illegally. That activity is not going to stop in my view. Anyone who is going to commit armed robbery, anyone who is going to commit a violent activity is not going to worry too much about acquiring a weapon in an illegal way to carry out that activity.
I received correspondence and I am sure other members of Parliament here today have as well. I hope she wrote to everyone. It is from Judith Ross, Ph.D., 34 Cavell Avenue, Toronto, Ontario. I think it is an excellent piece of work that she has done. She pretty well destroys all of the myths on The Coalition for Gun Control and brings in the facts. It is too bad that we do not have time to read it. I hope that everyone has read it.
I know it is not going to make any difference. I know that this bill is going to be enacted tomorrow. Bill C-17 will be passed in the House tomorrow and then it will go to the Senate and become law.
It really distresses me that this is going to become law and I am going to have to go back and talk to farmers, trappers and the native people in my community when it is absolutely second nature for them to carry and to use a gun in their daily lives. They do not use it in a destructive way. They use it in a very constructive way.
I now have to go back and say to them that they are breaking the law and can be charged by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, if the police happen to come to their house or stop them on the road and find a weapon in their pick-up truck. I cannot believe that we in this House of Commons cannot come to a better solution than Bill C-17.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Five minutes for questions and comments. The hon. member for Saint-Hubert.

Mr. Speaker, I can inform the hon. member who just spoke that to say guns do not kill people is a myth, and that will be subject of my comments.

Guns do not kill people. People kill people. The fact is that people without guns injure. People with guns kill. Gunshot wounds are 15 times more deadly than those from knives and far more deadly than those from weapons such as clubs or fists. Reducing the accessibility of guns may not reduce the number of violent confrontations but it will reduce the risk of fatal outcomes. It takes a less well formed motive to commit murder with a gun than with any other weapon because of the physical and psychological distance between the aggressor and the victim.

I think it is quite obvious, everybody has said so, but when we listen to the hon. member, he just doesn't make sense.
Nevertheless, I would like to ask him a question, and I hope that he will be able to give me a straight answer. I do not see why all those farmers and hunters and practically all the people in his riding will be breaking the law, because from now on, we will have legislation that will be a bit stricter on firearms. What it boils down to is that this legislation will turn restricted weapons into modified semi-automatic weapons. I do not think every single person in the hon. member's riding has a modified semi-automatic weapon.
I fail to see why everybody in his riding will be breaking the law from now on. I would appreciate it if the hon. member could answer that question.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question from my hon. friend. The storage provisions and the transportation provisions in the bill will make it illegal for a farmer to set his gun beside the back door or hang it up over the door. Yesterday I had a visitor from High Prairie who told me that two days prior to being here he shot a coyote in the back yard. It had come up nearly to the back porch.
I am passing this information on to you.
I asked him what he did with it. He said he shot it and then he had it buried because he did not know if it was rabid or not. He wanted to have the carcass buried. That

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
is something perhaps that my hon. friend does not understand.
He will not be able to leave his weapon, the .22 rifle, handy in an area close to the ammunition that it carries. He will have to store the weapon in one spot under lock and key, under regulation, or have a guard lock on the trigger mechanism and the ammunition in another spot. That is in the law. That will be in the law and is the regulation that is coming out.
The storage is in the legislation. It has to be under lock and key. Tell me how you are going to be able to do that.
Let me go back to the question brought up by my hon. friend. She said guns do not kill people, people kill people. That is a bumper sticker.
A Danish study differs greatly from American studies and finds that rather than being 15 times more lethal gunshot wounds range from 1.5 to 5 times more lethal than knife wounds. It depends on the calibre of the weapon. The information given by my hon. friend gives no consideration to penetration by a .22 calibre bullet. I would consider a knife wound much more lethal.
Those are spurious arguments. That is not the argument I am using. My argument is that there are honest people who have weapons. I have some. I have a number of shotguns. I have a couple of rifles. My sons, my children, have them. I have taught them to use them properly and they attend gun clubs. I do not see anything wrong with that. It is a legal activity. It was a legal activity and now we are zeroing in on an issue because there was a tragedy-and it was a tragedy that happened in Montreal-but because of those kinds of things happening we are zeroing in on legitimate, law-abiding citizens and to me that is wrong. That is wrong in my view.
Therefore, I cannot support the bill.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I wish to inform hon. members that the first five hours of debate at third reading stage are now expired. Pursuant to the Standing Orders of this House, the 10-minute maximum period, without questions or comments, is now starting. On debate, the hon. member for Victoria.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support Bill C-17.1 recognize, as I am sure all members do, that it is far from perfect in achieving the objective that I think virtually all Canadians want to see. That is effective gun control legislation. An overwhelming percentage of Canadians have come to the recognition that the first and primary responsibility of the state is to protect its citizens.
We are now facing an epidemic of violence in this country that has been created by a series of causes and will be dealt with, not simply by legislation of this kind. This legislation will only deal with a small part of it but at least it represents a step in the right direction.
Let me start by joining with other hon. members in a personal statement. I come from a very urban culture. Guns are foreign to me. I fired a gun a few times when I was in cadets in the army and later in the navy. I was not very good at it but I do recognize that it is necessary for the military of this country to be equipped with guns as part of the security of our country. I accept that in some circumstances police officers need guns, but beyond that I personally have a great deal of difficulty understanding why private citizens need guns.
I recognize as the previous member said there is a somewhat different culture, particularly in rural Canada. There are those who collect guns. To me that is a strange activity. I do not understand it at the personal level. There are those who hunt. That too is something that is strange to me. There are those who engage in shooting as part of a sport and in fact the sport is included in the Commonwealth Games, in the Olympics and so forth. To me that activity almost romanticizes the violence that is really inherent in guns. If we look back at history that is the role that guns played in our history and in our culture. They are part of war and war has become the bane of civilization.
So to me, guns symbolically have no place in a good society. However I recognize, and all legislators must recognize, that there are those who have a different culture. Further we must recognize that the criminal law cannot simply do the effective job of changing human behaviour. If we are going to tackle the causes of violence that led to the massacre in Montreal, that has caused 1,100 young people last year to commit suicide in Canada and the domestic violence some of which hap-
November 6, 1991

pens by guns, we cannot simply rely on the Criminal Code to do it.
But the argument that we should not try to use the Criminal Code to the full extent possible simply does not stand up. What distinguishes this country from the country to the south is that we recognize that the possession of a gun is not a right. It is a privilege which Parliament is entitled in the interests of the safety of the community to restrict.
What legislation in 1978 began to do, by providing certain restrictions on the acquisition and possession of guns, this legislation takes a step further. There is a huge amount of misinformation being put out about what is included in this bill. Let me be fairly specific about the bill and what it seeks to achieve.
It provides that first time applicants for firearms acquisition certificates, which have been in place in Canada since 1978, have to wait 28 days before receiving a certificate. It provides that for exceptions in certain areas, photographs would be necessary as part of the job of applying for a certificate. The bill changes the age limit for obtaining a certificate from 16 to 18. It increases the cost but provides that the cost on renewal is halved from that of a first time application. It bans the import and possession of fully automatic firearms converted to fire in a semi-automatic mode. It creates the enabling power to ban large capacity magazines through regulations.
The bill creates a new offence, the altering of a firearm or assembling parts to produce a fully automatic weapon. There is also the promise of prohibitions or restrictions of certain military and paramilitary type weapons following criteria to be developed by the Canadian Advisory Council on Firearms.
The Canadian Advisory Council on Firearms will have a major role in shaping the regulations and so too will this House because any regulation will have to come back to the House.
The previous member spoke of safe storage as if there is some terrible problem for those on farms. There is no provision in this legislation that will restrict a farmer from keeping a gun beside the door. What this legislation provides is for regulations to be developed for safe storage. Those regulations will have to be approved by the Canadian Advisory Council on Firearms and will
Government Orders
have to come back before this House. Members of this House will have an opportunity to see that there is a public debate on the regulations. Clearly the historic position of farmers will be taken into account.
Genuine gun collectors are defined in the regulation. It provides for record keeping requirements on gun collectors. How could any citizen complain about that? Remember, a gun remains a lethal weapon which can kill. As long as it is a lethal weapon which can kill human beings then it is entirely appropriate that the state should intervene to control and restrain it.
We also must remember, to come back to the point, that the Criminal Code has to deal with behaviour and make certain behaviour illegal. That is what this bill seeks to do.
I believe that Canadians generally accept the idea that we must have gun control. That control can be through education. As the previous member stated, a parent can educate his or her children in the use of guns. Society can train and educate people before they are allowed to acquire and possess guns. That is what this package provides for.
If the precise regulations do not work as effectively as they should then we will have to deal with them.
I would like to conclude by making this point again. This gun control legislation, so necessary as a step towards a safe society, is not all that we in Parliament must do to deal with the epidemic of violence in our society. We have to recognize the extent of the violence in our society. We have to recognize that violence is fundamentally gender specific. It is a male propensity to violence which is predominantly the problem in our society. We have to understand the reasons for that. We have to get to the heart of what it is that produces domestic violence, social violence and even institutional violence.
We have to work on social programs that get to the root of the difficulties. We have to fundamentally understand that people must have a fair, just and equitable society and they must see society as a family. In my view rampant individualism is at the heart of the increasing propensity of our society for violence. Further, it is the Americanization of our culture. The American belief

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
that to own a gun is a right is becoming a potential belief in this country.
What I am so proud of in this bill is the overwhelming support of all sides of the House for this step to bring under some kind legitimate control the acquisition and ownership of guns. It is a step in the right direction.
We on all sides in Parliament will monitor its effect. We must be ready to intervene to improve and make more efficient the procedures so that citizens are not burdened with bureaucracy. We must also be ready to continue to close the gap so that all in our society can feel safe that guns are not out of control in the end.

Mr. Speaker, since we are now under the 10-minute rule I will try not to ad lib too much. I am fortunate to be following the previous speaker, the member for Athabasca. His speech portrays in capsule form the two solitudes that are really involved in this whole debate of guns and gun control and/or the social domain.
It is interesting that I am now speaking because I frankly come in between as a happy negotiator, a happy compromiser and a happy ex-Conservative.
I am not a gun owner. I am not a gun collector. I do not own a gun. I could not shoot a deer if you paid me money for it.
I have listened to the debate and it is a troubled debate. As the hon. member for Victoria said sincerely and as the member from Athabasca sounded out certain practical problems that he felt, that is part of the problem that we have here tonight.
The thing that bothers me more than other matters is the process. Today really is the first time that under this interesting parliamentary system we have there has been an opportunity for members to debate publicly their views on C-17.1 know I only have 10 minutes and it goes very quickly. I think four have gone already. What really bothers me the most is the fact that this Bill C-17-and I admit that there has been a lot of preamble and a lot of history, C-80 which never came to the floor of the House-just came to the floor of the House on June 6. What we have is a mini Meech Lake. There was a mini Meech Lake with House leaders on June 6. Before the Minister of Justice even started to make her speech, the Leader of the Opposition stood up to say there were consultations among House leaders and it was decided
that one member would speak from each party and then the bill would be sent to committee. That is the way it was. The bells rang and then under the rules the Whips came.
Mr. Speaker, I wish you would get away from the interference with the member from wherever he is because this is a serious matter. Bells rang and under the rules that we have all agreed to the Whips come up and say: "No". That was Thursday, June 6. There were not many members around. "We will postpone the vote on second reading, which is usually a vote of some importance, we will postpone it until Monday at three o'clock", I believe.
Lo and behold, and frankly it is happening too often in this House, in the midst of Private Members' Business on the same day, the House leader of the NDP stood up twice and the second time he was successful. He said, among other things-of course I do not know how many members were in the House then, perhaps three, four or six-he then said: "Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding any other rules and procedures of the House of Commons, let it be deemed that this bill is passed and referred to the Legislative Committee H", et cetera. Some members said agree and there it was.
I admit that sincere members who were concerned about this matter debated it in committee. That is fine. They produced a report that finally came into the House as the amendment, or Bill C-17. The vote this afternoon on second reading at the report stage was the first time that members had a chance to express themselves by vote. Tonight and today is the first time members, besides the committee, have had a chance to speak on this bill.
If members want to know why the public out there feel that this place is irrelevant I would suggest that they look at the process that has been used in a very fundamental important bill that affects directly or indirectly all Canadians that they look at what has happened here with C-17.
Time moves so quickly in terms of the substance of the bill. As I said earlier, I am troubled by this bill. I know the popular feeling is to vote for it. However I finally got into it when it came on to the floor of the House. I read the report of the special committee on C-80 and I have read the minutes of the committee on C-17. There were the best of intentions to try to tighten up certain matters that affect lives. A blanket of bureaucracy on law-abid-
November 6, 1991

ing citizens is not going to solve the problem, as everyone wants.
I think there are some people in the gallery tonight who have experienced the agonies and the tragedies. I have two daughters and hopefully I will never have to share what some people have shared as a result of that tragedy in Montreal.
There has not been a member anywhere in the House, including the Minister of Justice, who has even tried to suggest that with this bill the tragedy in Montreal could have been avoided, or even the tragedy in Iowa where a brilliant Chinese honours student, distraught because he did not get the acclaim of his masters, went out and horribly shot a Chinese colleague who received the doctoral award and then he shot the professor who did not give it to him. There is not a member who has said that any of this would be corrected.
There are two solitudes here. We had that graphically illustrated earlier by the hon. member for Victoria and the hon. member for Athabasca. My problem is that the people I talked to are law-abiding citizens who wonder why they are going to have to comply with more bureaucracy when the penalties for using guns really have not been that fundamentally affected.
Time is of the essence here. The debate has been pretty good tonight because there have been different points of view. There is really no political capital in terms of partisanship in this. I want to compliment my seat-mate, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, who has taken a leading part in committee and in the debate of this bill. Frankly he has informed me of things that I did not understand about this bill. He has had the temerity perhaps but I say the intestinal fortitude to do what the people send us here to do, that is to stand up and say, as he said in his opening remarks on this bill and I was privileged to be here next to him when he said it: "Hey, we are looking at this through the wrong end of the telescope".
It is not the law-abiding citizens who have guns and have the .22 over the door, like my friend from Athabasca said, but the criminal out there that we are trying to get. We are not getting them with this bill. This bill, as I
Government Orders
said to the local press when I voted against the bill at second reading and at report stage earlier today-and I imagine I am most likely to vote the same way tomorrow-is a charade. This bill does not address the problem of the killers. There is not a killer that I heard of in the tragedies that we know about that would be affected by this bill.
You have indicated, Mr. Speaker, that I only have one minute-and 10 minutes does go very fast-but I want to compliment those who have worked sincerely on the bill. I compliment the Minister of Justice for trying to do something. Quite frankly I think more can be done with this advisory council to try to sort out where we go on this and to try to get the criminal. We should not try to pretend with the pressure of tragedy that gun control in this bill is going to solve the problem.
In conclusion, there are so many things that can be said. Obviously guns do not kill people. People kill people. Yes, I think we have a fundamental interest in legislating but I take exception to the pressure. However I am glad that we are at least debating it. This bill is a microcosm of members speaking and representing their constituents. Obviously you have a different point of view depending on where you come from. Mr. Speaker, you are indicating that I am just about through and I am through. I do not believe this bill solves the problem that we are trying to solve, the dilemmas of those who have sustained agony and those who are going to continue to sustain agony. That is because this bill does not address the fundamental issue of the criminal.

Mr. Speaker, before I begin my remarks let me with the greatest of respect correct my hon. colleague from Annapolis Valley- Hants. Indeed this bill, though flawed, though imperfect, would make a difference in at least one of the tragedies in which he noted. It has been reported by two separate independent studies that had this bill been in place, particularly relating to the size of the clip, that Marc Lepine would probably have killed fewer people at Ecole Polytechnique. Just the time it would have taken him to reload would have allowed more people to escape.
I trust that my hon. friend from Annapolis Valley- Hants will accept this most respectful correction of his statement.

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
It is not a perfect bill. It is not the bill that were I in a different position that I would have brought forward. It is at least a step in the right direction.
I think that some of the amendments are good steps. They will show the people of Canada particularly the women of Canada, particularly the parents of Canada who worry about their children and who are sickened at the tragedy that we saw in Montreal nearly two years ago, that here in Parliament we are trying to do something. I wish we could do more. I want us to do more. I hope that we will do more very soon. I support this bill as a start.
One of the reasons I support this bill is because of the situation in my own city of Halifax. Yesterday on my way to the airport to return to Ottawa I heard that a recent study had declared Halifax to be the city with the third most murders in the country, after Vancouver and Thunder Bay. I can tell you that that is news that comes in spite of the changes in our lives in the city of Halifax. It is news that is still shocking to Haligonians.
In the first 20 years of my life in that city I believe that there had been only one murder. In the last 20 the murder rate has risen steadily every year. Not all of those murders are done by guns but most of them are.
The other thing that brings me to support this bill and to support gun control generally also relates to the increase in crime in the province of Nova Scotia and the spate of spousal murders that we have seen in our province over the last few years, of young women shot to death by the men that they, one supposes at the very least, trusted most. Another reason I support it is that it sends a message that we are coming to grips with the question of guns in our society.
I think we sometimes suffer a great deal because of our nearness to the United States and our reliance on many of their communication facilities. Far too many Canadians tend to see themselves in the context of American society rather than in the context of our own. One of those things is the whole question of the right to bear arms which in the United States is a constitutional right. I will make no comment on the sensibility of that being a constitutional right. I will merely say that I am very happy that it is not something that appears to be in question or in any danger of going into our Constitution.
I remember some years ago, when I was living in Vancouver, British Columbia, and I was involved in a program for Canadian customs officers. They were telling us that one of their biggest problems was dealing with American tourists taking the Alaska Highway, going through the province of British Columbia to the state of Alaska. Every second car the customs officer told me had firearms which would be taken by Canadian customs officers, dismantled, sealed into special packages and given to the people when they left the province of British Columbia at the Alaska border.
The customs officer told me that his greatest difficulty was the complaints from Americans who kept saying: "We have the right to bear arms". As he said: "Yes, you do. In your country, you do not have the right to bear arms in my country".
I think that this is one of the differences between us and our neighbours to the south that gives me a certain sense of reassurance. We have not yet seen, although we have seen too much in the way of death by gun, some of the horrible tragedies that the Americans have seen.
I am thinking of a situation in Florida several months ago where a little boy was playing with a gun. He shot and killed his sister because a gun was something that was around the house and something that he played with.
I am thinking of a paperboy in a small town in Michigan about five years ago who was walking up the walk on his regular Thursday night rounds to collect money. A homeowner who had forgotten that it was the night of the paperboy thought he was an intruder and shot him dead on the front walk.
In both of those cases, the shooters were negligent but not murderers. The victims were no less dead. In those cases, guns did kill people even though the people wielding the guns probably did not want to.
I understand the needs of bona fide hunters, the farmers and of the true gun collectors to exercise their rights and their needs with regard to guns, but I think that a number of the people who complain that this bill is too severe have to walk a little bit in the shoes of those of us who live in the urban centres where people are afraid with reason to go out after dark. Women are afraid to park their cars in underground parking lots. Danger
November 6, 1991

lurks in cities that used to be safe and an entire Canadian way of life is disappearing as a culture of violence takes over.
If we do not, at the very least, support the minimum strengthenings to the gun law that this bill offers, then I think we will have to be ashamed to hold our heads up in front of our constituents. I do not think that this bill, as it stands, will interfere significantly with the rights of legitimate gun owners holding those guns for legitimate purposes.
I also do not think that this bill goes far enough in other ways to protect those of us who desire the protection against those who hold guns in an illegal manner.
As I said in the beginning, it is a step, it is a start. I hope it is a start of something that will make the Canadian society a safer place for all of us. I hope that this legislation is just the beginning toward what will be a permanent memorial and a just law so that the young women who died at Ecole Polytechnique and the other people who have died in Canada through the senseless violence and the senseless use of firearms will not have died in vain.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in this House in support of Bill C-17, a support based mainly on personal experience. First of all, I am an American by birth. Second, I spent three years in the U.S. Army, from the age of 17 to 20, and I know how extremely dangerous firearms are. I have seen first hand the damage they can cause as well as how they can literally transform normally peaceful people into violent, super machos all of a sudden.
I agree the bill is not perfect. I agree it does not do enough to defer criminals, as the hon. member for Annapolis Valley said just now. However, gun control is necessary, not because there are so many criminals who can purchase firearms but because the people who are killed, who are threatened and attacked with firearms, are not necessarily part of the Mafia or the underworld. They are people like you and me, Mr. Speaker. I am having a lot of trouble-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As an American by birth who was in the army for three years, I know what can happen with firearms, and how, in an environment where there are no firearms, innocent people can be affected and hurt by the absence of gun control.
There are some major flaws in this bill. The only reason I will vote for the bill is that it is a step in the right direction. It is the kind of step even the United States were unable to make. The same day someone in Killeen massacred twenty people and wounded ten others in a Texas restaurant, the U.S. Congress was considering a bill aimed at controlling firearms, but because of a powerful lobby group, the National Rifle Association, representatives in the U.S. Congress did not have the nerve to pass a bill that would prevent something like that from happening again. Here in Canada we have a bill that is a step in the right direction and that will at least save a few lives until the legislation is reinforced.
I have some reservations about this bill because I think there are some flaws, and I will mention them quickly.
First, there is no munitions control. Even when I was in the U.S. Army, they always made sure ammunition was not stored in the same location as the firearms.
Second, we should have a registration system that registers firearms when they are purchased. This bill does not provide such a system and in my view that is quite an important shortcoming.
Third, assault firearms should be forbidden, but that will only be decided in the regulations. That worries me in a way because we do not know exactly what assault weapons will be banned. I would really like to have that list as soon as possible so that we could end the trade in those weapons once and for all.
Fourth, another flaw of this legislation is that it contains a fairly important exemption for semi-automatic weapons that have been converted into automatic weapons. About 50,000 of these firearms will be exempt. I find that unacceptable, because these semi-automatic weapons cannot be used for hunting, except to hunt human beings. So I find that is a fairly important deficiency.
But, despite all these flaws, as I said, I find it is a step, albeit a small one, in the right direction. And I agree with those people like the lady whom I met, Mrs. Edwards, the mother of one of the women killed in the famous massacre at the Ecole Polytechnique in Montreal, who said: "Phil, pass the bill now. We will try to

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
strengthen it later. If we do not pass it now, we may never get another chance".
I trust that young woman's mother. I find that Quebecers are quite peaceful people with lots of common sense and they know that we really need to control firearms.
Having a law today to start the process is more important than not having a law at all. In general, that is why I will vote for this bill, based on my experience as an American citizen by birth and my three years of military service.
I know that firearms have had a frightful effect, right in the city where I was born, in Washington, in the United States, so much so that Washingtonians want to hold the manufacturers of firearms responsible for the murders committed with those weapons. It is an act of desperation because so far, the city of Washington has never been able to control the trade in these firearms. They are banned in Washington but it is a very profitable business in Virginia and Maryland. Now in Washington they are trying all they can to stop the killing.
I also want to talk to you about something else. In Fort Lauderdale, where my mother lives, people are allowed to transport firearms in their car provided these weapons are exposed for people to see. I even saw a man get out of his car when the car behind him honked at a red light. He took his gun and asked the other driver whether he wanted to get a bullet in the head. At least he was polite: He asked.
Frankly I do not want to see Canadian society become like that. It is true that in the United States everybody is armed to the teeth, which is extremely dangerous, but it is worse than that, because in your heart and soul, there is that pervasive fear that violence is waiting around the corner, and if you do not watch out, you will be the next victim. We do not have that here in Canada, and I am very glad about that.
Just one last word. It is true the legislation does not affect criminals who have firearms. I agree. I do not think any legislation would be able to keep firearms out of the hands of criminals, but there is also the problem of
young people, teenagers, who all of a sudden want to commit suicide. With this bill at least, we will have regulations on storage, and these young people will not have such easy access to firearms in order to commit suicide. Suicide is quite a serious problem among young people today.
There is also the problem of marital squabbles, when the husband loses his temper, grabs a gun and kills his wife. It is too easy. At least with this legislation, we will have a way to enforce proper storage of firearms.
In concluding I will vote in favour of Bill C-17 because it is a step in the right direction, but I expect Mrs. Edwards and all other Quebecers to take immediate action to reinforce the bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words on this legislation this evening.
Bill C-17 presents tough choices for many members in this House. The issues surrounding this legislation are difficult and profound. Bill C-17 requires that we choose between the conflicting goals of public safety and individual freedom, between the interests and perspectives of rural and urban Canadians, and between our obligations to represent as members of Parliament the views of our constituents while attempting to forward the national interest.
The mail I have received on this legislation has been for the most part opposed to this bill. Many of the letters were passionately and honestly written and argued. They raised some very good points. Those points were sincerely believed by those who took the time to write to me with them.
They suggested that the focus of Bill C-17 is wrong. It seeks to control guns when it is the criminal use of guns that needs to be controlled. It seeks to compensate, without compensation, the personal property of gun owners who have purchased weapons which as a result of this legislation will become illegal. It makes criminals out of law abiding responsible hunters and sportsmen. It fails to address adequately the need for training in the handling and the storage of firearms.
November 6, 1991

My understanding of this legislation and of gun control in Canada has been greatly helped by my discussions with one of those people from my riding who has taken the time to write and to intervene in this legislation, Kevin McMaster of Port Hastings. Kevin McMaster is a recreational marksman and a gun collector. He has devoted a great deal of time and energy toward understanding gun control in Canada and in other countries and its relationship to criminal activity. He is responsible, intelligent and well informed on these issues. Kevin McMaster has expressed to me serious reservations with Bill C-17. He has written:
I am deeply involved in the shooting sports and have invested a lot of time and money into it. If this legislation goes through as is, two of the guns I paid a lot of money for and bought legally will become outlawed. The government has said they will pay no compensation and this outrages me. I fully agree with stiffer penalties for criminal misuse of firearms and feel this to be a strong deterrent to crime. I would hope the government follows through on this.
I don't want to sound like someone who thinks everyone should have a gun. I just want a system that will work so that I will not have to worry about losing a sport that means so much to me. Every time I hear about a shooting I cringe, knowing that it makes gun owners look worse and worse. You can't even mention that you feel you should be allowed to carry a gun for self-protection without somebody thinking you are some kind of freak who wants to shoot somebody.
I can understand Kevin's concerns. Yet, while Kevin would not agree with my support for this piece of legislation, I believe we share the over-all objective of more effective gun control legislation. I support this legislation, flawed as it is, because I believe it is a step toward that objective. More important, it does not preclude some of the important measures that Kevin and others like him would advocate.
Bill C-17 is really one step in a process. It is a process which will address some of the important issues of firearms control and, as such, represents a step forward in making Canada a safer society.
For example, there are the enhanced requirements for obtaining an FAC: the 20-day waiting period, the photograph requirement, the minimum age raised to 18, requiring two references and allowing firearm officers to question spouses, family members, friends and other associates about an applicant's suitability for gun ownership. These will help control who gets guns, just as the law controls the guns that people get.
Government Orders
Even though these changes will cause some inconvenience for gun owners, I believe that the changes are reasonable and responsible under the circumstances. As well, the requirement that the FAC applicants complete a training course is a fundamental one in my view. Training has long been recognized as a tool for reducing accidents with firearms.
People must know that guns are not toys. They must be trained in their use and in the responsibilities that accompany their ownership. Even though serious questions remain about the structure and administration of firearms training, the fact that this bill reaffirms its importance is reassuring.
I should say in response to one of the issues which Kevin and others have made advocating further training,
I think it is important to note that this bill moves as far as the federal government can go constitutionally in presenting a framework to facilitate the provision of training for the use of guns which under our system must be administered and implemented by the provinces.
I would hope that the provincial governments will take up their responsibilities to encourage responsible licensing and training of firearms owners so that this objective toward gun control can be furthered.
I support as well the principle of safe storage, even though as I said before there will be certain people who will be inconvenienced by it. Many gun owners rightly believe that the criminal element of guns is what we must address. Yet these same people believe that lawful gun owners are totally unrelated to the criminal element.
From whom do criminals steal guns? From lawful gun owners in many instances. In 1990 there were almost
56,000	lost, stolen or missing firearms in Canada. Theft of firearms is not the only storage problem we have to address. We must address as well the accidental misuse of firearms, the kind which most often occurs with lawful gun owners.
Time and time again we hear on the news about tragic deaths resulting from children who have access to guns. I am not impressed with the government's inability or unwillingness to provide at this time a definition of safe storage for Parliament and Canadians to consider. I believe that definition would have brought a great deal

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
of reassurances to those who have reservations about this legislation.
Now we can only hope that the Firearms Advisory Council will think beyond the urban limits when it sets out storage requirements and makes them affordable, realistic and enforceable for all Canadians.
Increasing penalties for criminal misuse of firearms are welcome as well, as are the enforcement of prohibition orders. Despite the legislated sentences, though, it is important to educate judges and crowns alike as to the importance of applying these penalties in a serious and consistent manner. As with all laws, unless the penalties are properly enforced and administered, they are essentially pointless.
Although I support this legislation, I recognize as I said earlier that it is flawed in many instances and really represents only a first step. I have introduced some amendments which I believe would have strengthened the bill and which I would hope this government, in monitoring the legislation and developing the regulations that will accompany it, would take into account. In particular I would hope that the government would explore the issue of compensation for those people who must turn in their personal property, those guns that will be prohibited, so that these guns can be safely taken out of circulation.
Finally I also hope that the government will encourage the provinces in any way possible within the ambit of this law to establish standardized and rigorous training and licensing requirements for those who would purchase and use firearms in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this bill is about a lot of things. It is about gun control, supposedly. It is about better gun control, hopefully. I wish I felt that it would accomplish these kinds of objectives. I wish that I did not feel that it was really just a political bill, a bill to satisfy a series of events, a bill reacting to the fear of growing violence in Canada, and that somehow we would find a solution to the growth of this violence by restricting, controlling and enforcing.
After 17 years in the House of Commons, somehow I feel that again I am going to be cajoled by the pressure of party peers and this party kind of thing that happens in
voting to steal just another little chunk of my freedom and a little chunk of the freedom of my son.
I have hunted as a young person. I no longer hunt. I no longer own a gun. I have no interest in shooting at a target or at animals. I think the reason I feel that way is because I am a Canadian and I feel something about space. I had a chance to learn and to experience this kind of freedom. As a young man, I was able to take my father's shotgun and go from pond to pond and from field to field across the prairies and experiment and shoot and feel and satisfy that hunter instinct in me.
As young guys we would get a bunch of cans and put them up on those long, endless stretches across for miles and miles as far as you could see, and each try and make a few shots at it. You learn something from that about being Canadian, about being fee, about having space.
It is that sense of freedom and space that we have in the second largest country of the world that makes us non-violent. It is that education, that understanding. But that is not going to be there for my son. I cannot take my son out into the same field with pistol and set those glass balls, or an old glass insulator we would happen to find by the bottom of a pole and shoot at those. We learned something about ourselves and about our freedom, but my son cannot do that because he cannot get a permit to take his pistol to the field. In fact, he cannot take it anywhere except to a gun club of some kind that is properly registered, and that is only after he gets a registered permit.
By the time you have the learning experience, it is gone. At least the experience that I had that taught me about hunting, about life and guns and made me nonviolent so that I would never hunt again. I probably never would want to shoot a gun. That is how it was satisfied and that is why Canadians are less violent. That is why there are less murders in Canada by guns than in the United States or in the densities of city cores.
I believe our approach is a little bit wrong. This is really about space and Canadians feeling space. Here I go again applying a wrong solution and that concerns me. It concerns me that my son who is now 24 or 25, and his friend Ted, like to take the registered pistol and go out in the field and shoot a little bit at some targets. They cannot do that in the second largest country in the world.
November 6, 1991

There is no place in Canada that they can experience this kind of freedom.
They are willing to lose this freedom if they think that by losing it they are going to save the lives of all kinds of people. Quite frankly, I do not think it is going to work. For 17 years we have piled restriction upon restriction upon restriction, we voted again and again, to get tighter and tighter regulations, and here we go again. Has it worked? No. I do not think it has worked. I think our society is becoming more violent day by day, not less violent. I do not think this bill is going to add anything to it, other than the debate itself, where we express our anti-violence feelings and our sense of freedom. I just do not see that restricting my son's and his friends' freedom is going to give anyone security.
There is not that much in this bill. It is a rather useless kind of a bill now. Surely if you are going to do it do it then. I do not really think this is going to take any or many guns out of the system and I do not think it is going to make those who are shooting the guns less violent.
It seems we always have to choose a law for the lowest common denominator because there is an exception here and here, because there is mental illness here, because there is that person who does not have that sense of freedom or has been raised in a density and they become tight. That tight explodes and it explodes into violence, violence and guns and death. That is the lowest common denominator and so we place our freedoms on the same basis as the lowest common denominator. It concerns me that I will do this again.
My children and your children have had the good fortune to understand and perhaps have these freedoms. They have been able to afford to go to the gun club if that is where they have to go to shoot. To all these young people at university, school, college or newly into the work force, who want to have these experiences, we have suddenly said: "No. There is something very sinful and evil about this and if you do this you'll be violent". Guns are not about violence. It is the nature inside of us that causes us to act in a violent manner.
It seems that this bill is about politics. It seems to me it is about the career of the Minister of Justice who is a good Minister of Justice, a great politician and an intelligent woman whose motives are all right, but it
Government Orders
should not be about that. It should not be because there is a demand in our society to control violence that we throw in another restriction. That is not going to work. More and more laws piled upon us, reducing our freedom, are part of the pressure that causes the violence.
We have made this a useless bill. All it does is maybe take away a little bit of freedom. I have not decided how I will vote tomorrow on it. I guess I will go along. I do not know. As I go along I know that of the thousands of things I voted on, this is just one more small thing that I think I will regret if I think of it in terms of what I am as a Canadian, what Canada is to me, what freedom is to me and will I really whittle it down one more time. I do not really want to do it.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin my brief 10-minute remarks by lamenting the fact that I only have 10 minutes to discuss this bill. It is of great importance not only to many people in my riding but to our country, regardless of which way the vote goes. We have a general idea of which way it is going to go.
One of the unfortunate things about the so-called reforms of the House of Commons is that we are restricted to making comments of 10 minutes after five hours of debate, particularly on a subject like this where we did not have any debate, or very little debate on second reading. Of course I am going to have to restrict my remarks severely.
I do want to let the people of Scarborough West know what was involved in the decision making process of their member of Parliament. I want them to be able to feel that they can come to me and ask me to explain at greater length what my thinking was. I want them to know that they had the opportunity to impact and input on the decision that I have come to.
When I first approached this topic when the legislation was in its previous form under Bill C-80, I was determined to take a completely neutral role and listen to both sides of the argument with as little passion and as much reason as possible. I answered that search by examining the legislation and then inviting the people of Scarborough West to come to a public forum which I hosted in my riding.

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
To that public forum I invited two people, one person who I knew was in favour of that bill and one person who I knew was opposed to that bill. I gave each of those people an opportunity to express their point of view as to the reasons why they held the particular view that they did.
Mr. Speaker, I want to tell you that that forum to this very day had the greatest attendance of any forum that I have had. That really surprised me because I am an urban member of Parliament. I represent an urban riding. It is 100 per cent urban. Scarborough West is in metropolitan Toronto. I resent it greatly when I hear people attempting to turn this issue into an urban versus rural issue because it is not that.
There are people in my riding who passionately hold views on one side or another, and yet they all reside in the riding of Scarborough West, in the middle of Scarborough in the most populous area of Canada. It is not an urban versus rural problem.
It is a problem that we Canadians have to deal with. When I say "we Canadians", I mean Canadians of both sexes because violence affects everyone. Violence is a danger to everyone, and we all as human beings and as Canadians must be concerned about violence and its effects on everyone.
One of the interesting things that came out of that forum that I had was the strength of opinion on both sides. There were policemen there. There were lawyers, teachers, clergy, grandmothers-yes, grandmothers- husbands, wives, constituents. Very few people had no opinion, except perhaps me, and the atmosphere was a charged atmosphere. I took that into account.
It is interesting because there were more people there than there were at my public forum on the GST, my public forum on free trade, on abortion and on whatever topic you want to name. There were more people in Scarborough West in an urban riding at my forum on gun control than past or since to the present time.
That surprised me, so I sat back and analysed what I thought was the general consensus of that meeting. I had asked everyone to identify themselves as to whether they were in or out of the riding. To be sure, there were people there who were from outside the riding who expressed views opposed to the legislation.
I recognize that, but what else did I do. Of course, I received people in my office and had them explain to me at their leisure, one on one, their concerns with the legislation or their reasons why they felt I should support the legislation.
I sent a questionnaire to over 37,000 households in my riding. I represent approximately 100,000 people. I attempted to find out what those people were thinking. I asked them what their concerns were. Over 100,000 people at least had the opportunity to input on what their member of Parliament was going to do.
There were approximately 14 letters that I received regarding gun control, 14. Out of that, they were approximately half divided. Some were for, and some against. Of course, subsequently, we have received cards and representations from both sides.
I had the advantage of having one extra ability, and that was my ability as a member of Parliament and indeed, my privilege as a member of Parliament for the Liberal Party of Canada to be able to listen to the views of my caucus colleagues, to be able to explain to them the problems that I had with this legislation and to listen to what they had to say.
Make no mistake, Mr. Speaker, in my view there are very serious problems with this legislation. I want to just identify them quickly for the record because to me they are of great concern.
One of these amendments would impose what is known in law as a reverse onus. It would impose on a person who has been denied the opportunity to obtain a firearms acquisition certificate to prove that he is entitled to it. The citizen has to prove that he is entitled to something as opposed to the state having to prove that he is not entitled to it. That is called a reverse onus that is contrary to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and has been so stated by the Supreme Court of Canada on more than one occasion. That is in this bill and it is overkill. It is an attack on the individual rights of the citizen. I have a problem with this and I flag it for the hon. Minister of Justice and subsequent Ministers of Justice because I hope that they deal with it before the Supreme Court of Canada deals with it as it has done with previous reverse onuses. It is about time this House started taking responsibility for its own decisions instead of leaving the decisions to the Supreme Court of Canada.
November 6, 1991

Another concept that I have a problem with is confiscation without compensation. The bill provides that certain weapons will be illegal, cannot be possessed after a certain period of time. They will have to be turned in or whatever will happen to them, but there will be no compensation. This is dangerous. We have stood as a society against such things, against expropriation without compensation. Those people purchased weapons that were legal at the time of purchase and they will be denied compensation when those weapons are taken away from them.
There is a limitation on testamentary powers. What does that mean? That means that we are denying people the ability to give away their property by will. Is that what we want to do? A father cannot give this type of weapon in a gun collection to his or her children. Is that what we as a society want to tuck inside a criminal law bill? Have we thought about it? I do not think so.
Under the definition of genuine gun collector we have an open door to an attack on the sanctity of the home because a person who wants to be a genuine gun collector and he only has to own one restricted weapon has to agree in advance that his premises can be entered and searched to ensure that he complies with the regulations. What regulations? We have absolutely no way of knowing because there are no regulations and that is another problem.
As a former chairman of the scrutiny of regulations committee, I know the difficulty of scrutinizing regulations and of determining whether they are legal or not.
There are many other faults with this bill which I do not have time to express, however, having listened to my colleagues, I realized that these errors as I view them can be cured by this Parliament. We can change the law. We have that power. But there is one power that this Parliament does not have. This Parliament, no matter how hard it tries, whether there is the agreement of the Whips, whether it is the unanimous opinion of the House, we cannot give life to the lifeless. This bill may prevent the death of an innocent individual. I am prepared to give the bill the benefit of the doubt to save even one life because we can correct the errors.

Mr. Speaker, I want to start off by saying that I agree with my colleague from Scarborough West. I too have had a very difficult time in analysing this legislation and I must say
Government Orders
to my colleague, our critic for justice, that he has been very supportive in helping us through this legislation because it is complex and he has understood well that there are in fact two solitudes on this legislation. It is certainly not a rural-urban debate that is going on here. Like my colleague from Scarborough West, I have had representation here from caring, intelligent constituents who have presented briefs to me. The International Practical Shooting Confederation of Canada has been given the opportunity to make representation at the justice committee on Bill C-17. I must tell you, after reading their briefs it made it even more difficult because they pointed out in very vivid detail the flaws in this legislation. The central issue for all of us in public life today is the issue of trust. People are trusting us to make a decision on a piece of legislation like this, not just based on the headline of the bill. It is called the gun control bill, so how could you, as an urban member especially, possibly be voting against that says you are opposed to gun control? I mean, people in an urban centre, you just could not imagine doing that. Yet, when you get behind this legislation, you see that there are many, many faults in this bill. There is a lot of illusion in this bill. This is the one thing that frightens me deeply.
I am concerned that many of our constituents-and I go back to my colleague from Scarborough West- might think that this bill is really going to solve a lot of the problems that we have in terms of crime related to guns in this city, or wherever in our nation. The problem is that it is not.
I have talked to many of the people in my riding of Broadview-Greenwood, many of the policemen who walk the beat and who are exposed to firearms, day in and day out. I asked them to tell me honestly what they think of this legislation. They tell me, to a man, that they are not confident in this legislation. I spoke to Chief McCormick the other day and I said: "Chief, I have a very difficult time. I see you are on the list here of all the police chiefs in Canada supporting this legislation". He said: "Listen, Dennis, this bill is not perfect legislation, but it has things like the firearms acquisition certificate with a 28-day processing, the fact that we now put a picture on the firearms acquisition certificate. That is a plus. The training program is going to be much more extensive and in place. That is a plus to the legislation and the safeguards on storage". He did mention that he would like a national amnesty over a 90-day period. He

November 6, 1991
Government Orders
thought that that would go a long way. He said that for those reasons alone I should get behind this bill.
What distresses me about this whole process is the fact that this is such an important issue in our country, and yet we have only had, on the floor of the House of Commons, about six hours debate. I, quite frankly, find that not good for the people of this country. I particularly resent what happened to my fellow colleague from Willowdale last night. As he was standing on the floor of the House, and he was trying to put, not unlike my colleague from Scarborough West and not unlike myself, forward both views that exist in this important debate, the fact that there are law-abiding citizens who happen to have gun collections, who happen to be members of shooting clubs. He talked about their point of view in the debate. Debate is not just putting forward one point of view, it is listening to people in your community, or other people not just in your community but from across the country, as I listened today to the member for Timiskam-ing who I thought made a lot of sense. That is the purpose of this. He was doing that. I see a press release here that my colleague was accused of being a champion for the concerns of the gun lobby. There is nothing further from the truth. This is the kind of ruthless, uncaring emotion which can hurt a member for no just cause. The member was putting forward both sides of the debate, not unlike what we have been doing here tonight. I heard earlier the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants who was trying to do the same thing. It is only when we can get into listening to both sides of the debate, listening to all points of view, that we can ultimately craft a piece of legislation that is really going to serve the objective we are trying to attain.
I will be supporting this legislation, but I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I do not like it. I do not like this legislation. It is an illusory piece of legislation. I am frightened to death that we are misleading the Canadian public, that we are leaving the feeling that once this bill is passed crimes related to guns in this country are somehow magically going to disappear.
I think we are going to have to be vigilant in the implementation aspects of this legislation. As my colleague from Scarborough West said a few minutes ago the regulations have not been defined. We are handing this over to public servants who are basically going to be operating this without political input after we have passed the bill. That is not what I was elected to do when I came here. We were elected to craft legislation and after it was properly crafted, properly debated at length, put it over to the bureaucrats with all the definition attached.
What we are doing here is exercising blind faith in the bureaucracy of Canada, the Department of Justice, and I do it with trepidation. Like my colleague from Scarborough West, if it is to save just one life then we have done the right thing. I also do this because of my immense respect and trust for my colleague who is our justice critic.

Mr. Speaker, I come from a rural riding in Ontario. I believe that sometimes there is a real lack of understanding in this House on the ways of life in rural Canada. Sometimes in this House we have poorly thought-out bills that may seem reasonable to urbanites and people in urban Canada but really make no sense at all to rural Canadians, especially northern Canadians.
Hunting predators of livestock is really a way of life in rural Canada, as is hunting for food and livelihood in the native and northern communities. I believe law abiding Canadian hunters and many tourists who visit Canada will also be penalized under this bill.
Many urban Canadians do not understand the way of life in rural Canada. Unless one has lived on a farm or in an isolated part of the north it is really difficult to relate to the needs of these Canadians. That does not mean that they do not have rights or that they do not have any right to be heard on this issue.
A whole sector of society is being ignored by the minister and the government in that they have proposed such a vague and ambiguous bill. I speak of it as being ambiguous in the sense that a lot of what is in this bill will be brought down through regulation. I heard the House leader of the government suggest earlier that Parliament will have the right to look at the regulations in this case. Clearly they will not. Parliament has made changes in the bill which give a lot of people who are

concerned with the regulation some sense of hope that their voice will be heard. What he failed to relate to the public is that in fact we will not be able to change these regulations. Mr. Speaker, as many have said Bill C-17 is a very difficult decision for all members of Parliament. Many people feel that the bill goes too far and many people feel that the bill does not go far enough.
For example, we all remember the massacre at l'Ecole Polytechnique in Montreal. We all hear demands to defend against violence and to control guns such as were issued just this week by Justice David Dickson of the Supreme Court of New Brunswick as he conducted the trial of Allen Leger, who was convicted of multiple murders in the Miramichi area in New Brunswick last year. It is natural that Parliament should wish to express its serious concerns in very tangible and legislative ways. Bill C-17 is such an expression. Yet there is another serious side to this issue, and that is the restraint of rights of law abiding citizens, of men and women who
shoot for sport, who collect guns as artistic treasures, who hunt wildlife and game birds as a means of enjoying the great natural resources of Canada. There are also some very well organized youth training and education programs in Canada which are at risk of compromise and frustration within the umbrella of this bill.
In Fredericton we have a very active shooting fraternity. The head coach of the Shooting Federation of Canada lives in my riding, Bob Kiersttead. He has been very successful in guiding the shooting team of Canada to medal performance in international competition such as in Cuba earlier this year. In fact the president of the Shooting Federation of Canada, Mr. David Hitchcock, also resides in Fredericton-York-Sunbuiy. He has has been very helpful and instrumental in informing me about the points of view of those who are enthusiasts and collectors of firearms.
In communication with the Shooting Federation of Canada as this bill has come to the House, some concerns have been expressed which I would like to put on the record. The Shooting Federation of Canada feels that this bill, with all its good intent and purposes, in its present form prior to regulations actually inhibits the youth training and education programs which it conducts in the sense that it limits firearms acquisition certificates to those who are 18 years of age or older. I am advised that this still does not prevent those who are under 18 from using borrowed guns under the permit regime.
The shooting federation points out that the definition of firearms inhibits many of the air gun types of target pistols and rifles that youth use in competition. I was advised by the minister's office today that subsequent regulations emanating from this bill will address the youth education and training programs of the Shooting Federation of Canada and specify in regulation form the provisions that will make those programs effective once again.
It is going to be a commitment on my part to follow in this House the emergence and the advancement of those regulations so that in fact the works of the Shooting Federation of Canada are not compromised or inhibited in the ways it now fears.
The shooting fraternity in Canada is by and large a very responsible and effective constituency. Those in the Fredericton area, as I say, have conducted very responsi-

ble and comprehensive communication in consultation with me throughout the process of considering this bill. I believe that much has been accomplished as a result of those consultations not only by myself, the representations that I have made to my caucus colleagues and the consultations with those shooting enthusiasts from my riding, but the same process has existed right across Canada.
Some of the really significant evidence of the political process at work has been the fact that Bill C-80, which was badly flawed and unacceptable, was withdrawn. Bill C-17 has received many amendments both in committee and here in the House.
The definition of genuine gun collectors has been cast in the legislation, which is an advancement. There has been an identification of sport shooting with respect to restricted weapons. There has been an improvement generally in the normal firearms acquisition process. But perhaps most profound of all the accomplishments that I believe has been achieved is that the process of regulations has been cast in such a way that every regulation, as opposed to emanating from a bureaucratic source without challenge, under this bill must come to this House, must be available for 30 sitting days, not during vacations, not during election campaigns, to be examined by the appropriate committees of this House and of the Senate so that they might report to members of this House upon the ramifications of those regulations, so that this House might in fact debate and approve or reject those regulations.
It is my understanding that is only the second time in the legislative history of this House that such a process for pre-examination of regulations has been used in terms of a bill such as this one.
There is no doubt in my view that legitimate gun owners are unfairly penalized by this legislation which does attempt to offer a balance of comfort and confidence to those who fear for the safety of a violent society.
I understand, sympathize and support the concerns of all such responsible and careful citizens who do safely practice the use and ownership of firearms. However, the political process, the way of life in a free and

democratic society is balanced and I believe we have achieved a form of balance in this case.
Perhaps more than most other bills, this legislation reflects the true nature of our political process in Canada. There is really no call to vote the party line on this bill. It is largely a matter of individual judgment and conscience.
Through the consultation process with our citizens, both those who use guns and those who abhor them, we have considered all sides of this issue. Through the caucus process we have wrung every amendment possible to achieve a balance and to reach a consensus.
On the basis of that balance-in respect for the concessions and compromises which have been achieved, in respect to the consensus which I have shared with my colleagues, both in caucus and in this House, and in respect for the deep concerns which are held by my constituents on both extremes of this issue-I have come to the conclusion that I will support this bill on third reading tomorrow to achieve two purposes.
Some say two solitudes, but it is two purposes that are closely integrated by this bill. The first is to contribute my own message for a less violent society in Canada and second, to contribute an equally strong message for recognition of the integrity of the legitimate gun collecting and shooting fraternity in Canada who are paying their share of a high price of freedom to achieve the purposes of this bill with respect to a more stable society.
Let us earnestly hope that their sacrifice of further limited rights will not be wasted and that Canada will in fact become a safer and more secure model of contemporary life.
If the balance of those two purposes can be achieved and served by this bill, then it will truly be an optimum demonstration of responsible consensus among the members of this Parliament.

We were asked not to participate at second reading and there were very few speeches given. Now that it has proceeded through committee, through report stage and on to third reading, those of us who have had an interest in it but have not been able to participate immediately in the process of bringing this legislation through to this
