stage are being given this brief opportunity, although it is only 10 minutes, to state our view on it.
It is something that I have been anxious to do for the record. I have made no secret since I came here in 1988 of my belief that there should be stronger and more complete regulation of firearms in Canada. I say that without equivocation and I say that in support of this bill. I say it also while acknowledging the fact that many of my constituents have come to see me and have spoken to me of their concerns about this bill.
Many of my constituents, be they urban or not, are owners of firearms. They use them regularly either in hunting or in sports and they feel strongly that this bill does not serve their interests fairly. To them I say: I have heard your concerns. I have much sympathy for some of the technical problems that have been raised with respect to this bill, but I want to address it in more general terms on the basic philosophy behind this legislation.
I think we have heard quite eloquent speeches tonight on both sides of this issue. Where they tend to focus in criticism of the approach to control firearms, and have made notes as I listened to various speakers, they have said this bill does not get to the issue of the killers. They have said it only penalizes those who are law-abiding. They have said in essence that by trying to control firearms you are not controlling criminals because criminals do not seek firearms acquisition certificates or whatever.
I have a fundamental disagreement with that notion. My friend from Annapolis Valley-Hants said that we are looking at this from the wrong end of the telescope. I suggest that the opposite is true, that he is looking at it from the wrong end of the telescope.
The notion that we should be inhibited from regulating activities which are otherwise lawful and carried on by law-abiding people in a democratic society is simply wrong. It is a fallacious principle. We have in our Constitution a very eloquently drafted Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It speaks of fundamental freedoms, freedom of conscience and religion, freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression, freedom of peaceful assembly, freedom of association, democratic rights, legal rights, equality rights and so on.
I believe I came to this House partly because of my great conviction of the importance of fundamental and
more general freedoms. But freedoms do not exist in a vacuum. Freedoms exist because of the rule of law. Our freedom to act is inhibited by the rights of others and without that inhibition, their freedoms indeed are restrained and lost.
To look at the fact, yes, firearms may be lawful. Their possession may be in order. To begin to impose regulation on those things is to take away freedoms. To me that is completely nonsensical in a modem society. What can we do in this society without addressing law or regulation in some form or other? We cannot be employed without having registered to obtain a social insurance number. We cannot drive a car without being licensed, having taken training, having passed tests. Whatever you do in our society you confront rules, regulations of some form of other.
Surely in modem society to impose regulations on the acquisition and possession of firearms is a minimal and reasonable limitation on something that is fundamentally dangerous and also frightening to many Canadians.
Look at the statistics. I think they speak for themselves. The member who spoke earlier said they do not work. I do not understand how anyone can say gun control does not work. Look at the comparisons between Canada and the United States in these numbers. For example, I am told there was a study done comparing Seattle, Washington, with Vancouver. Despite similar over-all crime rates, Seattle had a much higher murder rate than Vancouver. The Seattle rate of murder with hand guns is almost five times higher than in Vancouver. The rate of assault using a firearm is seven times higher.
Is that because people living in Vancouver are somehow nicer than people who live in Seattle? Is it because for some reason Canadians have all of the space that my friend opposite was talking about earlier, they are more peaceful? No. It is because we have built a society in which the acquisition and use of firearms and their control has been accepted as natural and normal. The result of that has reaped for us in much lower rates of crime. Those are the indisputable facts I believe.
When we approach issues like this, let us not get the thing upside down. Let us recognize the fact that a proliferation of firearms that would result with lessened regulation would also result ultimately in more crime, in more murders and more homicides, in more assaults

with firearms. That to me is indisputable. As for those who pursue shooting as a sport, I have no problem. I earnestly hope that if there are technical problems in this bill that do interfere in some way that is unfair, those problems will be addressed in future legislation at an early time.
I speak, I admit, as one who does not possess, has never possessed, a firearm, but I think I speak on behalf of many Canadians who look in our daily newspapers and see classified ads for the sale of firearms, who pick up the Canadian Tire catalogue and see with some fright photographs of firearms readily available, who can walk into stores and see them on shelves.
To me, it is a very simple thing. This is something that requires regulation and control by government to protect freedom. I am not one who sees this as a further limitation on freedom but rather as a method of ensuring the most basic of freedoms, the freedoms to walk our streets and to live in peace, and to believe that we will not be assaulted. That is the fundamental freedom. That is the most important thing.
If there are concerns that those freedoms are not fully enjoyed then surely they must be addressed. That limitation is one to which we should willingly subscribe as we do to so many others.
Without having the time to go through technical details and argue for points of change or other things that I would like to see added to the legislation, I simply want to add my voice to those who say that this is a reasonable limitation of our freedom in a democratic society, to use the words of the charter of rights, and one which I think is welcome by the vast majority of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I take the floor tonight to speak on a difficult subject, particularly at a time of seemingly increasing intolerance and violence. Everyday we hear about tragedies like suicides, serial murders or even murders related to petty larceny. It is sad that such tragedies are now a common occurrence.

The most tragic of those incidents we hear of is about a child who has injured a playmate, using a gun that just happened to be in the house.
Bill C-17 is a beginning, a first step. The stricter control of firearms in our country can only help in diminishing the likelihood of a gun being used in anger or frustration or despair. If you do not have one, if you cannot get one, you cannot use it.
The first letter I ever got on gun control came from Africa. It came from a constituent living in Nigeria, I think it was, who wrote me saying: "I just got a magazine from the gun society to which I belong. It is encouraging me to write you to oppose gun control legislation". He said, "I am writing you for exactly the opposite reason.

No responsible gun collector, no responsible hunter opposes good gun control legislation".
Since then I have received many more letters on both sides of the issue. I have read carefully all letters to me from both those interested in increased gun control and those against control.
The most persistent thing I have heard from those who do not want to see this bill pass and do not want an increase in gun control is that it does not control criminals. Hopefully, it will keep more guns out of the hands of criminals. The RCMP estimates that there are
53,000	lost or stolen guns unaccounted for in Canada. The safe storage requirements in this bill may go some way toward ensuring that number is not increased dramatically in the future.
These letters say this bill does not punish the criminal. That is true. I do not think we want a lot of criminals to punish. I think what we want to do is prevent crimes of violence. We want to prevent deaths. Our whole policing system in this country is turning toward preventative approaches to policing. The 28-day cooling off period helps ensure that guns are getting into fewer and fewer hands where they will be misused.
They say it does not reduce violent crime. However since gun control legislation was brought in, in 1978, the percentage of homicides due to firearms has dropped from 39 per cent to 29 per cent.
I have heard tonight that more people die in automobile accidents. That is true too. However there are 16 million automobiles in Canada and only 6 million gun owners. The rate of death by guns is 50 per cent higher. That totally ignores the fact that cars are used every day for many hours a day and driven many miles a day.
The 40,000-plus police officers across this country, the ones who face the threat of those guns on the street, are the ones who have asked us to pass this legislation. In fact they have asked us to pass tougher legislation than what is before us. Can we who sit here comfortably say to them who suffer the consequences of our inaction that we will not act? I cannot.
I have heard a lot of talk about freedom. I was particularly concerned when I heard the member from Fraser Valley West, who is a member I admire and

respect for many reasons, say with almost tears in his eyes that his son would never enjoy the pleasures of shooting a gun across the prairies. Does the freedom to enjoy the vast spaces of our prairies mean we have to be able to shoot a bullet across it? To me the important freedoms are the freedom to live, the freedom to walk the streets, the freedom for my daughter to walk into her structural engineering class and know she is a little safer than those girls in Montreal were two years ago.
Some people have asked me: "Is this a different issue for women?" Yes, it is. It is a different issue because we know from the time we are very little that even when we grow up we are going to be smaller, physically weaker and more vulnerable because of it. It is something we live with every day of our lives. Our activities are constrained by it. There is a tinge of fear in our lives far more often than in those who are not women.
Anything that extends that sense of vulnerability and fear we feel is something that further limits the way we live our lives.
I do not think that the limits imposed in this law are unreasonable for the privilege of possessing something that is capable of killing and maiming. Is it unreasonable to say that you should be 18 years of age before you own a gun? I do not think so. Is it unreasonable to say there should be a more secure screening process for gun applicants? I do not think so. Is it an unreasonable limit on freedom to say you have to wait 28 days between the time you apply to acquire a gun and the day you can actually get the permit to buy that gun? I do not think so. Is it unreasonable to require that somebody has to have two people to vouch for them before they can walk out of the store with something in their hands that can kill the very next person they see? I do not think that is unreasonable.
Is it unreasonable that your photograph appear on your firearms acquisition certificate so that it is clear that you are the person who has that certificate and that you have a right to have the gun you have. I do not think there is anything at all unreasonable about that. I do not think that is an extreme infringement on anybody's freedom. My photograph is on my driver's licence. Why

We live beside the most violent society in the world, largely because of the constitutionally entrenched right to bear arms. We do not want to be like that society in the level of violence. I think one way of putting our children first is to say that we want a society where violence is not the way we solve problems. I think putting reasonable limits as this bill does on the use of guns is one small step toward that better world for children.

I am not going to require a whole lot of time, but I do have a few words that I would like to share with you and the House.
We have heard very much tonight and several people in the debate said things to the effect that we did not have enough time to debate. I would suggest to them that they have not taken advantage of the tremendous opportunity we have had in the past to discuss and debate this issue. It seems like a long time ago when I
had my first opportunity to speak and that was on second reading on Bill C-80. Following that I was given the opportunity to sit on a special committee that came out of Bill C-80. I felt that committee had several recommendations that would have probably improved Bill C-17 more than it is had the minister and her officials chosen to take all of those recommendations.
The committee put a tremendous amount of study and work into it. A number of groups came in front of us. We received many briefs, presentations and letters, and I think we researched the issue very, very thoroughly.
Based on our report, the minister did make some changes and modifications and brought in Bill C-17. Although I did not volunteer, I was asked again to sit on the legislative committee on Bill C-17 and I did so very willingly.
For those who felt the debate was limited, I would offer to share my files, the briefs, the letters I received that cover an entire shelf in my office. We had them piled on my desk and they covered my entire desk to a depth of about 18 inches. My staff has offered the observation that reading through all of them is the equivalent of reading an encyclopaedia. We received a tremendous volume of input and suggestions.
I agree with many of the people tonight who have said that this bill is not perfect. My own personal preference was that we should be licensing users rather than looking at their weapons and firearms. We are not there. Perhaps some day we can get there, but we are not there yet.
We do have a bill that will improve firearms control and safety. The training requirements before issued with a firearms acquisition certificate, are something that have been supported by absolutely everyone. People on both sides of the issue, hunters and shooting club members have a vested interest in making sure that those who hunt with them and stand beside them on the range are qualified, competent and handle their weapons safely.
There have been a few misconceptions tonight that I would like to touch on briefly. It is my personal feeling that this bill will not impact on 99.9 per cent of those who hunt or shoot competitively.
The storage restrictions that were talked about earlier refer to collectors and those with restricted weapons. I do not think the farmer who is worried about predator control needs to be worried about storage requirements,

at least not legislated ones. I would hope that person knows enough to store his weapons safely anyway.

Elected representatives are going to have the opportunity to look at them, vet them, discuss them in committee and comment on them before they are gazetted. No Canadian need worry about regulations being snuck in. It is something that is going to become very public and open to debate.
It is very late in the day. You have been very patient. Members who are still with us tonight have been very patient. I will conclude by saying something that I have said in our committee several times. That is, I honestly believe that people in the Hunting and Shooting Federation and the Canadians who are concerned about gun control both have something in common. They and every

sensible Canadian want effective firearms legislation. The only debate we have had is to determine what defines effective and what is going to work.
I am going to be supporting this bill. I pray it will help provide more effective control of the criminal use and abuse of firearms in this country.
